definition: A classic text classification dataset of Usenet postings across twenty topics.
related_terms: AG News; CIFAR-100; ImageNet-21k; Iris Dataset
student_friendly_explanation: The 20 Newsgroups dataset is a collection of messages from different online forums, organized into 20 distinct categories or 'topics'. It's commonly used by researchers and students to train machine learning models to classify text data.
example: For instance, you might have messages discussing politics, sports, technology, and entertainment. A model trained on this dataset could be taught to recognize and categorize new posts based on their content.

definition: A real-time rendering technique representing 3D scenes as Gaussian primitives with color, opacity, and covariance. Unlike NeRF's implicit representation, uses explicit primitives rasterizable at 100+ FPS with comparable quality.
related_terms: NeRF (Neural Radiance Field); 3D Vision; Difference of Gaussians (DoG); Gaussian Blur
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're looking at a 3D scene, like a room filled with objects. Instead of trying to describe every single tiny detail, 3D Gaussian Splatting takes big chunks of this scene and represents them using something called 'Gaussian primitives.' These primitives have colors, how much they show through (opacity), and how spread out they are (covariance). It's like painting big blobs on a canvas instead of drawing every little thing. This method is really fast and can handle lots of details without slowing down the computer too much.
example: In a virtual reality game, 3D Gaussian Splatting could be used to quickly render a complex scene with many objects, such as a bustling city street with cars, trees, and people. The system would take large portions of the scene, each represented by a Gaussian primitive, and quickly draw them on the screen, making the scene appear smooth and detailed even when moving around.

definition: Combining data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism to train models too large for any single axis.
related_terms: Model Parallelism; Tensor Parallelism (TP); Pipeline Parallelism (PP); Sequence Parallelism (SP)
student_friendly_explanation: 3D Parallelism is a technique used to distribute the workload of very large machine learning models across multiple computers. It combines three types of parallelism: data parallelism, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism. This allows the model to be trained more efficiently than if it were handled by just one type of parallelism alone.
example: Training a deep neural network with hundreds of millions of parameters using a distributed system where the model's parameters are split among different nodes, each processing a portion of the data in parallel.

definition: Computer vision techniques perceiving and reconstructing 3D information from 2D images or sensors. Includes depth estimation, 3D reconstruction, and novel view synthesis. NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruct photorealistic 3D scenes from sparse photos.
related_terms: NeRF (Neural Radiance Field); Depth Estimation; Point Cloud; Novel View Synthesis
student_friendly_explanation: 3D Vision is about using computer vision to see and create 3D models from 2D pictures. It helps us understand how objects look in real life, even when we can't see them all at once. This technology is used in many ways, like making virtual tours of buildings or creating realistic animations.
example: A 3D model of a building created from multiple 2D aerial photographs using 3D Vision techniques.

definition: An object's full three-dimensional position and orientation.
related_terms: Pose Estimation for Objects; Pose Graph; Category-Level Pose Estimation; Task Space
student_friendly_explanation: A 6D pose describes where an object is located in space, including both its position (where it is) and orientation (how it is facing). This information is crucial for robotics and autonomous systems to understand the environment and interact with objects accurately.
example: When a robot arm picks up a cup from a table, its 6D pose includes the position of the cup (where on the table) and the orientation (which way the cup is facing).

definition: An optimizer holding momentum and variance buffers in eight-bit blocks with dynamic scaling.
related_terms: Optimizer State; Muon Optimizer; Quantized Optimizer; Lion Optimizer
student_friendly_explanation: An 8-Bit Optimizer is a type of optimization algorithm that uses special memory buffers to store information about how quickly it learns (momentum) and how much it varies (variance). These buffers are very small, only using 8 bits of memory, which makes them fast and efficient. The algorithm also adjusts the size of these buffers dynamically based on the learning process.
example: A neural network training system that uses an 8-Bit Optimizer to speed up the training process by storing and updating learning rates and variance estimates in tiny, 8-bit memory units.

definition: A randomized comparison of two model versions on live traffic.
related_terms: Traffic Splitting; End-to-End Test; Integration Test; Online Metric
student_friendly_explanation: An A/B test for models is when we compare two different versions of a machine learning model by testing them on real data, like how a website handles traffic. It helps us see which version works better and makes decisions based on the results.
example: A company uses an A/B test to compare two different versions of their recommendation system. One version recommends products based on past purchases, while the other uses user behavior data. They then analyze the performance of each version on a portion of their users' traffic to decide which one performs better.

definition: The share of searches where a user leaves without clicking any result.
related_terms: Zero Result Rate; Query Result Cache; Blended Results; Result Deduplication
student_friendly_explanation: The abandonment rate is a metric that measures how often users leave a search engine or database without interacting with any of the results. It's important because it helps us understand if our search system is engaging enough for users to find what they're looking for.
example: A university research portal has an abandonment rate of 30%. This means that out of every 100 users who search for information, 30 users do not click on any of the search results, indicating that the search interface may need improvement to keep users engaged.

definition: Linking an acronym to the full form it stands for within a document.
related_terms: Text Normalization for Speech; Sentence Segmentation; Pronoun Resolution; Coreference Resolution
student_friendly_explanation: Abbreviation resolution is the process of converting abbreviations into their full forms within a text, making the document easier to read and understand.
example: In a research paper discussing the use of machine learning techniques, the abbreviation 'ML' is resolved to 'Machine Learning' to ensure clarity for the reader.

definition: Inferring the most plausible explanation for observed evidence.
related_terms: Qualitative Reasoning; Explanation Facility; Monotonic Reasoning; Non-Monotonic Reasoning
student_friendly_explanation: Abductive reasoning is about figuring out the best guess or hypothesis when you see certain things happening. It's like trying to solve a mystery by making the most logical conclusion based on the clues you have.
example: A computer system detects unusual network traffic patterns. Using abductive reasoning, the system infers that this might be an attack rather than normal user behavior, even though it hasn't been confirmed yet.

definition: Systematically removing components to measure each one's contribution.
related_terms: Ablation Transparency; Ablation Study for Components; Mean Ablation; Zero Ablation
student_friendly_explanation: An ablation study is a method where we deliberately remove parts of a system or model to see how it affects the overall performance. This helps us understand which parts are most important and which can be adjusted or removed without significantly impacting the outcome.
example: In a neural network, an ablation study might involve temporarily removing certain layers to observe if the network still performs well on tasks like image classification. This helps researchers decide which layers are essential for good performance.

definition: Removing model parts to determine each one's contribution to behaviour.
related_terms: Mean Ablation; Zero Ablation; Resample Ablation; Path Patching
student_friendly_explanation: Ablation study is like taking out the pieces of a puzzle one by one to see how each piece fits into the big picture. In deep learning, we remove different parts of a model to figure out which part contributes most to its performance.
example: In a neural network designed to recognize images, an ablation study might involve removing certain layers or neurons to see if the network still performs well on image recognition tasks. This helps researchers understand which parts of the network are crucial for its accuracy.

definition: Clearly reporting which components contributed to a claimed improvement.
related_terms: Ablation Study; Ablation Study for Components; Transparency about Limitations; Mean Ablation
student_friendly_explanation: Ablation transparency is about showing which parts of a system or model made the biggest difference when they were removed. It's like taking out different pieces of a puzzle and seeing how much the picture changes. This helps other people understand why certain features work better than others.
example: In a machine learning model, researchers might remove different layers one by one to see which ones are most important for accuracy. They then report which layers had the biggest impact, making their findings more transparent and easier to understand.

definition: A Markov chain state that, once entered, can never be left.
related_terms: Markov Chain; Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC); Stationary Distribution; Markov Inequality
student_friendly_explanation: An absorbing state is like a final destination in a game of chance. Once you reach this state, you can't go back to any other states. It's a special kind of state in a Markov chain where you stay put forever.
example: In a weather model, if it's raining (an absorbing state), you can't leave the rain state. You'll always stay in the rain state.

definition: How often a system declines to answer rather than guessing.
related_terms: Acceptance Rate of Suggestions; Hallucination Rate; Answer Extraction; Task Success Rate for Users
student_friendly_explanation: The abstention rate measures how frequently a system chooses not to provide an answer or response, especially when it's uncertain or lacks enough information to make a guess. It's a way to evaluate the system's reliability and confidence level.
example: A language model uses machine learning to generate text responses. If the model is trained on a limited dataset, it might sometimes abstain from answering questions that require knowledge beyond its training data, thus showing a high abstention rate.

definition: Statically analyzing programs by executing them over approximate abstract values.
related_terms: Program Synthesis; Abstract Syntax Tree (AST); Rule Engine; Syntax-Guided Synthesis (SyGuS)
student_friendly_explanation: Abstract interpretation is like running a program through a simplified version of itself, using approximate values instead of exact ones. It helps us understand what the program does without actually executing it line by line.
example: Imagine you have a complex algorithm that processes data. Instead of stepping through each line of code to see how it works, abstract interpretation allows you to analyze the overall behavior of the algorithm using simpler, more manageable values.

definition: Answering in generated prose rather than by extracting a span.
related_terms: Extractive Question Answering; Question Answering (QA); Multi-Hop Question Answering; Closed-Book Question Answering
student_friendly_explanation: Abstractive Question Answering is a type of natural language processing where we generate a detailed answer in our own words, rather than just copying a specific part from the given text. It's like when you read a story and then write your own version of how you imagine the characters might feel or what they did next, instead of just quoting a single sentence.
example: A system that generates a detailed response about the plot of a book, describing the main character's journey and emotions in its own words, based on the information provided in the book.

definition: Producing a summary in new wording rather than copying source sentences.
related_terms: Text Summarization; Extractive Summarization; Summarization Compression Ratio; Multi-Document Summarization
student_friendly_explanation: Abstractive summarization is when we create a shorter version of text by rewriting it in our own words, instead of just copying parts of the original text. It's like taking a long story and making it into a brief summary, but using different words to convey the same information.
example: Given a long news article about climate change, an abstractive summarization would take key points and rephrase them into a concise summary, avoiding direct quotes from the original text.

definition: A route for users and researchers to report harmful system behaviour.
related_terms: Responsible Disclosure; Abuse Detection; User Override; Verification Regime
student_friendly_explanation: The Abuse Reporting Channel is a special way for people to tell when something in a computer system isn't fair or safe. It's like a hotline, but for computers, where you can report if you see someone being mean or doing something wrong online. This helps make sure everyone uses the system nicely.
example: When a new social media platform is released, the developers set up an Abuse Reporting Channel so users can report any inappropriate behavior they notice, helping the platform improve and stay safe for all.

definition: Identifying plagiarism or undisclosed automated assistance in submitted work.
related_terms: Evidence Integrity; Cheat Detection; Claim Detection; Signal Detection in Safety Data
student_friendly_explanation: Academic Integrity Detection is like a smart detective that looks at your homework to make sure you didn't cheat by copying someone else's work or using an AI to help you write it.
example: A university uses this technology to check if students have copied parts of their essays from other sources, or if they've used an AI tool to generate some of their work.

definition: Speech whose pronunciation patterns differ from a model's dominant training distribution.
related_terms: Speech Corpus; Accessibility in Speech Technology; Frame Rate in Speech; Speech Enhancement
student_friendly_explanation: Accented speech refers to how someone speaks when they have a different accent compared to the way most people speak. It means their pronunciation might be slightly different, like adding extra emphasis or changing the way certain sounds are made.
example: A speech recognition system trained on standard English might struggle with recognizing accented speech, such as the pronunciation of 'th' in words like 'think' by someone with a Scottish accent.

definition: Terms specifying what customers may and may not do with a service.
related_terms: Terms of Service Enforcement; Model Usage Policy; Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP); Know Your Customer for AI
student_friendly_explanation: An Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) is like a set of rules you have to follow when using a service, just like how your school has rules for being a good student. It tells you what you can and cannot do with the service, so everyone uses it safely and fairly.
example: A college uses an online platform for submitting assignments. The AUP might state that students can only submit their work through this platform and cannot download or share it outside the system to avoid cheating.

definition: The specific measurable conditions a system must meet before release.
related_terms: Acceptance Rate of Suggestions; Release Readiness Review; Quality Gate; Acceptance Criteria for Agents
student_friendly_explanation: Acceptance criteria are like a checklist that tells you if a new software or product is ready to be used by everyone. It's a set of rules that make sure everything works as it should before it goes live.
example: A new app needs to have features like a search function, user profiles, and a payment system working properly. These features are the acceptance criteria that developers check to ensure the app is ready for users.

definition: Explicit conditions an agent's output must satisfy to be considered complete.
related_terms: Termination Condition; Agent Specification; Acceptance Criteria; Acceptance Threshold
student_friendly_explanation: Acceptance criteria for agents are like rules that tell us when an agent's actions are good enough. These rules ensure that the agent's output meets certain standards before we consider it complete. It's about making sure the agent has done everything it was supposed to do.
example: An AI chatbot designed to provide customer service needs to meet specific acceptance criteria. For instance, it must be able to answer at least 90% of common customer inquiries correctly within 3 seconds to be deemed fully functional.

definition: The fraction of speculatively drafted tokens the target model confirms, which determines achieved speedup.
related_terms: Speculative Decoding; Cache Hit Rate; Acceptance Rate of Suggestions; Acceptance Rate of Completions
student_friendly_explanation: Acceptance Rate is a measure of how many of the guesses or predictions made by an AI system are actually correct. It tells us how often the AI's predictions are accepted and acted upon.
example: In a language translation system, the Acceptance Rate measures how often the system correctly translates sentences from one language to another. If the system translates 80 out of 100 sentences correctly, its Acceptance Rate would be 80%.

definition: How often users keep a system's proposed output rather than discarding it.
related_terms: Acceptance Criteria; Task Success Rate for Users; Abstention Rate; Hallucination Rate
student_friendly_explanation: The acceptance rate of suggestions measures how frequently users choose to accept the system's proposed output instead of rejecting it outright.
example: In an AI-driven virtual assistant, the acceptance rate of suggestions indicates how often users opt to follow the system's recommendation for tasks or actions, rather than dismissing them.

definition: The specific numeric criterion a candidate must exceed to proceed.
related_terms: Alert Threshold; Deployment Gate; Acceptance Criteria; Acceptance Criteria for Agents
student_friendly_explanation: The acceptance threshold is like a magic number that a candidate needs to reach to be accepted into a program or system. It's a specific value that, if exceeded, allows someone or something to move forward. For instance, in a software deployment process, this threshold could be the minimum score required on a test to ensure the software meets quality standards before being deployed to users.
example: In a machine learning model deployment process, the acceptance threshold could be the minimum accuracy score required for the model to be deployed. If the model's accuracy score exceeds this threshold, it can be trusted to make predictions and decisions without human intervention.

definition: Enforcing document permissions at query time rather than after results are returned.
related_terms: Access to Justice; Permission-Aware Retrieval; Control Testing; Enterprise Search
student_friendly_explanation: Access Control in Retrieval is like having a lock on your documents before you ask for information. Instead of checking who has access only after you've asked, this system makes sure everyone can only see what they're allowed to see right from the start. It's like making sure people know which doors they can open before they even try to enter.
example: A university uses an enterprise search system where each document has specific permissions set up. When a student searches for information, the system checks immediately if the student has the necessary access rights to view the requested document. This ensures that no unauthorized access occurs during the search process.

definition: Efforts to make legal help available to people who cannot afford representation.
related_terms: Criminal Justice Risk Assessment; Access Control in Retrieval; Legal Research Automation; Accessibility Technology
student_friendly_explanation: Access to Justice is about ensuring that everyone, regardless of their financial situation, can get the help they need with legal matters. This might include free legal clinics, pro bono services, or programs that provide legal aid based on income level.
example: A university law school implements an Access to Justice program where students volunteer to provide free legal advice to local residents facing eviction or other legal issues, especially those who cannot afford private attorneys.

definition: Designing voice systems that work for diverse speech patterns and abilities.
related_terms: Low-Resource Speech; Speech Corpus; Frame Rate in Speech; Accented Speech
student_friendly_explanation: Accessibility in speech technology means making voice systems usable by people with different speech patterns and abilities, such as those who speak with accents or have speech impairments.
example: A speech recognition system that can accurately transcribe speech from speakers with strong regional accents, even when they speak quickly or with varying pitch.

definition: Ensuring generated output works for people using assistive technology.
related_terms: Attribution of Generated Work; Curation of Generated Output; Localization of Generated Content; Compliance Review of Generated Content
student_friendly_explanation: Accessibility of generated content means making sure that the text produced by AI tools can be used by everyone, including those who rely on special devices or software to read information. This includes ensuring that the content is accessible through screen readers, which help visually impaired users navigate web pages and documents.
example: A university website uses an AI tool to generate course descriptions. To ensure accessibility, the system is programmed to convert these descriptions into a format that can be easily read by screen readers, allowing visually impaired students to access the same information as their sighted peers.

definition: Tools enabling people with disabilities to access information and services.
related_terms: Educational Technology; Speech Recognition (ASR); Public Service Delivery; Access to Justice
student_friendly_explanation: Accessibility technology is software and devices that help people with disabilities use computers, websites, and other digital tools more easily. It includes features like screen readers for visually impaired users, keyboard navigation for those who can't use a mouse, and text-to-speech software for those who have difficulty reading.
example: A screen reader that reads aloud the contents of a web page, allowing a visually impaired user to navigate and interact with the website.

definition: A structured representation of interface elements that an agent can read instead of pixels.
related_terms: Accessibility Technology; Accessibility Standard; Accessibility by Default; Synthetic Accessibility
student_friendly_explanation: An Accessibility Tree is like a map of all the parts of a user interface, such as buttons, text boxes, and images, that a special kind of software (an agent) can understand instead of just seeing the picture on a screen. This helps people with disabilities interact with websites or apps more easily.
example: When a visually impaired person uses a screen reader to navigate a website, the screen reader reads out information about different parts of the page, like links and text fields, based on the Accessibility Tree.

definition: Harm caused by a system behaving unexpectedly rather than by malicious intent.
related_terms: Misuse Risk; Residual Risk; Risk Matrix; Systemic Risk
student_friendly_explanation: Accident risk refers to harm that occurs when a system behaves unpredictably, not because someone is trying to cause trouble, but simply due to unforeseen circumstances or bugs in the system.
example: A self-driving car accidentally hits a pedestrian during an unexpected software glitch, which was not designed to handle such scenarios.

definition: The assignment of responsibility for an AI system's decisions and consequences to identifiable people.
related_terms: Responsibility Gap; Algorithmic Accountability; External Accountability; Algorithmic Accountability Advocacy
student_friendly_explanation: Accountability structure is about making sure that when an AI makes a decision or causes an issue, there are specific individuals who can be held responsible. It’s like having a chain of command where mistakes can be traced back to a person, instead of just blaming the AI itself.
example: A hospital uses an AI system to predict patient readmissions. The system makes a prediction based on historical data, but sometimes it gets it wrong. In an accountability structure, the hospital assigns a specific doctor or nurse to review the AI's predictions and take responsibility for any errors in their decisions.

definition: The playback signal captured by a microphone, which must be removed for duplex conversation.
related_terms: Acoustic Feature; Acoustic Simulation; Acoustic Scene Classification; Acoustic Speech Token
student_friendly_explanation: Acoustic echo occurs when you speak into a microphone, and the sound from your voice is picked up again, causing a delayed version of your speech to be heard back. This can interfere with clear communication, especially in environments with reflective surfaces like classrooms or conference rooms.
example: In a classroom with hard walls, your voice echoes back to you, making it difficult to hear yourself and others at the same time.

definition: A numeric summary of a short audio frame used as input to a speech model.
related_terms: Acoustic Speech Token; Acoustic Simulation; Acoustic Scene Classification; Semantic Speech Token
student_friendly_explanation: Acoustic features are numbers that represent small parts of a sound clip, like tiny snapshots of how the sound looks. These numbers help speech models understand and process the sounds more effectively.
example: In a speech recognition system, acoustic features are extracted from short segments of audio to train the model on different types of speech sounds.

definition: Determining the environment a recording was made in from its ambient sound.
related_terms: Acoustic Simulation; Acoustic Feature; Acoustic Speech Token; Acoustic Echo
student_friendly_explanation: Acoustic Scene Classification is about figuring out where a recording was taken by listening to the background sounds, like if it's a park, a classroom, or a city street.
example: A system that can tell if a recorded voice is from a coffee shop or a library based on the ambient sounds around it.

definition: A discrete audio unit capturing detailed sound qualities needed for faithful reconstruction.
related_terms: Semantic Speech Token; Acoustic Feature; Acoustic Simulation; Acoustic Scene Classification
student_friendly_explanation: An acoustic speech token is a small segment of audio that contains all the important details about how a particular word or sound is produced, allowing it to be accurately recreated later.
example: A recording of a single spoken vowel sound, isolated from a sentence, which captures all the nuances of its production.

definition: The criterion a Bayesian optimizer maximizes to decide where to sample next.
related_terms: Entropy Search; Probability of Improvement (PI); Expected Improvement (EI); Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're playing a game where you have to guess a secret number chosen by your friend. The 'Acquisition Function' is like a smart strategy that helps you guess the correct number faster. It tells you which number to guess next based on how close you think you are to guessing right. This way, you can make better guesses and find the secret number quicker.
example: In a machine learning experiment, an acquisition function might be used to decide which data points to collect next. For instance, if the model is trying to predict the price of a house based on various features, the acquisition function could suggest which new house features to test next, helping the model learn more efficiently.

definition: A cognitive architecture modelling human cognition through modular memory and production systems.
related_terms: Production Memory; Chunking in Cognitive Architecture; Procedural Memory in Architectures; Declarative Memory in Architectures
student_friendly_explanation: ACT-R is a model that helps us understand how our brains think and learn. It uses different parts of our brain (like memory banks) to store information and use rules to solve problems. This model is used by computer scientists to make smart programs that can think like humans.
example: Imagine you're learning a new language. ACT-R would help simulate how your brain stores words and rules for grammar, allowing you to quickly adapt and use new vocabulary.

definition: A choice an agent makes that influences the environment's next state.
related_terms: Multi-Discrete Action; Action Masking; Parameterized Action; State
student_friendly_explanation: In reinforcement learning, an action is like making a decision that can affect how the world around you changes. It's what you do to try and achieve something, like choosing which button to press on a machine to get a reward.
example: A robot learning to navigate through a maze. The robot has to decide which direction to go next (left, right, or straight) based on its current position and the rewards it gets for reaching certain points.

definition: An explicit enumeration of permitted operations, denying anything not listed.
related_terms: Action Grounding; Action Space for Agents; Compensating Action; Agent Specification
student_friendly_explanation: An Action Allowlist is like a list of approved actions that an AI can perform. It's a way to specify which operations are allowed, making sure the AI only does what you want it to do. This helps prevent unwanted or unintended actions from happening.
example: A robot vacuum cleaner has an Action Allowlist that defines the specific cleaning patterns and areas it can operate in. If the allowlist includes 'clean living room' and 'avoid kitchen', then the robot will only clean those areas and avoid the kitchen, ensuring it follows your instructions.

definition: Predicting what action will occur before it begins.
related_terms: Temporal Action Localization; Action Recognition; Action Space; Video Understanding
student_friendly_explanation: Action Anticipation is about predicting which action will happen next in a video sequence, like anticipating a person's move before they make it.
example: A self-driving car uses Action Anticipation to predict the actions of other vehicles and pedestrians on the road, allowing it to make safe driving decisions.

definition: Converting continuous control into a finite grid of choices so discrete methods apply.
related_terms: Discrete Action Space; Parameterized Action; Multi-Discrete Action; Action
student_friendly_explanation: Action Discretization is a technique used in reinforcement learning where we take a continuous range of possible actions and break it down into a smaller, finite set of discrete options. This allows us to use simpler, more manageable methods to make decisions within the system.
example: In a self-driving car scenario, the car's decision-making system might have a continuous action space that includes all possible steering angles from -10 degrees to +10 degrees. By discretizing this action space, we could limit it to only five discrete values (e.g., -6, -2, 2, 6, 10 degrees), making it easier to implement and manage.

definition: Converting a model's intended action into a concrete executable command in an environment.
related_terms: GUI Grounding; Action Module; Action Space for Agents; Action Preview
student_friendly_explanation: Action grounding is the process of translating a model's planned actions into specific, actionable commands that can be executed within a real-world environment. It ensures that the abstract intentions of an AI system are transformed into practical steps that can be carried out by the system or by other components in the environment.
example: A robot navigating a warehouse uses action grounding to convert its navigation plan (e.g., 'move forward until reaching the storage area') into a series of precise movements (e.g., 'step left, step right, step forward, step forward, ...').

definition: Identifying commitments and tasks agreed during a conversation.
related_terms: Clause Extraction; Item Response Theory (IRT); Document AI; Meeting Summary
student_friendly_explanation: Action Item Extraction is about finding all the tasks and responsibilities mentioned during a meeting or discussion. It's like picking out the 'to-do' list from what people say.
example: During a project planning meeting, the AI system extracts action items such as 'Schedule weekly meetings with team members' and 'Review progress every two weeks.'

definition: Ensuring follow-up work identified after an incident is actually completed.
related_terms: Cost Monitoring; Data Incident; Incident Classification for ML; Communication During Incidents
student_friendly_explanation: Action Item Tracking is like keeping a list of tasks that need to be done after something happens, such as a problem with technology or data. It makes sure that all the items on this list are finished and completed.
example: After a software bug was fixed, the team created a list of actions to ensure that all necessary updates were made to prevent future issues. This list included tasks like testing new features, updating documentation, and checking system performance.

definition: Preventing selection of actions that are invalid in the current state.
related_terms: Parameterized Action; Discrete Action Space; Action; Action Repeat
student_friendly_explanation: Action Masking is a technique used in reinforcement learning where the system prevents you from choosing actions that would lead to impossible or undesirable outcomes based on the current situation.
example: In a game environment, if an agent is trying to move towards a goal but the action space includes jumping over a cliff, Action Masking ensures that the agent cannot take such an action, thus preventing it from falling.

definition: The component translating an agent's decisions into effects on its environment.
related_terms: Perception Module; Action Grounding; Side Effect; Compensating Action
student_friendly_explanation: An action module is like a smart controller in a robot or virtual agent. It takes the robot's or agent's choices (decisions) and turns them into actions that affect the robot's surroundings, such as moving its arms or changing its behavior.
example: A self-driving car's action module decides to slow down when it detects an obstacle ahead, which then causes the car to apply brakes and adjust its speed accordingly.

definition: Showing exactly what an agent intends to do before it does it.
related_terms: Diff Preview; Action Grounding; Action Module; Action Space for Agents
student_friendly_explanation: Action Preview is a feature where an AI system shows you, in advance, what actions it plans to take before actually executing them. This helps in understanding the AI's intentions and can be useful for debugging or testing purposes.
example: A virtual assistant that previews its actions, such as scheduling a meeting, before actually sending the invitation email.

definition: A computer vision task that identifies human actions or activities in video sequences. Methods range from two-stream networks (spatial + temporal) to 3D CNNs and video transformers. Applications include surveillance, sports analytics, sign language recognition, and human-computer interaction.
related_terms: Video Understanding; Pose Estimation; Image Recognition; Temporal Action Localization
student_friendly_explanation: Action Recognition is about teaching computers to understand what people are doing in videos. It looks at how people move and do things, like running, jumping, or signing. This helps in many ways, such as watching security cameras, analyzing sports performances, recognizing signs in sign language, and making computers understand human actions better.
example: A system that watches a video of a basketball game and can tell which player is shooting, dribbling, or passing the ball, helping coaches and analysts to analyze the game more effectively.

definition: Holding an action constant for several steps, which shortens effective horizons and aids exploration.
related_terms: Action Masking; Parameterized Action; Discrete Action Space; Multi-Discrete Action
student_friendly_explanation: Action Repeat is when you keep performing the same action over multiple turns in a game or simulation. This helps you explore different scenarios without having to start from scratch each time, making your learning process more efficient.
example: In a video game where you control a character that can move left or right, Action Repeat allows you to repeatedly move the character in one direction (say, left) for several turns before changing directions. This way, you can better understand how the environment reacts to your actions.

definition: The set of operations an agent may invoke, including tools, code, and messages.
related_terms: Resource; Action Grounding; Compensating Action; Observation Space
student_friendly_explanation: The action space for agents is like a list of all the things an agent can do. This includes using tools, running code, or sending messages. It's about what actions the agent can take within a system.
example: In a robotics simulation, the action space might include actions like 'move forward', 'turn left', 'open door', and 'activate sensor'. These actions define what the robot can do in the virtual environment.

definition: Storing intermediate values in reduced precision to fit longer sequences in memory.
related_terms: Scalar Quantization of Vectors; Context Compression; Model Compression for Edge; Memory Compression
student_friendly_explanation: Activation Compression is a technique used in machine learning to save memory by storing some values of neural network activations in a simpler, lower-precision format. This allows the model to handle longer sequences without running out of memory.
example: A deep learning model processes sequences of data, such as text or time series. By using Activation Compression, the model can store intermediate values of its activations in a less precise form, allowing it to process longer sequences than it would otherwise be able to.

definition: A mathematical function applied to a neuron's output in a neural network that introduces non-linearity into the model. Without activation functions, stacked layers would collapse into a single linear transformation regardless of depth. Common activation functions include ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit), sigmoid, tanh, GELU, and SwiGLU.
related_terms: Neural Network (NN); Deep Learning (DL); Backpropagation (BP); Model
student_friendly_explanation: Activation functions add non-linearity to neural networks, which allows them to learn complex patterns in data. Without them, neural networks would behave like simple linear models, unable to capture the intricate relationships between inputs and outputs.
example: Imagine a neural network trying to classify images of cats and dogs. An activation function like ReLU can help the network distinguish between the brightness levels of pixels, making it easier to separate cat from dog images.

definition: The output produced by applying a convolutional filter to an input in a neural network, visualizing which features the network detects at each spatial location. Also called feature maps. Visualizing activation maps helps understand what patterns each layer of a CNN learns, from simple edges to complex objects in deeper layers.
related_terms: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN); Feature Map; Spatial Dropout; Hierarchical Feature Map
student_friendly_explanation: An activation map is like a picture taken by a special lens (convolutional filter) on top of another image (input). This lens shows us which parts of the original image the neural network has noticed as important. It's like seeing through a magnifying glass to find interesting details.
example: Imagine you have a photo of a cat. When a CNN looks at this photo, it might see the cat's whiskers as one feature and the fur texture as another. Each part of the photo where the CNN notices something interesting creates a small dot in the activation map, showing where those features were detected.

definition: Moving stored activations to host memory or disk to free accelerator capacity.
related_terms: Parameter Offloading; Activation Memory; Sequence Parallelism (SP); Cognitive Offloading
student_friendly_explanation: Activation offloading is a technique where data, called activations, that are temporarily stored during neural network computations are moved to the host's main memory or storage device to make more space available on specialized hardware like GPUs or TPUs. This allows these powerful processors to perform more tasks without waiting for the slower transfer of data.
example: During a deep learning training process, the activation values from intermediate layers are frequently transferred back to the host's memory to be processed by the CPU. By offloading these activations, the GPU can handle more computations simultaneously, improving overall efficiency.

definition: An interpretability method substituting activations between runs to identify which components cause a behaviour.
related_terms: Path Patching; Activation Sparsity; Concept Activation Vector (CAV); Activation Function
student_friendly_explanation: Activation Patching is a technique used in deep learning to see how different parts of a neural network contribute to its output. By temporarily replacing certain parts of the network's internal workings, we can figure out which elements are most important for generating specific results.
example: Imagine you have a complex model that predicts whether an email is spam or not. Using Activation Patching, you could replace parts of this model with simpler ones and observe how the prediction changes. This helps you understand which features of the emails (like keywords or sender's address) are crucial for the model to make its decision.

definition: Reducing the precision of intermediate values, which enables faster arithmetic but is more error-prone.
related_terms: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ); Weight-Only Quantization; Activation Sparsity; Activation Patching
student_friendly_explanation: Activation quantization is a technique used in deep learning models where we reduce the number of bits used to represent certain values, like numbers in the middle of calculations. This makes the model run faster because it needs less processing power, but it can lead to more errors in the results.
example: In a neural network, activation quantization might be applied to the values between layers, reducing their precision from 32-bit floating point to 8-bit integers. While this speeds up the computation, it may cause some inaccuracies in the final output.

definition: The proportion of zero activations, which efficient inference kernels can exploit to skip work.
related_terms: Sparsity Ratio; N:M Sparsity; Activation Patching; Concept Activation Vector (CAV)
student_friendly_explanation: Activation sparsity refers to the number of zeros among the many possible activations in a neural network. Efficient inference kernels can take advantage of these zeros to skip unnecessary computations, making the network faster and more energy-efficient.
example: In a convolutional neural network, if a certain layer has many activation values set to zero due to spatial or feature invariance, the inference kernel can skip over these zeros, thus saving computational resources.

definition: Modifying internal representations at runtime to control output characteristics.
related_terms: Steering Vector; Dictionary Learning for Activations; Activation Sparsity; Activation Patching
student_friendly_explanation: Activation steering is a technique used in deep learning where we adjust the internal data structures (representations) of a neural network during its operation to influence how it processes information and produces outputs. It's like tweaking the settings of a machine to get the desired results, but done automatically by the system.
example: During training, a neural network learns to recognize patterns in images. Activation steering can be used to fine-tune these learned features, ensuring that certain parts of the image are emphasized or suppressed based on the task at hand, such as focusing on edges or textures.

definition: An inequality constraint satisfied with equality at the solution, actively shaping the optimum.
related_terms: Equality Constraint; Inequality Constraint; Active Set Method; Chance Constraint
student_friendly_explanation: Active constraints are like rules that are always followed exactly at the best solution. They're important because they help us find the very best outcome in a problem.
example: In a manufacturing process, an active constraint could be the minimum quality level that must be met at all times. This ensures that the product meets the required standard without any room for deviation.

definition: Choosing which unlabelled data to include in training to maximize benefit per token.
related_terms: Model Selection; Active Learning Query Strategy; Active Learning (AL); Exemplar Selection
student_friendly_explanation: Active Data Selection is about picking which examples of data to use during training so that we can learn the most from them. It's like choosing the best examples to teach a machine learning model, ensuring it learns effectively with less data.
example: A machine learning system analyzing images of animals to recognize different species. The system uses Active Data Selection to decide which animal images to study more closely, focusing on those that are most helpful for improving its recognition accuracy.

definition: A machine learning approach where the algorithm selects the most informative unlabeled examples to query an oracle (typically a human annotator) for labels. By strategically choosing which data points to label, active learning can achieve target accuracy with significantly fewer labeled examples than random sampling, reducing annotation costs.
related_terms: Semi-Supervised Learning; Transfer Learning (TL); Algorithm; Accuracy
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're trying to teach a computer to recognize cats in pictures. Instead of labeling every single picture, active learning lets the computer pick the most tricky ones to ask humans about. This way, it can learn faster and more efficiently, using fewer human labels.
example: In a study, an AI system uses active learning to identify images of cats. It first looks at many unlabeled images and decides which ones are hardest to classify. Then, it asks a human to label those images, focusing on the most uncertain cases. This targeted approach helps the AI learn better with fewer human efforts.

definition: Choosing which experiment to run next to maximize information gained.
related_terms: Self-Driving Laboratory (SDL); Closed-Loop Discovery; Active Experimentation; Experiment Tracking
student_friendly_explanation: Active learning for experiments is about deciding which new experiment to perform next to get the most useful information. It's like choosing the best puzzle piece to solve a mystery, ensuring you learn the most with each step.
example: A scientist uses machine learning algorithms to analyze data from previous experiments. Based on this analysis, the system recommends which new experiment should be conducted next to refine a specific hypothesis or uncover new insights.

definition: The rule choosing which unlabeled examples to send for annotation next.
related_terms: Active Learning (AL); Query by Committee; Active Data Selection; Uncertainty Sampling
student_friendly_explanation: Active Learning Query Strategy is a method used in machine learning to decide which data points need human labeling the most. It selects the unlabeled examples that, when labeled, will provide the greatest improvement in the model's performance.
example: In a spam detection system, an Active Learning Query Strategy might choose emails that have a high chance of being spam but haven't been labeled yet. This way, the system can learn more effectively by focusing on tricky cases.

definition: A large untrimmed video benchmark for temporal action localization and detection.
related_terms: Kinetics; Temporal Action Localization; ARC Benchmark; Benchmark Lifespan
student_friendly_explanation: ActivityNet是一个大型的视频基准，用于时间动作定位和检测。它包含大量的未经修剪的视频数据，帮助研究人员评估和改进识别和检测视频中动作的能力。
example: 研究人员使用ActivityNet来训练他们的算法，以便能够准确地识别和定位视频中的特定动作，例如跑步、握手等。

definition: The component of a reinforcement learning system that selects actions.
related_terms: Distributed RL; Ape-X; IMPALA; Safe Reinforcement Learning
student_friendly_explanation: An actor in a reinforcement learning system is like a decision-maker. It takes into account the current situation (state) and decides what action to take next (like choosing between walking or running). This choice is based on rewards received from previous actions, helping the system learn and improve over time.
example: In a game where an AI learns to navigate through a maze, the actor decides which direction to move next based on how well it performed in previous moves, aiming to reach the end goal as quickly as possible.

definition: A distributed design separating experience collection from gradient computation.
related_terms: V-Trace; Dyna Architecture; Distributed RL; Experience Replay
student_friendly_explanation: Actor-Learner Architecture is a method used in artificial intelligence where the part of the system that learns (the actor) and the part that calculates how much it should learn (the learner) work separately. This separation helps in making the learning process more efficient and manageable.
example: In a complex game environment, the actor decides actions based on the current state, while the learner updates its understanding of the environment's dynamics. This architecture allows the system to adapt quickly to new situations without getting overwhelmed by too much data.

definition: A statistical model of risk and reserving used in insurance and pensions.
related_terms: Insurance Pricing Model; Insurance Claim Estimation; Statistical Arbitrage; Claims Triage
student_friendly_explanation: An actuarial model is a tool that helps insurance companies predict how much money they might need to pay out in claims based on historical data and current trends. It's like a smart calculator that can forecast future costs, helping insurers set fair prices and manage their finances effectively.
example: An insurance company uses an actuarial model to estimate the average cost of claims for different types of policies over the next five years. This helps them set premiums that cover potential payouts and ensure they have enough reserves to handle any unexpected claims.

definition: The condition where a commanded action exceeds what hardware can deliver.
related_terms: Series Elastic Actuator (SEA); Time-Optimal Trajectory; Fault Tolerance in Robotics; Integral Windup
student_friendly_explanation: Actuator saturation happens when the robot tries to move faster or stronger than what its actuators can handle. It's like trying to push a heavy box with your arms, but they get tired and can't push any more.
example: A robotic arm trying to lift a very heavy object, but the motor is too weak and reaches its maximum capacity, causing the arm to stop moving further.

definition: Selecting which audiences see which advertisements based on predicted relevance.
related_terms: Privacy-Preserving Advertising; Creative Optimization; Frequency Capping; Lookalike Audience
student_friendly_explanation: Ad targeting is like sending personalized invitations to your friends based on what you like. It uses smart algorithms to show ads to people who are most likely to be interested in them, making sure everyone sees ads they might find useful.
example: A social media platform uses machine learning to analyze user behavior and interests. It then shows targeted ads to users based on their past interactions and preferences, such as recommending a new movie or product based on similar users' experiences.

definition: A boosting algorithm reweighting misclassified examples so later weak learners attend to them.
related_terms: Ensemble Learning; Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM); Decision Stump; Boosting
student_friendly_explanation: AdaBoost is like a team of detectives solving a crime. Each detective (weak learner) gets a chance to solve the case, but if they get it wrong, the next detective gets a bigger clue (reweighted importance). This way, the team focuses more on solving cases that were initially harder to solve.
example: Imagine you have a group of students trying to predict whether it will rain or not based on weather conditions. Each student makes a prediction, but some predictions are more correct than others. AdaBoost would then give extra weight to the incorrect predictions, making the next student (or 'detector') focus more on those tricky cases to improve overall accuracy.

definition: An adaptive optimizer removing the need for a global learning rate by tracking update magnitudes.
related_terms: Muon Optimizer; Lion Optimizer; LAMB; Maximal Update Parameterization
student_friendly_explanation: AdaDelta is an advanced optimization technique that automatically adjusts how much each parameter should be updated during training. It does this without needing a single, fixed learning rate, which makes it more flexible and efficient.
example: During training a neural network, AdaDelta updates the weights of the network's layers based on the differences between the current and previous values of those weights. It uses a running average of these differences to determine the new weight values, ensuring that the updates are always small enough to avoid overshooting the minimum.

definition: A memory-efficient adaptive optimizer factoring second-moment statistics into row and column vectors.
related_terms: Optimizer State; Quantized Optimizer; Zero Redundancy Optimizer; Fused Optimizer
student_friendly_explanation: AdaFactor is an advanced optimization technique that helps adjust how much weight we give to each step when training machine learning models. It does this by looking at both the rows (individual features) and columns (examples) of data, and figuring out the best way to update the model parameters efficiently without using too much memory.
example: During the training of a neural network, AdaFactor analyzes the data to determine the optimal learning rate for each parameter, taking into account the unique characteristics of both the input features and the examples, thus improving the model's performance.

definition: An optimizer scaling each parameter's step by the inverse square root of its accumulated squared gradients.
related_terms: Diagonal Preconditioning; Shampoo Optimizer; RMSProp; Zero Redundancy Optimizer
student_friendly_explanation: AdaGrad is an optimization technique that adjusts how much we update each parameter during training. It does this by looking at how much the parameter has changed (its gradient) and then scales the update based on the size of these changes. The more the parameter has changed, the smaller the update will be, which helps prevent overshooting the optimal solution.
example: Imagine you're trying to find the lowest point in a hilly landscape. Each time you take a step downhill, you adjust your step size based on how steep the hill is at your current position. If you've been going down a very steep hill recently, you'll take a smaller step next time to avoid falling off the edge. This way, AdaGrad helps you navigate the landscape efficiently.

definition: A variant of Adam applying weight decay directly to parameters rather than through the gradient, improving generalization.
related_terms: Decoupled Weight Decay; Gradient Descent Variant; Step Decay; Exponential Decay
student_friendly_explanation: AdamW is an advanced version of the Adam optimizer that adds a form of weight decay (a technique to prevent overfitting) directly to the parameters instead of using the gradients. This helps in making the model generalize better by penalizing large weights during training.
example: In a machine learning project, a researcher uses AdamW to fine-tune a neural network. By adding weight decay directly to the parameters, AdamW ensures that the model doesn't become too complex and overfits the training data, leading to improved performance on unseen data.

definition: Modifying a retrieved past solution to fit the current problem's differences.
related_terms: Case-Based Reasoning Cycle; Means-End Reasoning; Qualitative Reasoning; Monotonic Reasoning
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptation in case-based reasoning is about tweaking a previously solved problem's solution to make it work for the new situation, even if some details have changed.
example: A software system uses historical data to diagnose issues with computer hardware. When diagnosing a new type of error, it adapts the previous diagnostic steps by adjusting the specific tests and checks based on the new error's characteristics.

definition: Small trainable modules inserted between pre-trained model layers while original weights remain frozen. Add minimal parameters (1-5%) but match full fine-tuning performance. Multiple task-specific adapters can share one base model.
related_terms: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT); LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation); Fine-tuning; Adapter Module
student_friendly_explanation: Adapter modules are like little helpers that you can add between parts of a big, complex model. These helpers don't change the main parts of the model, but they can make the model better at doing specific tasks. It's like giving your model some extra training wheels to help it learn new things without changing everything.
example: Imagine you have a very smart robot that can do many tasks. Now, you want this robot to be really good at understanding and responding to emails. You can use adapter modules to teach just the part of the robot that handles emails, making it more specialized without changing the rest of its abilities.

definition: Changing a model's active fine-tuned adapter without reloading base weights.
related_terms: Model Swap; Hot Reload; Adapter Merging; Adapter Pattern
student_friendly_explanation: Adapter Hot Swap is a process where you can update or modify parts of a pre-trained model (like an adapter) without having to start over with the entire model from scratch. It's like changing a small part of your car engine while it's running, but for a machine learning model.
example: When developing a language model, you might want to tweak some parts of it to better suit a specific task. With Adapter Hot Swap, you can make these changes quickly and efficiently, without having to retrain the whole model from the beginning.

definition: Folding a trained adapter back into base weights so inference adds no extra computation.
related_terms: Adapter; Adapter Module; SLERP Merging; DARE Merging
student_friendly_explanation: Adapter Merging is a technique used in deep learning where we take a part of a model (called an adapter) that has been trained on some data, and fold it back into the main model's weights. This way, when the model makes predictions, it doesn't need to do any extra calculations, making it faster and more efficient.
example: Imagine you have a big neural network model that can classify images. Sometimes, you might want to add a small tweak to this model to make it better at recognizing a specific type of image. Adapter Merging allows you to add this tweak (the adapter) without making the model run slower. So, when the model looks at new images, it can still recognize them quickly and accurately, just like before.

definition: A small trainable bottleneck inserted into a frozen model so only a few parameters change.
related_terms: Adapter; Adapter Merging; Inception Module; LoRA Rank
student_friendly_explanation: An adapter module is like a tiny, trainable part that you can add to an already trained model. It's designed to make changes to just a few important parts of the model, without having to retrain the whole thing from scratch. This way, you can tweak the model to better fit your specific needs without starting over.
example: Imagine you have a pre-trained image recognition model that works well but needs to recognize a new type of object. An adapter module allows you to add a small, trainable part to this model, which can learn to recognize the new object without changing the rest of the model. This makes it much more efficient and faster to update.

definition: A model permitted to update in deployment under an agreed governance plan.
related_terms: Predictive Model in Medicine; Automation Bias in Medicine; Precision Medicine; Adaptive Trial Design
student_friendly_explanation: An adaptive algorithm in medicine is like a smart doctor that can learn from new data and improve its decisions over time, following a set of rules to ensure safety and accuracy.
example: A drug trial where the dosage and frequency of a medication are adjusted based on how patients respond, allowing the treatment to become more effective and safer as more data is collected.

definition: Spending more computation on harder inputs and less on easy ones.
related_terms: Adaptive Retrieval; Conditional Computation; Easy Example Removal; Morphological Computation
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive computation is like giving more effort to solve tricky problems and less effort to simple ones. It's a way of making machines smarter by focusing more on difficult tasks.
example: A machine learning model that improves its performance by spending extra time and resources on hard cases, such as recognizing images with complex patterns or identifying rare diseases.

definition: Letting a network decide how many processing steps a given input requires.
related_terms: Stochastic Depth; Parameter Sharing Across Depth; Recurrent Depth; Network Depth
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive Depth allows a neural network to dynamically adjust the number of layers or processing steps needed to handle different inputs, making it more flexible and efficient.
example: In a convolutional neural network (CNN) used for image recognition, Adaptive Depth can automatically reduce the number of convolutional layers when dealing with smaller images, thus saving computational resources.

definition: Augmenting discriminator inputs at a rate tuned to prevent overfitting on small datasets.
related_terms: Discriminator Overfitting; Discriminator; Adversarial Loss; Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
student_friendly_explanation: An adaptive discriminator augmentation is a technique used in machine learning, particularly with generative adversarial networks (GANs), to make the discriminator more robust and less likely to memorize the training data. It involves randomly altering the input to the discriminator in a way that helps it learn from a wider range of examples, thus preventing it from becoming too specialized on the training set.
example: In a GAN where the generator creates images and the discriminator classifies them, an adaptive discriminator augmentation might involve slightly changing the appearance of the generated images each time they are shown to the discriminator. This ensures that the discriminator learns to recognize patterns across different types of images rather than just memorizing specific examples.

definition: Scaling gradients relative to parameter magnitude rather than a fixed threshold, enabling normalizer-free networks.
related_terms: Gradient Value Clipping; Gradient Norm Clipping; Gradient Descent Variant; Gradient Underflow
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive Gradient Clipping is a technique used in machine learning to adjust the size of the gradients (the changes in the model's parameters) based on their importance rather than using a fixed limit. This method helps prevent the model from becoming too sensitive to small or large parameter values, which can cause issues during training.
example: During the training of a neural network, adaptive gradient clipping ensures that the gradients do not become too large or too small, thus helping the network learn more effectively without getting stuck in local minima.

definition: A sequence of material adjusted to each learner's demonstrated needs.
related_terms: Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT); Content Recommendation in Education; AI in Education; Language Learning Application
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive Learning Path is like having a personalized textbook that changes based on what you know and don't know. It's smart software that figures out which topics you need to learn more about and adjusts the lessons accordingly, making your learning experience more efficient and effective.
example: A language learning app that starts with basic vocabulary and gradually introduces more complex words and phrases based on how well you understand each level.

definition: Pooling that adjusts window size so the output has a fixed shape regardless of input size.
related_terms: Pooling; Average Pooling; Max Pooling; Global Average Pooling
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive pooling is a technique used in deep learning where the size of the pooling window can be adjusted automatically based on the input size. This ensures that the output always has a consistent shape, no matter how large or small the input image is.
example: In a convolutional neural network, adaptive pooling can adjust the size of the pooling window to ensure that the output feature maps have a fixed shape, such as 3x3 or 5x5, regardless of the input image size.

definition: Deciding dynamically whether and how much to retrieve for each query.
related_terms: Query Generation for Retrieval; Corrective Retrieval; Adaptive Computation; Retrieval Necessity
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive Retrieval is about figuring out what information to fetch based on your question. It's like when you ask a smart friend for advice, they quickly decide which details to share to help you best.
example: A search engine using Adaptive Retrieval can analyze your search query and adjust how much information it retrieves, showing more relevant results or less if the query is too broad.

definition: Choosing a different cutoff per region to handle uneven illumination.
related_terms: Thresholding; Otsu's Method; Illumination Robustness; HSV Color Space
student_friendly_explanation: Adaptive thresholding is a technique used in computer vision to automatically adjust the threshold value based on the local image intensity distribution, rather than using a fixed global threshold. This method helps in handling images with uneven lighting by identifying regions with similar brightness levels and applying a threshold within those regions.
example: In an image of a room taken at different times of day, adaptive thresholding can be used to segment the image into different regions where the light conditions vary. For instance, during the day, the threshold might be set higher to separate bright areas like windows from dark areas like walls, whereas at night, the threshold could be lower to better distinguish between the darker parts of the room and the brighter ones.

definition: An adaptive oversampling method concentrating synthetic examples where the minority class is hardest to learn.
related_terms: SMOTE; Adaptive Retrieval; Synthetic Data Ratio; Adaptive Computation
student_friendly_explanation: ADASYN is a technique used in machine learning to help computers better understand data from groups that have fewer examples. It creates new, artificial examples of these underrepresented groups by analyzing how similar they are to existing examples. This helps the computer learn more effectively from all types of data.
example: Imagine you're working on a project to classify different types of fruits based on their images. If there are many apples but only a few bananas, ADASYN can create additional banana images that are similar to the real ones, making it easier for the computer to learn to tell them apart.

definition: A model treating a series as the sum of its trend, seasonal, and residual parts.
related_terms: Multiplicative Decomposition; STL Decomposition; Residual Component; Seasonal Hybrid ESD
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you have a time series data set showing sales over years. The additive decomposition model helps us break down this data into three main parts: the overall trend (like the general direction of sales), the seasonal pattern (like how much more or less we sell during certain times of the year), and the random fluctuations (like unexpected spikes or drops). By adding these parts together, we can better understand the underlying patterns in the data.
example: A retail store tracks its monthly sales over several years. Using an additive decomposition model, the data is separated into a long-term trend showing an increasing sales pattern, a seasonal component indicating higher sales during holiday seasons, and random variations from month to month. This analysis helps the store predict future sales more accurately.

definition: The general family of count adjustments preventing zero probabilities in discrete models.
related_terms: Laplace Smoothing; Label Smoothing; Dirichlet Smoothing; Additive Decomposition
student_friendly_explanation: Additive smoothing is a technique used in machine learning to avoid assigning zero probability to any category in a model. It adds a small constant to the counts of each category, making all probabilities non-zero.
example: When training a text classification model with 5 categories, if a category never appears in the training data, additive smoothing ensures that this category has a very small but non-zero probability in the final model.

definition: A scene parsing dataset annotating a wide variety of objects and surfaces across scene types.
related_terms: Visual Genome; SVHN; Cityscapes; GQA
student_friendly_explanation: ADE20K is a large dataset containing images from various scenes, each annotated with details about different objects and surfaces within them. This helps researchers and developers improve computer vision systems by teaching them to recognize and categorize elements in real-world images accurately.
example: In one image from ADE20K, you might see an annotated scene showing a kitchen countertop with a glass bottle, a wooden cutting board, and a red plate. Each object and surface is carefully labeled to help machine learning models learn to identify and classify such elements correctly.

definition: Estimating whether a patient will follow a prescribed treatment plan.
related_terms: Treatment Response Prediction; Clinical Guideline Adherence; Return Prediction; Compliance Automation
student_friendly_explanation: Adherence Prediction is a type of artificial intelligence (AI) that helps doctors predict if patients will stick to their medication or therapy plans. It uses data from previous treatments to forecast future behavior.
example: An AI system analyzing electronic health records to determine which patients are likely to take their medications on time, thereby improving overall treatment outcomes.

definition: A similarity score between two partitions, corrected so random agreement scores zero.
related_terms: Learned Index; Davies-Bouldin Index; Index Rebuild; IVF Index
student_friendly_explanation: The Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) is a way to measure how similar two groups of data points are, even if they were created randomly. It corrects for chance agreement, making sure that if the groups are just by luck, it won't give a high score.
example: Imagine you have a list of students sorted into two groups based on their favorite colors (red and blue). If you randomly sort them again, the ARI will show how much the new grouping matches the original one, but it will adjust for the fact that random sorting could look similar by coincidence.

definition: The set of variables that must be controlled for to render a causal comparison valid.
related_terms: Causal Representation Learning; Causal Discovery; Independent Causal Mechanisms; Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP)
student_friendly_explanation: An adjustment set is like a group of factors you need to consider when comparing how one thing affects another. It's important because if these factors aren't accounted for, your results might not make sense.
example: In a study examining the effect of diet on health outcomes, an adjustment set might include age, gender, and exercise habits. These factors could influence both diet and health outcomes, so they need to be taken into account to accurately assess the diet's impact.

definition: Estimating a compound's absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity computationally.
related_terms: Readmission Prediction; Yield Prediction; Length of Stay Prediction; Protein Structure Prediction
student_friendly_explanation: ADMET Prediction is a method that uses computer models to predict how a new drug will behave in the body. It helps scientists understand if a drug can be absorbed by the body, how it will move around the body, how it will be broken down, and if it might cause any harmful effects.
example: A pharmaceutical company uses ADMET Prediction to determine if a newly developed drug can effectively treat a disease without causing severe side effects.

definition: The property of a heuristic that never overestimates the true remaining cost.
related_terms: Consistency of a Heuristic; Planning Heuristic; Minimum Remaining Values (MRV); Safety Property
student_friendly_explanation: Admissibility is a quality of a heuristic function used in artificial intelligence. It means that the heuristic can never guess the remaining cost too high. In simpler terms, it's like when you're planning a route, and your map always shows you will reach your destination sooner than it actually takes.
example: In a pathfinding algorithm, an admissible heuristic ensures that the estimated distance to the goal is never less than the actual distance. For instance, if you're trying to find the shortest path from your house to the park, an admissible heuristic would never underestimate how far away the park is, ensuring you don't miss any shortcuts.

definition: Rejecting or deferring requests at the edge to protect a system from overload.
related_terms: Request Isolation; Edge AI; Overflow Handling; Model Compression for Edge
student_friendly_explanation: Admission control is like a traffic cop for your computer system. It decides whether new tasks can join the queue or if they need to wait until others finish first. This helps prevent your system from getting too busy and crashing.
example: When a server receives a large number of requests to process images, admission control ensures that only a certain number of requests are processed at once, preventing the server from becoming overwhelmed and stopping all work.

definition: Control that produces motion in response to measured external forces.
related_terms: Impedance Control; Traded Control; Shared Control; Robust Tube Control
student_friendly_explanation: Admittance control is a type of robotic control that adjusts the robot's movement based on the forces applied to it by an external object or person. It helps the robot respond to touch or manipulation, making it useful in applications like teleoperation or haptic feedback systems.
example: A surgeon using a robotic arm to perform surgery can adjust the arm's movements based on the pressure and force applied by their hands. This allows them to feel the resistance of tissues and organs, which enhances precision and control during delicate procedures.

definition: A census-derived tabular dataset widely used in fairness research despite known limitations.
related_terms: German Credit Dataset; Titanic Dataset; Yelp Dataset; Dataset Licence
student_friendly_explanation: The Adult Income Dataset is a collection of data about people's income levels, gathered from a census. It helps researchers study how different factors can affect income, but it has some issues that make it tricky to use.
example: Researchers might use this dataset to analyze how education level and occupation impact an individual's income, taking into account potential biases in the data.

definition: A policy gradient method using an advantage estimate from a learned value baseline.
related_terms: Soft Actor-Critic (SAC); DDPG; Deterministic Policy Gradient (DPG); TD3
student_friendly_explanation: Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) is a method used in artificial intelligence to teach machines how to make decisions. It combines the idea of learning from rewards (advantages) with a way to estimate values based on past experiences. This helps the machine improve its decision-making skills over time, making it more efficient at solving problems.
example: In a game where a robot learns to navigate through a maze, A2C can help the robot learn which actions lead to better outcomes by comparing the immediate benefits (advantages) of each action with the overall value of those actions based on previous experiences.

definition: Computing how much better an action was than average, the signal that drives policy gradient updates.
related_terms: Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE); Selective State Update; Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C); MAP Estimation
student_friendly_explanation: Advantage Estimation is a method used in machine learning to figure out how much better one action is compared to others. It helps algorithms learn which actions lead to better outcomes by comparing them to what would have happened if they had taken the average action.
example: In a reinforcement learning scenario, an agent learns to navigate a maze. The advantage estimation calculates how much more efficient each path is compared to the average path. This information guides the agent to choose paths that lead to quicker completion of the maze.

definition: Assigning an agent to actively find flaws in another agent's output.
related_terms: Self-Correction; Red Team Prompt; Automated Red Teaming; Diff Preview
