student_friendly_explanation: Deepfake detection is a method used to identify videos or audio clips that have been altered to look like real people but are actually fake. This technology analyzes the content to determine if it has been manipulated.
example: A deepfake detection system might analyze facial expressions, body movements, and voice patterns in a video to check if they match the original person's behavior. If the system detects inconsistencies, it can flag the video as a deepfake.

definition: An open-weight model family notable for efficient training techniques and strong reasoning results.
related_terms: Qwen; Falcon; Gemma; Flux
student_friendly_explanation: DeepSeek is an open-weight model family known for its effective training methods and impressive reasoning outcomes. These models learn and improve their performance through iterative processes, making them highly adaptable and capable of complex tasks.
example: For instance, DeepSeek can analyze large datasets and identify patterns more efficiently than traditional models, allowing it to make accurate predictions and classifications.

definition: A sensible baseline setting that works acceptably without tuning.
related_terms: Configuration Management; Configuration Sweep; Hyperparameter Configuration File; Baseline Model
student_friendly_explanation: Default configuration is a set of initial settings that work well enough for basic operations without needing to adjust them further. It's like having a basic recipe that gets you a good meal without needing to tweak every ingredient.
example: In training a machine learning model, a default configuration might be a set of hyperparameters (like learning rate and batch size) that have been found to perform well across various datasets, allowing the model to start learning effectively without extensive tuning.

definition: Automatically identifying flawed products on a production line from sensor or image data.
related_terms: Poaching Detection; Claim Detection; Signal Detection in Safety Data; Fraud Detection
student_friendly_explanation: Defect detection is a process where machines automatically spot mistakes in products as they come off a factory line using information from sensors or cameras.
example: A defect detection system might analyze images of car parts coming down an assembly line. If it detects a part that's not aligned properly, it can trigger a warning signal to stop the line and fix the issue before the defective product goes to market.

definition: The limit of what a parent agent permits a delegated one to do.
related_terms: Model Specification; Rate Limit; Worker Agent; Subagent
student_friendly_explanation: The delegation boundary is like a rule that limits what a main AI system (parent agent) can allow another smaller system (delegated agent) to do. It's about setting boundaries to control actions.
example: Imagine you have a big robot (parent agent) that controls a small helper robot (delegated agent). The delegation boundary decides how much the big robot can tell the small robot to do, such as moving an object or playing music, without overstepping its own limits.

definition: The process of forecasting and reconciling expected demand across an organization.
related_terms: Demand Sensing; Demand Response; Public Transit Optimization; Workforce Planning
student_friendly_explanation: Demand planning is like predicting how much of something will be needed in the future, and making sure everyone knows about it so they can prepare accordingly. It's like when you know there will be more people at a party next week, so you buy more food and drinks.
example: A grocery store uses demand planning to predict how much milk will be sold each day. They then adjust their supply chain to ensure they have enough milk on hand to meet customer needs without overstocking.

definition: Shifting electricity consumption in response to grid conditions and prices.
related_terms: Price Elasticity; Energy Grid Optimization; Item Response Theory (IRT); Demand Planning
student_friendly_explanation: Demand Response is about changing when you use electricity based on what the power grid needs at that time. It's like adjusting your shower timing to match the water supply, but for electricity.
example: During peak hours, a smart home system might automatically lower the temperature of the air conditioning to save energy, which helps the local power plant avoid using more expensive backup generators.

definition: An autoencoder trained to reconstruct clean inputs from corrupted ones, learning robust features.
related_terms: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE); Autoencoder Bottleneck; Contractive Autoencoder; Autoencoder Anomaly Detection
student_friendly_explanation: A Denoising Autoencoder is like a smart helper that learns to fix mistakes. Imagine you have a picture, but some parts of it are blurry or unclear. A Denoising Autoencoder can take this blurry picture and make it clear again, even if it's not perfect. It does this by understanding the important parts of the image and ignoring the noisy parts.
example: Consider a Denoising Autoencoder being used to improve images captured by a camera in low light conditions. The encoder takes the noisy image as input and tries to recreate a clearer version. This process helps the AI learn to recognize the essential features of an image, making it better at distinguishing between different objects.

definition: One iteration of a diffusion sampler that partially removes noise from the current estimate.
related_terms: Sampling Steps; Step Count Tuning; Sampler Comparison; Reverse Diffusion Process
student_friendly_explanation: The Denoising Step is one cycle in a process called a diffusion sampler. During this step, the sampler tries to remove some random errors (noise) from an initial guess (estimate) of something complex, like a picture or a model.
example: Imagine you have a blurry image, and you want to make it clearer. The Denoising Step would be like taking a guess at what the original clear image might look like, then making small adjustments to reduce the blur, trying to get closer to the true image.

definition: Frequent feedback that guides learning at every step but risks encoding unintended shortcuts.
related_terms: Reward Function; Reward Misspecification; Reward; Sparse Reward Problem
student_friendly_explanation: Dense reward is frequent feedback that helps you learn at each step of your journey, but it can sometimes lead you down unintended paths if not used carefully.
example: Imagine you're training an AI model to recognize cats in images. Dense reward might tell you right away if the model is correct or incorrect, but if the feedback is too specific (e.g., pointing out every single pixel), it could create shortcuts that aren't always the best way to improve the model's performance.

definition: Clustering that defines groups as regions of high point density separated by sparse areas.
related_terms: Noise Point; Spectral Clustering; Consensus Clustering; DBSCAN
student_friendly_explanation: Density-based clustering is a method where we group data points into clusters based on their density in the space. Points within a cluster are close to each other, while points in different clusters are far apart. This approach doesn't require specifying the number of clusters beforehand, making it more flexible.
example: Imagine you have a set of data points scattered across a map. In density-based clustering, we look at the local density around each point. If a point has many nearby neighbors (high density), it's likely part of a cluster. Conversely, if a point has few neighbors (low density), it might be an outlier or separate cluster.

definition: Learning the probability distribution that generated observed data.
related_terms: Histogram Density Estimation; Score Matching; Capability Density; Confidence Estimation for Routing
student_friendly_explanation: Density estimation is like guessing the shape of a cloud based on scattered raindrops. It helps us understand how likely it is to find an event at any point in space or time.
example: Imagine you have a bag of marbles of different colors. By looking at the marbles you've already drawn out, density estimation can help you guess how many red, blue, green, etc., marbles might be left in the bag.

definition: A representation linking each word to its syntactic head, capturing grammatical relations directly.
related_terms: Dependency Parsing; Universal Dependencies (UD); Head Word; Syntactic Ambiguity
student_friendly_explanation: A dependency tree is a visual way to show how words in a sentence relate to each other based on their grammatical roles. Each word points to the one it's directly connected to, which is called its 'head.' This helps us understand the structure of the sentence and how different parts work together.
example: In the sentence 'The cat chased the mouse,' the dependency tree would have 'cat' pointing to 'chased' and 'mouse' pointing back to 'chased.' Here, 'chased' is the head of both 'cat' and 'mouse,' showing that 'chased' is the main verb and 'cat' and 'mouse' are its direct objects.

definition: The task of predicting the distance from the camera to each pixel in an image. Monocular depth estimation uses a single image; stereo methods use two views. Deep learning models like MiDaS and DPT produce dense depth maps from single images. Critical for autonomous driving, robotics, and AR applications.
related_terms: 3D Vision; Point Cloud; Monocular Depth Estimation; Depth Map
student_friendly_explanation: Depth estimation is about figuring out how far away objects are in a picture taken by a camera. It's like guessing how close things are without touching them. We can do this using just one picture (monocular) or by looking at two different pictures (stereo). Some smart computer programs can even make a detailed map showing distances everywhere in the picture.
example: Imagine you have a camera taking a picture of your room. Depth estimation helps the computer understand how far each object in the picture is from the camera. This way, it can tell you if the bookcase is closer to the wall than the table.

definition: A per-pixel record of distance from the camera to the scene.
related_terms: Depth Completion; Disparity Map; Depth Estimation; Metric Depth
student_friendly_explanation: A depth map is like taking a snapshot of how far away different parts of an image are from the camera. It records distances pixel by pixel, giving us a detailed view of the scene's geometry.
example: Imagine you have a camera taking pictures of a room. A depth map would show you how close or far each object in the picture is from the camera, helping you understand the layout and dimensions of the room.

definition: Content substantially based on an existing work, raising rights questions.
related_terms: Attribution of Generated Work; Commercial Use Rights; Consent for Training; Model Output Ownership
student_friendly_explanation: A derivative work is a new version of an existing work where it has been significantly changed or improved. This can include adding new features, fixing bugs, or translating it into different languages. However, this change means that the original creator may have rights over the new work, which can sometimes lead to legal issues.
example: When a software company modifies an open-source library to add new features and fixes, it creates a derivative work. If someone wants to use this modified version, they need to get permission from the original creators, as they might own the copyright.

definition: The table stacking every example's feature vector as a row, the standard input to a fitting routine.
related_terms: Stacking; Affinity Matrix; Word Co-Occurrence Matrix; Support Vector Regression (SVR)
student_friendly_explanation: A design matrix is like a spreadsheet where each row represents a different data sample, and each column shows a specific characteristic or feature of that sample. This matrix helps machine learning algorithms understand the patterns in the data.
example: Imagine you're analyzing images of handwritten digits. Each row in your design matrix could represent an image, and columns might show pixel intensity levels at different positions on the image. This way, the algorithm can learn to recognize patterns in the images based on their visual characteristics.

definition: A second generation stage adding fine texture to an otherwise complete image.
related_terms: Refinement Pass; Face Enhancement; Prompt Enhancement; Hierarchical Generation
student_friendly_explanation: Detail Enhancement Pass is a process where a computer algorithm adds more subtle details to an image that has already been mostly completed. It focuses on making the image look more realistic and less pixelated.
example: During the Detail Enhancement Pass, an AI algorithm might add finer textures to a partially drawn portrait, such as shading around the eyes and lips to make the face appear more lifelike.

definition: How often a synthetic content detector is right, which is often lower than claimed.
related_terms: Base Rate Problem in Detection; Invisible Watermark; FAST Detector; Two-Stage Detector
student_friendly_explanation: Detector reliability refers to how accurately a synthetic content detector identifies what it's supposed to find. It's often less effective than advertised because it can sometimes mistake non-synthetic content for synthetic.
example: A content detection system might flag a document as containing copyrighted material when it actually doesn't, due to its imperfect ability to distinguish between genuine and fake content.

definition: Evaluation configured so repeated runs produce identical results.
related_terms: Score Variance Across Runs; Task Decomposition in Evaluation; Evaluation Pipeline; Continuous Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: Deterministic evaluation means that when you run an experiment or test multiple times, you get the same results every time. It's like flipping a coin; if it's deterministic, you'll always get heads or tails, no matter how many times you flip it.
example: Imagine you're testing a new algorithm for image recognition. In a deterministic evaluation, running the test 10 times will consistently yield the same accuracy score, whereas in a non-deterministic (randomized) evaluation, the scores might vary each time.

definition: A measure of conversational quality across turns rather than single responses.
related_terms: Dialogue State Tracking (DST); Conversational Memory; Open-Domain Dialogue; Task-Oriented Dialogue
student_friendly_explanation: Dialogue Evaluation Metrics (DEMs) are tools used to assess the overall quality of conversations between systems or humans, focusing on how well different parts of a dialogue flow together rather than just individual responses.
example: Imagine you're chatting with a virtual assistant about your upcoming project. A DEM could evaluate not just the quality of your last response but also how well it fits with the assistant's previous turn, ensuring a smooth conversation.

definition: A behavioural or physiological indicator derived from device sensor data.
related_terms: Digital Therapeutic; Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI); Exclusion Risk in Digital Systems; Wearable Health Data
student_friendly_explanation: A digital biomarker is a signal from your body that can be read by machines, like sensors on your clothes or in your home. It's like a message your body sends out, but it's captured by tech tools instead of words.
example: Imagine you have a special shirt with tiny sensors that track how you move and how your heart beats. These sensors send information to a computer, which then looks at patterns in your movements and heartbeat to see if there might be something going on inside your body that needs attention.

definition: A photorealistic, AI-driven virtual human representation engaging in real-time conversation with natural expressions. Combines computer graphics, facial animation, speech synthesis, and conversational AI. Applications: customer service, healthcare, entertainment.
related_terms: Computer Vision (CV); Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI); Exclusion Risk in Digital Systems; Digital Biomarker
student_friendly_explanation: A digital human is an AI-driven virtual human that looks and acts like a real person through advanced technology. It uses computer graphics and facial animation to create lifelike appearances, and speech synthesis to produce natural-sounding voices. These virtual humans can interact with people in real time and show emotions through their expressions.
example: A digital human assistant in a customer service chatbot, which can understand your questions, respond naturally, and show empathy through its animated face and voice.

definition: Shared foundational systems such as identity and payments that many services build on.
related_terms: Public Service Delivery; Exclusion Risk in Digital Systems; Digital Biomarker; Digital Therapeutic
student_friendly_explanation: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) refers to shared foundational systems like identity and payments that many digital services rely on.
example: A common example of DPI is the use of a single national ID system that allows citizens to access various online services securely and efficiently.

definition: Software delivering an evidence-based clinical intervention, sometimes regulated as a device.
related_terms: Therapeutic Alliance; Digital Biomarker; Mental Health Support Tool; Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI)
student_friendly_explanation: Digital therapeutics are computer programs designed to help treat medical conditions using scientific evidence. They can be regulated like medical devices if necessary.
example: A digital therapeutic app that uses machine learning to analyze sleep patterns and provides personalized sleep recommendations based on this analysis.

definition: A morphological operation expanding bright regions, closing small gaps.
related_terms: Morphological Operation; Closing; Erosion; Opening
student_friendly_explanation: Dilation is a process in computer vision where we expand bright areas in an image, effectively filling small gaps between them.
example: Imagine you have a black-and-white image with some white spots representing objects. Dilation makes those spots bigger by adding white pixels around them, which helps connect isolated objects.

definition: Publishing results broken out by subgroup rather than pooled.
related_terms: Best-of-N Reporting; Inference Budget Reporting; Error Bar Reporting; Multi-Metric Reporting
student_friendly_explanation: Disaggregated reporting is when we separate and show the results of our study based on different groups or categories instead of just looking at them all together as one big group. This way, we can see how each part of the study performed better.
example: Imagine you did an experiment where you tested different types of soil for plant growth. Instead of just saying 'this soil helped plants grow', disaggregated reporting would tell us which type of soil worked best for which kind of plant, and how much it helped.

definition: A finite set of possible actions, such as the buttons of a game controller.
related_terms: Parameterized Action; Action Discretization; Multi-Discrete Action; Action Masking
student_friendly_explanation: In reinforcement learning, a discrete action space is a collection of possible actions that can be taken, like pressing different buttons on a game controller. Each action in this space is chosen from a predefined set, and the learner doesn't have to make continuous decisions.
example: Imagine playing a video game where you can move left, right, jump, or shoot. These actions form a discrete action space because you can only take one of these actions at a time, and there's no middle ground between them.

definition: A classifier modelling the boundary or conditional label probability directly without describing the inputs.
related_terms: Discriminative Model; Generative Classifier; Evaluation of binary classifiers; Maximum Margin Classifier
student_friendly_explanation: A discriminative classifier is a type of machine learning model that tries to find a decision boundary between different classes. Unlike generative models, it doesn't need to understand the underlying distribution of the data; instead, it focuses on directly predicting the class labels based on the input features.
example: For instance, consider a spam email classifier. This model learns from examples of emails labeled as 'spam' or 'not spam' and then predicts whether new emails are spam or not based on their content and structure, without needing to know the probability distribution of all possible email features.

definition: The network in an adversarial model that tries to distinguish real data from generated samples.
related_terms: Discriminator Overfitting; Adaptive Discriminator Augmentation; Generative Adversarial Network (GAN); Adversarial Loss
student_friendly_explanation: A discriminator is like a judge in a game of classification. It's a part of a system that tries to tell the difference between real things and things that were made up. In artificial intelligence, it helps decide if something is genuine or fake.
example: Imagine you have a magic box that can create pictures. A discriminator would look at both real photos and the ones created by the magic box and try to figure out which ones are real and which ones are fake. This way, it helps improve the magic box's ability to make better pictures.

definition: A per-pixel record of horizontal shift between stereo views, inversely proportional to depth.
related_terms: Depth Map; Stereo Matching; Depth Estimation; Depth Completion
student_friendly_explanation: A disparity map is like a special picture that shows how different parts of an image look when you have two cameras looking at the same scene from slightly different angles. It tells us how far away objects are by recording how much the pixels move between the two images. Closer objects make bigger changes than farther ones.
example: Imagine you have two cameras taking pictures of a room. A disparity map would show which parts of the room look closer and which look farther based on how the pixels move between the two images.

definition: Monitoring incoming data for changes that would invalidate a deployed model's assumptions.
related_terms: Label Shift; Covariate Shift; Mean Shift; Importance Weighting for Shift
student_friendly_explanation: Distribution shift detection is like watching for changes in the type of cookies arriving at a cookie factory. If the types of cookies suddenly change (like if chocolate chip cookies start appearing instead of oatmeal ones), it might make the cookie-sorting machine (our model) work less well. This helps us know when our machine (model) might need an update.
example: Imagine you have a model that predicts which students will pass a difficult exam based on their study habits. Over time, the distribution of study habits (the 'distribution') shifts because some students start using different methods (like group study instead of individual study). Distribution shift detection would notice this change and alert you that your model might not perform as well now.

definition: One unit of text in a corpus, such as an article, email, or web page.
related_terms: Retrieval Corpus; Multi-Page Document Understanding; Document Classification Pipeline; Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)
student_friendly_explanation: A document is a single piece of text found within a collection of texts called a corpus. This could be anything like a blog post, a research paper, or even a tweet. In the context of artificial intelligence, understanding documents is crucial for various tasks.
example: When you search for information on a topic using a search engine, it analyzes documents from websites, emails, and other sources to find relevant content. This process involves breaking down the text into smaller units, which helps in understanding the overall meaning and relevance.

definition: AI systems understanding and extracting information from documents including PDFs, forms, invoices, and contracts. Combines OCR, layout analysis, table extraction, and key-value extraction. Models like LayoutLM process both text and visual layout.
related_terms: Information Extraction (IE); Intelligent Document Processing (IDP); Invoice Processing; Clause Extraction
student_friendly_explanation: Document AI is a technology that allows AI systems to understand and extract information from various types of documents such as PDFs, forms, invoices, and contracts. It uses techniques like Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to read text, layout analysis to understand the structure of the document, and key-value extraction to identify specific pieces of information.
example: A document AI system can analyze an invoice PDF and automatically extract the invoice number, date, total amount, and other details, making it easier for businesses to manage their financial records.

definition: Routing incoming documents to the correct processing path by type.
related_terms: Inverse Document Frequency (IDF); Document; Text Classification; Multi-Page Document Understanding
student_friendly_explanation: The document classification pipeline is like sorting mail into different folders based on its content. It takes incoming documents and decides which way to send them next, depending on what they say.
example: Imagine you have a pile of emails. A document classification pipeline would look at each email's text and decide if it should go into the 'spam' folder, the 'important' folder, or the 'regular' folder based on keywords and phrases it finds.

definition: Identifying forged or altered identity and financial documents.
related_terms: Fraud Detection; Fraud Detection in Public Programmes; Intelligent Document Processing (IDP); AI in Finance
student_friendly_explanation: Document fraud detection is about finding fake or changed documents, like ID cards or bank statements, to make sure we're dealing with real people and money.
example: A document fraud detection system might analyze a photo of a driver's license. It checks if the photo matches the person's face using facial recognition technology.

definition: Adjusting scores so long documents are not unfairly favoured by having more term matches.
related_terms: Pivoted Length Normalization; Chunk Retrieval; Document Static Features; Dirichlet Smoothing
student_friendly_explanation: Document Length Normalization is a technique used in Information Retrieval to make sure that longer documents aren't given an unfair advantage because they have more words to match search queries. This is done by adjusting the scores of documents based on their length, ensuring that shorter documents aren't penalized just because they contain fewer terms.
example: Imagine you're searching for information about 'Artificial Intelligence' using a search engine. If a document is very long (say, 5000 words) and another document is short (say, 1000 words), the search engine might score the long document higher simply because it has more terms to match your query. Document Length Normalization would adjust these scores so that both documents are considered fairly.

definition: Query-independent signals such as popularity, freshness, and quality.
related_terms: Document Length Normalization; Index Freshness; Freshness Ranking; Chunk Retrieval
student_friendly_explanation: Document static features are signals about a document that don't change over time, like how popular it is, how new it is, and how good it is. These features help search engines understand documents better without needing to look at the text itself.
example: A document's freshness feature might be used to rank a recent research paper higher than an older one, even if both papers have similar content.

definition: Manipulating a web page through its document structure rather than simulated clicks.
related_terms: Indirect Prompt Injection; Web Agent; Browser Automation; Episodic Agent Memory
student_friendly_explanation: DOM (Document Object Model) interaction involves changing parts of a webpage without using typical mouse clicks. Instead, it uses JavaScript to directly manipulate the HTML elements on the page.
example: A script can change the text color of an element on a webpage by accessing the element's ID and setting its CSS style property.

definition: Adjusting a model trained in one distribution to perform well in a related but different one.
related_terms: Domain Generalization; Unsupervised Domain Adaptation; Test-Time Adaptation (TTA); Domain Weighting
student_friendly_explanation: Domain adaptation is like training a smart helper to understand new situations better after it has already learned from old ones. Imagine you have a robot that can recognize cats in photos. If you want it to also recognize dogs, you tweak its learning process to make it more flexible, so it can adapt to new types of images without forgetting what it already knows.
example: Suppose you train a machine learning model to classify images of cats and dogs. After some time, you notice it performs well on the training set but struggles with a new dataset of images taken under different lighting conditions. Domain adaptation techniques allow you to fine-tune this model, making it more robust against variations in the environment, so it can still accurately classify cats and dogs even when the lighting changes.

definition: A measure of real-world outcomes rather than intermediate model quality.
related_terms: Efficiency Metric; Metric Definition Drift; Scale-Free Metric; Scale-Dependent Metric
student_friendly_explanation: Downstream impact metrics are tools used to assess the practical effects of a model or system, focusing on real-world results rather than just the quality of the model itself.
example: For instance, when training a machine learning model to predict housing prices, a downstream impact metric might evaluate how accurately the model predicts actual sales prices, rather than just measuring the model's accuracy in making predictions.

definition: A regularization technique where randomly selected neurons are temporarily ignored during training by setting their outputs to zero. This prevents co-adaptation of neurons and acts as an implicit ensemble of exponentially many sub-networks. At inference time, all neurons are used but outputs are scaled. Dropout is one of the simplest and most effective regularization methods for neural networks.
related_terms: Regularization; Overfitting; Neural Network (NN); Inference
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're building a big neural network brain. Sometimes, this brain can get too good at remembering everything, even things it shouldn't. Dropout is like playing a game where we pretend some of our brain's neurons don't exist for a while. We pick random neurons and make them forget what they know. This helps the brain learn better and not overthink things.
example: When training a neural network, we might use dropout to prevent it from memorizing the training data instead of learning general patterns. During training, we randomly turn off some neurons, making the network think it has fewer connections than it really does. This makes the network more robust and less likely to overfit to the training data.

definition: Executing an agent's plan without applying effects so its intentions can be reviewed.
related_terms: Dry Run Verification; Plan Cost Model; Side Effect; Plan Execution
student_friendly_explanation: A dry run mode is when you go through the steps of running an AI agent's plan without actually making any changes or affecting the environment. This allows you to check if the plan makes sense and what it would do before actually executing it.
example: Imagine you have a robot that needs to navigate a maze. In dry run mode, you could simulate the robot moving through the maze without actually moving it, just to see if it follows the correct path and turns at the right spots.

definition: Executing a plan in a mode that reports intended effects without applying them.
related_terms: Dry Run Mode; Verification Step; Verification Before Completion; Plan Cost Model
student_friendly_explanation: A dry run verification is when you go through a process step-by-step to see what it would do, but don't actually make any changes or use resources. It's like practicing a dance routine before performing it in front of an audience.
example: Imagine you're writing a program to sort data. A dry run verification would allow you to check if your sorting algorithm works correctly by running it on a small set of test data, ensuring it sorts the data as expected without making any actual changes to the real data.

definition: Near-identical records split across train and test, inflating measured accuracy.
related_terms: Temporal Leakage; Pipeline Leakage; Target Leakage; Surrogate Split
student_friendly_explanation: Duplicate Leakage happens when similar data is spread between training and testing sets, making it seem like the model performs better than it really does.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of emails labeled as spam or not spam. If some emails are accidentally duplicated across both training and testing sets, the model might look very good on the test set because it has seen those emails before, even though it hasn't learned from them.

definition: The failure mode where a unit outputs zero for all inputs and receives no gradient thereafter.
related_terms: Parametric ReLU (PReLU); Zero Initialization Problem; Leaky ReLU; He Initialization
student_friendly_explanation: When using a ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function, if a neuron's output is always zero for any input, it means that neuron will never learn anything from the data because it doesn't get any updates. This happens when the weights of the neuron are initialized to zero or when the network is trained without proper initialization.
example: Imagine a neuron with a ReLU activation function. If the weights of this neuron are initialized to zero, then for any input, the neuron will output zero. As a result, the neuron will not receive any gradient during backpropagation, meaning it won't adjust its weights, and thus, it will remain stuck at zero output.

definition: Automatically adjusting the loss scale in response to detected overflow during mixed-precision training.
related_terms: Loss Scaling; Loss Spike; Loss Surface Visualization; Gradient Underflow
student_friendly_explanation: Dynamic Loss Scaling is a technique used in deep learning training, especially when using mixed precision. It automatically adjusts the loss scale based on whether the loss value might cause an overflow (when it gets too big). This helps prevent numerical issues that can occur during training.
example: Imagine you're trying to train a neural network with both floating-point and half-precision numbers. If the loss value becomes extremely large, Dynamic Loss Scaling will automatically increase the loss scale to make the loss more manageable, thus avoiding potential overflow errors.

definition: Adjusting prices automatically in response to demand, inventory, and competition.
related_terms: Insurance Pricing Model; Demand Response; Price Elasticity; Demand Planning
student_friendly_explanation: Dynamic pricing is like magic pricing that changes automatically based on how many people want something, how much you have left to sell, and what your competitors are doing. It's kind of like when you adjust the price of your lemonade depending on how thirsty people are and how much you still have.
example: A ride-sharing service might lower the price of a ride if it notices that more people are asking for rides than usual, and it has some empty cars available. This helps them make sure everyone gets a ride without wasting resources.

definition: Input dimensions that vary at runtime, which complicate compilation and kernel selection.
related_terms: Static Shape; Just-in-Time Compilation (JIT); Shape Polymorphism; Layer-Wise Learning Dynamics
student_friendly_explanation: Dynamic Shape refers to input dimensions that change during runtime, making it harder to compile code and select kernels efficiently.
example: In a neural network, if the number of input features varies based on user input, the Dynamic Shape allows the model to adapt without recompiling, but this can slow down performance compared to Static Shape where dimensions are fixed.

definition: The income effect on people whose work generative systems substitute for.
related_terms: Consent for Training; Compensation Model; Opt-Out Mechanism; Hash Matching for Known Harm
student_friendly_explanation: When artificial intelligence systems replace human creators' work, it can reduce their income. This is known as economic harm to creators.
example: A music creation software might replace a composer's income if it generates music similar to what the composer creates. This could lead to a decrease in the composer's earnings.

definition: Running AI models directly on edge devices (smartphones, IoT sensors, cameras) rather than in cloud data centers. Edge AI provides lower latency, reduced bandwidth usage, improved privacy, and offline capability. Trade-offs include limited compute power, memory constraints, and the need for model compression techniques like quantization and pruning.
related_terms: Model Compression; Quantization; Pruning; Compute
student_friendly_explanation: Edge AI allows running AI models on devices like smartphones and IoT sensors instead of sending all data to cloud servers. This makes processes faster and more secure, but it also limits what can be done due to device limitations.
example: A smartwatch uses edge AI to analyze heart rate data locally without needing to send information to a distant server, providing immediate health insights while conserving battery.

definition: The minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions to turn one string into another.
related_terms: Levenshtein Distance; Edit Generalization; Edit Locality; Ripple Effect of Edits
student_friendly_explanation: Edit Distance is a way to measure how different two strings are by counting the minimum number of operations needed to change one string into the other. These operations include inserting, deleting, or substituting characters.
example: To transform the word 'kitten' into 'sitting', you need to make 2 changes: replace 'k' with 's', and add 'g' at the end. This process shows that the Edit Distance between 'kitten' and 'sitting' is 2.

definition: Software supporting teaching, learning, and assessment.
related_terms: Learning Analytics; Accessibility Technology; Language Learning Application; Personalized Learning Content
student_friendly_explanation: Educational technology refers to software tools designed to enhance teaching methods, facilitate learning processes, and support assessments. It includes various applications that can adapt to individual learners' needs and track their progress.
example: A personalized learning platform that adjusts the difficulty level of math problems based on a student's performance, providing additional resources when needed and offering more challenging questions as the student progresses.

definition: The portion of a long context a model actually uses well, often shorter than its nominal limit.
related_terms: Effective Context Utilization; Effective Depth; Infinite Context Approximation; Effective Receptive Field
student_friendly_explanation: Effective Context is the part of a longer input that a model can understand and use effectively. It's usually smaller than what the model is designed to handle, like a model that can process up to 10 words but only uses the first 3 or 4 words well.
example: Imagine you have a very smart AI system that can analyze text. This system has a limit of understanding up to 10 words at once. However, it only truly understands the first 3 or 4 words of any given sentence. So, if you give it a sentence like 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog', it will understand the first few words better than the rest.

definition: A measure combining quality with the resources required to achieve it.
related_terms: Downstream Impact Metric; Metric Definition Drift; Scale-Free Metric; Scale-Dependent Metric
student_friendly_explanation: An efficiency metric is a way to evaluate how well something works while also considering how much effort or resources were needed to make it work. It combines both the quality of the result and the amount of resources used to get there.
example: For a machine learning model, an efficiency metric might be the accuracy (quality) of predictions along with the time it takes to train the model (resources). A good model should have high accuracy but also be trained quickly.

definition: A convolutional family scaling depth, width, and resolution together according to a compound rule.
related_terms: Width Scaling Rule; Wide ResNet; ResNeXt; S4
student_friendly_explanation: EfficientNet is a type of neural network model that adjusts its depth, width, and resolution simultaneously based on a specific set of rules. This allows it to efficiently learn from data without needing as many parameters as other models.
example: Imagine you have a deep neural network that can classify images. EfficientNet might start with a smaller number of layers and gradually add more layers as it learns more complex patterns in the data. This way, it can capture both fine details and broader features effectively.

definition: Sorting incoming correspondence by urgency and required action.
related_terms: Triage Chatbot; Triage Protocol; Claims Triage; Triage System
student_friendly_explanation: Email triage is like sorting your inbox into different piles based on how important the emails are and what you need to do with them.
example: A triage chatbot might prioritize emails from clients who have urgent questions over those from colleagues who just want to check in. It sorts them into 'urgent' and 'normal' categories, then directs them to the appropriate person for action.

definition: A dense vector representation of data (words, sentences, images, or other entities) in a continuous vector space where similar items are mapped to nearby points. Embeddings capture semantic relationships: the classic example is that vector('king') - vector('man') + vector('woman') ≈ vector('queen'). Cosine similarity typically outperforms Euclidean distance for comparing embeddings.
related_terms: Vector Database; Word2Vec; Semantic Search; Vector Space
student_friendly_explanation: Embeddings are like special codes that computers use to understand words, sentences, or even pictures. These codes are arranged in a big space where similar things are close together. It's kind of like how you can find your favorite toy near your bed because it's similar to other toys you like.
example: Imagine you have a codebook where each word has its own unique code. If we take the code for 'king' and subtract the code for 'man', then add the code for 'woman', we get a new code that's very close to the code for 'queen'. This shows how similar words can be grouped together.

definition: The size of the vector representing each token or item.
related_terms: Head Dimension; Embedding; Multimodal Embedding; Hidden Dimension
student_friendly_explanation: The embedding dimension is the number of dimensions (or numbers) used to represent each word or piece of data in a model. It's like giving each word a unique set of numbers to help the model understand and process it better.
example: In a neural network, each word in a sentence might be represented as a vector with a certain number of dimensions. For instance, if the embedding dimension is 100, then each word could be represented as a 100-dimensional vector, where each number in the vector helps the model learn different aspects of the word.

definition: Change in embedding distribution over time that degrades a fixed vector index or downstream model.
related_terms: Concept Drift; Matryoshka Embedding; Tied Embeddings Tradeoff; Metric Space Embedding
student_friendly_explanation: Embedding drift is when the meaning of words or data changes over time, which can make it harder for models to understand and use this information correctly.
example: Imagine you have a set of word embeddings that represent different words in a way that captures their meanings. If these representations change gradually over time, it's like the words start to mean slightly different things. This can confuse machine learning models that were trained on the old embeddings, making them less effective at tasks like translation or classification.

definition: A learned dense vector per category, letting a model discover similarity between levels.
related_terms: Category utility; Rare Category; Embedding Drift; Target Encoding
student_friendly_explanation: In machine learning, an embedding layer for categories is a way to represent different categories as dense vectors. These vectors help the model understand how similar one category is to another, making it easier to analyze data.
example: For instance, if we have categories like 'Artificial Intelligence', 'Computer Vision', and 'Natural Language Processing', the embedding layer would assign each category a unique vector. This allows the model to recognize that 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'Computer Vision' might be more similar than 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'Natural Language Processing'.

definition: A model whose purpose is producing vectors for retrieval and similarity rather than generating text.
related_terms: E5 Embedding Model; BGE Embedding Model; Instructor Embedding; GTE Embedding Model
student_friendly_explanation: An embedding model transforms textual information into numerical vectors. Unlike models that generate text, it focuses on creating vectors for retrieval and measuring similarities between them.
example: For instance, an embedding model might convert the sentence 'Artificial intelligence is fascinating' into a vector representation. This vector could then be used to compare this sentence with others, even if they use different words but convey similar meanings.

definition: The property that vector differences between embeddings can encode analogical relationships.
related_terms: Analogy Task; Cross-Lingual Embedding; Word Embedding; Sentence Embedding
student_friendly_explanation: Embedding space arithmetic refers to the ability of embedding vectors to represent analogies between words or phrases in a way that vector differences can capture these relationships.
example: In an embedding space, if 'king' - 'man' + 'woman' = 'queen', this arithmetic operation shows that the embedding space can encode the analogy between 'man' and 'woman' as opposites, leading to the expected result 'queen'.

definition: A control that immediately removes power or halts motion in a hazardous situation.
related_terms: Safety-Rated Monitored Stop; Capture Point; Emergency Change; Stop Sequence
student_friendly_explanation: The Emergency Stop is a safety feature that quickly cuts off power or stops movement when something dangerous happens. It's like pressing the 'stop' button on a car if you're about to crash into something.
example: In a robot that moves around, if it detects an obstacle, the Emergency Stop will instantly halt the robot's movement to prevent accidents.

definition: Rules governing the use of automated tools in hiring and promotion.
related_terms: Bias in Hiring Algorithms; Business rules engine; Sectoral Regulation; AI Regulation
student_friendly_explanation: Employment Decision Regulations are guidelines that dictate how companies can use automated systems to make decisions about hiring new employees or promoting existing ones.
example: A company uses an AI algorithm to evaluate job applications. This algorithm is subject to Employment Decision Regulations, which ensure it doesn't unfairly discriminate against candidates based on race, gender, or other factors.

definition: A neural network architecture where an encoder processes the input into a fixed representation and a decoder generates the output from this representation. The architecture is fundamental to machine translation, image segmentation (U-Net), and generative models (VAE). Modern encoder-decoder models use transformer attention for both components.
related_terms: Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq); U-Net; Transformer; Encoder
student_friendly_explanation: An encoder-decoder model is a type of neural network that takes an input and converts it into a fixed format, which is then used to generate an output. Imagine you have a secret message (input) that needs to be understood by another person (output). The encoder turns your message into a universal code (fixed format), and the decoder decodes this code back into understandable language (output). This process is crucial for tasks like translating languages or creating images.
example: In a machine translation task, the encoder might take a sentence in one language and convert it into a series of numbers or vectors. Then, the decoder uses these numbers to generate the equivalent sentence in another language, effectively translating the meaning without needing to know the exact words.

definition: A segmentation architecture downsampling to capture context then upsampling to restore detail.
related_terms: Image Segmentation; Semantic Segmentation; Motion Segmentation; Zero-Shot Segmentation
student_friendly_explanation: Encoder-Decoder Segmentation is a method used in computer vision where we first reduce the information (downsampling) to understand the overall structure of an image, and then we increase it again (upsampling) to see the details clearly. It's like zooming out to see the big picture and then zooming in to see the small parts.
example: Imagine you have a photo of a city skyline. First, the encoder segmentations might look at the broad strokes of buildings and streets, capturing the general layout. Then, the decoder segmentations would focus on the finer details, such as individual windows and signs, making the image clearer and more detailed.

definition: Balancing electricity supply and demand across a network in real time.
related_terms: Demand Response; Predictive Grid Maintenance; Inventory Optimization; Building Energy Management
student_friendly_explanation: Energy Grid Optimization is about making sure there's always enough electricity to power all the devices and appliances in a city while using as little energy as possible. It's like managing a big game of musical chairs, but instead of people, it's electricity and devices.
example: Imagine a smart city where buildings can adjust their heating and cooling based on the weather forecast and the number of people inside. This helps save energy and reduces costs.

definition: The consequence applied when content or an account violates policy.
related_terms: Appeals in Moderation; Action Item Extraction; Predictive Policing Critique; Next Best Action (NBA)
student_friendly_explanation: An enforcement action is like a consequence you get when something you did doesn't follow the rules set by the group or community. It's what happens when someone breaks the rules, like getting a warning or a punishment.
example: In a social media platform, if a user posts inappropriate content, the platform might take an enforcement action such as removing the post and possibly suspending the user's account for a certain period.

definition: A measure of how much a user interacts, which must be interpreted carefully as a quality signal.
related_terms: Text Quality Metric; Dialogue Evaluation Metric; Writing Assistance Metric; Honorifics
student_friendly_explanation: An engagement metric is a way to quantify how actively users engage with something, like a website or a chatbot conversation. It's important because it helps us understand if people are using the system effectively.
example: In an online course platform, an engagement metric might look at how often students log in, read articles, or participate in discussions. This can help instructors see which parts of the course are most popular and where they might need to improve.

definition: The degree to which ensemble members make different errors, the property that makes averaging help.
related_terms: Weighted Ensemble; Ensemble Learning; Ensemble Distillation; Snapshot Ensemble
student_friendly_explanation: Ensemble diversity refers to the variety of mistakes made by individual models within an ensemble. This diversity helps improve overall performance because it allows the ensemble to capture different aspects of the data, reducing the risk of overfitting.
example: Imagine you have three machine learning models predicting house prices. Model A might often underestimate prices, Model B might often overestimate, and Model C might be quite accurate but occasionally miss the mark. By combining their predictions, you can get a more reliable estimate than any single model could provide on its own.

definition: A technique that combines multiple models to produce predictions more accurate and robust than any single model. Methods include bagging (Random Forest), boosting (XGBoost, AdaBoost), and stacking. Ensemble methods reduce variance, bias, or both.
related_terms: Random Forest; Gradient Boosting; Bagging; Bias-Variance in Ensembles
student_friendly_explanation: Ensemble learning is when you use many different machine learning models together to make better predictions than any single model could make on its own. It's like having a team of experts working on a problem instead of relying on one person.
example: Imagine you have a group of friends trying to guess the number of candies in a jar. Each friend makes their own guess. If you take the average of all their guesses, it's likely to be closer to the actual number than any individual guess would be. This is similar to ensemble learning, where multiple machine learning models work together to improve the accuracy of predictions.

definition: Retrieval across an organization's internal documents, messages, and systems.
related_terms: Document Summarization in Enterprise; Translation for Global Operations; Access Control in Retrieval; Intelligent Document Processing (IDP)
student_friendly_explanation: Enterprise search is like having a super smart search engine that can look through all the information your company has, including emails, files, and other digital stuff, to find what you need quickly.
example: Imagine you work at a big tech company. If you need to find a specific document about a project, the enterprise search system can scan through all the documents on your computer network and show you the one you want, even if it's buried deep in a folder.

definition: Choosing which real-world entity a name refers to among candidates sharing that name.
related_terms: Entity Grid; Nested Entity Recognition; Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD); Named Entity Substitution
student_friendly_explanation: Entity disambiguation is about figuring out which specific thing a name points to when there could be multiple possibilities. For example, if you see 'New York' in a text, it might refer to the city or the state, and the system helps decide which one.
example: In a document about New York, an entity disambiguation system would look at context clues like 'the Big Apple' to determine whether 'New York' refers to the city or the state.

definition: Connecting a mention in text to a specific entry in a knowledge base.
related_terms: Nested Entity Recognition; Entity Grid; Claim-Evidence Linking; Entity Disambiguation
student_friendly_explanation: Entity Linking is like connecting a name or term mentioned in a text to a specific entry in a database of information. Imagine you have a list of names and addresses, and you want to find out which one belongs to whom. That's what Entity Linking does, but for more complex data like people, places, and things in texts.
example: In a news article about a scientist, Entity Linking can connect the scientist's name to their profile in a scientific database, linking the text to real-world information.

definition: A tree splitting measure based on information content, closely tracking Gini impurity in practice.
related_terms: Split Criterion; Gini Impurity; Gini Importance; Entropy Minimization
student_friendly_explanation: The entropy criterion is a method used in machine learning to decide which feature to split data on during the creation of decision trees. It measures how much information we gain about the target variable by splitting the dataset into subsets. This measure helps create more homogeneous groups of data points, making it easier to predict outcomes.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of emails labeled as spam or not spam. Using the entropy criterion, you can determine the best email attribute (like the presence of certain words) to split the data. This way, you can create a decision tree where each branch represents a different email characteristic, leading to better predictions.

definition: The external system a reinforcement learning agent interacts with and receives observations and rewards from.
related_terms: Reinforcement Learning (RL); Unsupervised Environment Design (UED); Observation; Vectorized Environment
student_friendly_explanation: In reinforcement learning, the environment is like a playground where an AI agent learns by interacting with it. It provides the agent with information about its state (observations) and feedback in the form of rewards, which helps the agent improve its performance over time.
example: Imagine you're playing a video game where your score (reward) changes based on your actions. The game itself (environment) gives you clues about your position and speed (observations), and your goal is to maximize your score (rewards).

definition: The external system an agent perceives and acts upon, such as a terminal, browser, or API.
related_terms: Browser Automation; Environment Reset; Headless Browser; Agent Architecture
student_friendly_explanation: An environment for agents is like a sandbox where an AI can interact with the outside world. It could be a web page you browse, a game you play, or even a set of rules for a simulation. This sandbox helps the agent learn and make decisions based on what it sees and does.
example: Imagine you're building a chatbot that needs to understand different websites. The chatbot's environment would be the web pages it visits, allowing it to gather information and respond appropriately.

definition: Returning an environment to its initial state for a new episode.
related_terms: Episode; Environment Snapshot; Environment for Agents; Observation Space
student_friendly_explanation: In AI, when we reset the environment, we're essentially making it like it was at the start of a game or task. It's like restarting a level in a video game, but for our AI system. This means all the variables and conditions are set back to their original state, ready for a fresh round of interactions.
example: Imagine you have an AI agent playing a game where it learns to navigate through a maze. After every successful round (episode), the AI resets the maze to its initial state, allowing it to learn from its mistakes and improve without forgetting past experiences.

definition: One complete run of an agent in an environment from start to termination.
related_terms: Environment Reset; Trajectory; Premature Termination; Termination Condition
student_friendly_explanation: An episode is like a single game or task that an AI agent performs in a virtual world. It starts when the agent begins interacting with the environment and ends when the task is completed or fails according to certain rules.
example: In a video game where the AI character navigates through levels, one episode would be the character's journey from the first level to the final boss fight, including all actions taken and decisions made.

definition: Uncertainty from limited knowledge or data, reducible by collecting more evidence.
related_terms: Predictive Uncertainty; Aleatoric Uncertainty; Deep Ensemble; Bayesian Neural Network (BNN)
student_friendly_explanation: Epistemic uncertainty is the doubt we have about our knowledge or understanding of a system because we don't have enough information or data. It's like when you try to guess the outcome of a coin toss but haven't flipped it yet; you're uncertain about the result.
example: Imagine you're training a machine learning model to predict house prices based on various features like location, size, and age. Even if your model performs well on the training data, there might be some houses whose prices it can't accurately predict due to missing or insufficient data. This uncertainty is epistemic because it comes from a lack of knowledge rather than randomness.

definition: A simple exploration rule choosing a random action with small probability and the best known action otherwise.
related_terms: Thompson Sampling (TS); Random Search Baseline; Probability of Improvement (PI); Random Search
student_friendly_explanation: Epsilon-Greedy is a strategy used in decision-making processes, especially in artificial intelligence algorithms. It balances between exploring new options (randomly) and using what we know (best known actions). Imagine you're playing a game where you have to choose between different moves. With Epsilon-Greedy, you pick a move randomly some of the time, but mostly you stick with the one you think is best.
example: Suppose you're training an AI agent to play a video game. The agent has learned from previous trials that moving left is often the best choice. However, sometimes it's better to explore other moves to find out if they perform well too. Epsilon-Greedy helps the agent balance this exploration and exploitation by occasionally making random moves while mostly following the learned best moves.

definition: A requirement that an expression equal a fixed value exactly.
related_terms: Active Constraint; Inequality Constraint; Chance Constraint; Slack Variable
student_friendly_explanation: An equality constraint is like a rule that says one thing must be exactly equal to a specific number. It's a type of optimization problem where we want something to match a fixed target value precisely.
example: In a machine learning model, an equality constraint might ensure that the output of a neural network layer equals a certain threshold value, which could be used to activate a particular neuron or set a decision boundary.

definition: A morphological operation shrinking bright regions, removing small specks.
related_terms: Morphological Operation; Dilation; Opening; Closing
student_friendly_explanation: Erosion is a process used in computer vision where a bright region shrinks as it removes small specks, similar to how sand erodes from a beach.
example: Imagine an image of a city skyline with buildings. Erosion can be applied to this image to remove small noise points, like tiny specks of dust, making the buildings clearer.

definition: Including uncertainty intervals so readers can judge whether differences are meaningful.
related_terms: Best-of-N Reporting; Inference Budget Reporting; Disaggregated Reporting; Multi-Metric Reporting
student_friendly_explanation: Error bars reporting is a method used to show how much uncertainty there is around a measurement or an estimate. It helps us understand if the difference between two measurements is significant or just due to natural variation.
example: In a study comparing the effectiveness of different machine learning algorithms, error bars on the mean performance scores can help you see if the differences between the algorithms are meaningful or if they could be due to random chance.

definition: The shape of a model's errors, whose skew or heavy tails often matter more than the mean.
related_terms: Mean Absolute Error (MAE); Relative Error; Median Absolute Error (MedAE); Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
student_friendly_explanation: Error distribution is like looking at the mistakes a model makes when predicting something. It shows us if the errors are mostly small or if there are some really big ones. This helps us understand how well our model is doing.
example: Imagine you have a weather prediction model that tries to guess the temperature. If the model mostly gets close to the actual temperature but sometimes wildly overestimates or underestimates, we would see an error distribution with a few large deviations from the mean temperature.

definition: How often automated handling hands a case to a human.
related_terms: Safety Escalation in Wellbeing Apps; Deflection Rate; Case Management; Escalation Path
student_friendly_explanation: The escalation rate is a measure of how frequently an automated system decides to hand over a case or task to a human being when it can't handle it on its own. It's like a traffic light for decisions: if the system can't make a decision, it signals to a human helper.
example: Imagine you're using a chatbot for customer service. If the chatbot can't answer a complex question, it might escalate the case to a human representative. This happens at a certain rate, which we call the escalation rate.

definition: Straight-line distance between two points, the default metric for continuous features.
related_terms: Minkowski Distance; Distance Metric Learning; Distance Concentration; Damerau-Levenshtein Distance
student_friendly_explanation: The Euclidean distance is a way to measure the straight-line distance between two points in space. It's like drawing a line connecting them on a map, and the length of this line is the Euclidean distance.
example: Imagine you have two cities, City A and City B, on a map. If you want to know the shortest path to travel from City A to City B, you would use the Euclidean distance to calculate the straight-line distance between them.

definition: Documentation describing an evaluation's purpose, construction, and known limitations.
related_terms: Deterministic Evaluation; Task Decomposition in Evaluation; Evaluation Pipeline; Continuous Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: An evaluation card is a document that clearly states what the evaluation aims to achieve, how it was created, and any potential issues it might have. It helps ensure that everyone understands the criteria being used and the methods applied.
example: An evaluation card for a machine learning model includes sections on the dataset used, the metrics chosen (like accuracy, precision, recall), and any preprocessing steps taken. This ensures that when the model performs well, it’s clear why it succeeded based on the defined criteria.

definition: The compute and money required to run a benchmark, which limits how often it can be used.
related_terms: LM Evaluation Harness; Private Evaluation Set; Dynamic Benchmark; Sample Size for Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: Evaluation cost is the amount of computational effort and financial resources needed to run a benchmark test. It affects how frequently you can perform such tests, as higher costs limit their use.
example: For instance, running a machine learning model on a large dataset might require significant computing power and time, making it less practical to evaluate the model's performance frequently.

definition: Evaluation of a binary classifier typically assigns a numerical value, or values, to a classifier that represent its accuracy. An example is error rate, which measures how frequently the classifier makes a mistake.
related_terms: Generative Classifier; Discriminative Classifier; Maximum Margin Classifier; Nearest Centroid Classifier
student_friendly_explanation: The evaluation of a binary classifier involves assigning a score that reflects how well it predicts whether an item belongs to one category or another. This score helps us understand how often the classifier makes correct or incorrect predictions.
example: Imagine you have a binary classifier that predicts if an email is spam (1) or not spam (0). The error rate would be calculated as the number of emails the classifier incorrectly labeled divided by the total number of emails. If the classifier made 5 mistakes out of 100 emails, the error rate would be 5%.

definition: The automated system generating, scoring, and reporting model assessments.
related_terms: Continuous Evaluation; Adversarial Evaluation; Deterministic Evaluation; Blind Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: An evaluation pipeline is an automated process that takes in model outputs, scores them based on predefined criteria, and then reports the results. It's like a conveyor belt where models go through a series of checks and scoring steps.
example: In a machine learning project, the evaluation pipeline might take the predictions made by a model and compare them against actual outcomes. It could score the model based on accuracy, precision, recall, and other metrics, and then generate a report summarizing the performance.

definition: A subset of the sample space to which a probability can be assigned.
related_terms: Sample Space; Mutually Exclusive Events; Probability Measure; Conditional Probability
student_friendly_explanation: An event is like a group of outcomes from an experiment where we can assign a chance (probability) to happen. It's a part of all possible outcomes (sample space). For example, if you roll a die, getting a 4 is one event.
example: When flipping a coin, landing on heads is an event. We can say there's a 50% chance (or 0.5 probability) of this event happening.

definition: Ensuring digital material is unaltered and its handling fully documented.
related_terms: Academic Integrity Detection; Weight of Evidence (WoE); Chain of Custody; Integrity of Relationships
student_friendly_explanation: Evidence integrity is about making sure that data stays unchanged and that everyone knows who handled it at every step. It's like keeping track of who signed a document and making sure no one can change the document without leaving a record.
example: In a study using machine learning algorithms, evidence integrity ensures that the training data used to teach the models hasn't been altered and that all changes to the dataset are logged, allowing researchers to verify the process.

definition: Optimization inspired by biological evolution using selection, mutation, crossover, and fitness evaluation. Types: genetic algorithms, genetic programming, evolutionary strategies, neuroevolution. Excel at complex multi-modal optimization.
related_terms: Genetic Algorithm (GA); Neural Architecture Search (NAS); Fitness approximation; Stability of an Algorithm
student_friendly_explanation: An evolutionary algorithm is like a smart guessing game where solutions to problems evolve over time. It uses ideas from nature, such as selection, mutation, and crossover, to find better solutions. Think of it as a group of creatures trying to solve a puzzle, passing on their best traits to the next generation.
example: Imagine you have a function that takes a number and returns another number. An evolutionary algorithm can be used to find the input number that makes this function output the highest possible value. It does this by creating many 'creatures' (potential solutions), comparing them, and gradually improving the ones that perform better.

definition: The danger that people unable to use a system lose access to essential services.
related_terms: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI); Digital Biomarker; Digital Therapeutic; Risk Parity
student_friendly_explanation: Exclusion Risk in Digital Systems refers to the risk that users who can't effectively use a digital system are denied access to important services provided by that system.
example: A hospital might implement an exclusion risk management system to ensure that patients with certain conditions can still receive necessary medical care even if they struggle with using the electronic health record system.

definition: Information from running code or tools that an agent uses to correct itself.
related_terms: Plan Execution; Cost Estimation Before Execution; Compiler Error Feedback; Code Interpreter
student_friendly_explanation: Execution feedback is information provided when a program runs, which helps the AI system adjust and improve its performance. It's like getting a score after you play a game, but instead of a score, it gives details on what went wrong and how to fix it.
example: When you run a script, if there's a syntax error, the interpreter provides execution feedback, such as 'SyntaxError: invalid syntax' along with line numbers where the error occurred. This feedback guides you to correct the mistake and refine your code.

definition: Choosing a small representative subset of data that preserves the structure of the whole.
related_terms: Coreset Selection; Model Selection; Active Data Selection; Gradient Matching Selection
student_friendly_explanation: Exemplar selection is about picking a few key examples from a large dataset. These key examples should be chosen carefully so that they represent the overall data well. This helps in making decisions or training models more efficiently.
example: Imagine you have a huge dataset of images of cats and dogs. Exemplar selection would involve choosing a few dozen images that best represent the variety of cat and dog appearances in the entire dataset. These selected images can then be used to train a model to recognize cats and dogs, making the training process faster and more effective.

definition: The average gap between predicted confidence and observed accuracy across confidence bins.
related_terms: Isotonic Regression Calibration; Expected Model Change; Reliability Diagram; Confidence in Association Rules
student_friendly_explanation: The Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is a measure used in machine learning to evaluate how well a model's predicted confidence levels match its actual performance. It calculates the average difference between what a model predicts it will achieve (confidence) and what it actually achieves (accuracy) within different confidence intervals.
example: Imagine you have a model predicting whether an email is spam or not. If the model predicts a 90% chance of being spam but only gets 85% of emails right, the ECE would help you understand if the model's confidence level is too high or too low, and adjust accordingly.

definition: The average penalty of a classifier's decisions given error costs and class frequencies.
related_terms: Cost Matrix; Annotation Cost per Judgment; Threshold Selection; Operating Point
student_friendly_explanation: The expected cost is a measure used to evaluate how much a classifier might lose if it makes a wrong decision. It takes into account both the cost of making an error and the frequency of different classes in the data.
example: Imagine you have a spam filter for emails. If it incorrectly labels a non-spam email as spam (false positive), you might get a notification about a potential scam, which could be annoying. If it incorrectly labels a spam email as non-spam (false negative), you might miss out on important information. The expected cost would help you decide the best threshold to set for your spam filter, balancing between these two types of errors.

definition: Extracting and validating spending records from receipts and statements.
related_terms: Invoice Processing; Intelligent Document Processing (IDP); Suspicious Activity Report (SAR); Border Processing Automation
student_friendly_explanation: Expense Report Processing is about taking information from documents like receipts and bills, checking if it's correct, and using that data to create a report of all the money spent.
example: A software system automatically reads through all the receipts from a company's monthly expenses, verifies the amounts and categories, and generates a comprehensive report that includes total costs, itemized details, and sometimes even flags any unusual spending patterns.

definition: An RL technique storing past experiences in a buffer and sampling random mini-batches for training. Breaks temporal correlations, improves data efficiency, and stabilizes training. Prioritized replay samples more important transitions.
related_terms: Deep Q-Network (DQN); Reinforcement Learning (RL); Replay Buffer; Prioritized Experience Replay
student_friendly_explanation: Experience Replay is a method used in reinforcement learning where we store past experiences in a buffer and then randomly select mini-batches of these experiences to train our model. This helps break the order of events, making the training process more effective and stable.
example: Imagine you're playing a video game where your score increases based on actions you take. Experience Replay would be like saving all your previous game states and actions, then choosing a random subset of them to learn from, which helps improve your gameplay strategy over time.

definition: A regression metric similar to R-squared but insensitive to systematic bias.
related_terms: R-Squared in Prediction; Score Variance Across Runs; Brier Score Decomposition; Faithfulness Metric
student_friendly_explanation: The Explained Variance Score (EVS) is a measure used in regression analysis to assess how well a model explains the variability of the data. It's like R-squared, but it doesn't get fooled by systematic errors.
example: Imagine you have a model predicting house prices based on square footage. If EVS is high, it means your model explains a lot of the price variation, even if some of the variation is due to other factors not included in the model.

definition: Reducing the learning rate by a constant multiplicative factor each step or epoch.
related_terms: Step Decay; Decoupled Weight Decay; Exponential Moving Average of Weights (EMA); Multiplicative Weights Update
student_friendly_explanation: Exponential decay in optimization means gradually reducing the speed at which we adjust our model's parameters over time. It's like slowing down when you're running a race; you start fast but then slow down as you get tired.
example: Imagine you're trying to find the lowest point on a hill. At first, you take big steps downhill. But as you get closer to the bottom, you take smaller and smaller steps, eventually stopping. This is similar to exponential decay, where the learning rate decreases over time.

definition: Adjusting overall brightness to recover detail in over or underexposed regions.
related_terms: Gamma Correction; Vignetting Correction; Underwater Image Correction; Blob Detection
student_friendly_explanation: Exposure correction is like adjusting the brightness of an image so that it looks more natural and has better details. It helps fix images that are too dark (underexposed) or too bright (overexposed).
example: Imagine you take a photo of a scene at sunset. If the photo is too dark, exposure correction can make the colors pop and show more details in the sky and the horizon.

definition: The declared structure a system must fill when pulling information from text.
related_terms: Nested Extraction; Zero-Shot Extraction; Open Information Extraction (OpenIE); Information Extraction (IE)
student_friendly_explanation: An extraction schema is like a set of rules that tells a computer system how to organize and collect data from text. It's a way to define what parts of the text should be extracted and how they should be arranged.
