example: Imagine you have two groups of colored balls: red and blue. Each group has its own 'center' based on where most of the balls are. The Nearest Centroid Classifier would then decide which group a new ball belongs to by seeing which center is nearest to it.

definition: Resizing by copying the closest pixel, preserving hard edges but producing blockiness.
related_terms: Bilinear Interpolation; Bicubic Interpolation; Resize Interpolation; Iterative Closest Point (ICP)
student_friendly_explanation: Nearest Neighbor Interpolation is a method used to resize images or data. It works by finding the closest pixel to the desired location and copying its color value. This process preserves the sharp edges of the image but can make it look blocky.
example: Consider an image where you want to increase its size. Nearest Neighbor Interpolation would find the nearest pixel to each new point on the resized image and copy its color. This results in clear edges but makes the image appear chunky.

definition: The distribution of trials until a fixed number of successes, also used to model overdispersed counts.
related_terms: Binomial Distribution; Multinomial Distribution; Geometric Distribution; Beta Distribution
student_friendly_explanation: Negative Binomial Distribution is a way to count how many times you need to try something before getting a certain number of successful outcomes. It's like flipping coins until you get a specific number of heads.
example: Imagine you're trying to sell lemonade until you've sold 5 cups. If the probability of selling a cup is 0.4, the Negative Binomial Distribution can tell you the average number of tries it will take to sell those 5 cups.

definition: A description of content to steer generation away from.
related_terms: Prompt Weighting; Text Encoder for Generation; Prompt Length Effect; Prompt Enhancement
student_friendly_explanation: Negative Prompt is a type of input used in generative AI models to instruct the model to avoid generating certain types of content. It's like telling the model what not to include in its output.
example: For instance, if you want to generate an image of a cat but don't want it to have any ears, you can use a Negative Prompt to tell the AI model to exclude ear features from the generated image.

definition: The number of sequential transformation stages between a network's input and output.
related_terms: Effective Depth; Parameter Sharing Across Depth; Recurrent Depth; Depth Pruning
student_friendly_explanation: Network depth refers to the total number of layers or transformations in a neural network model. Each layer processes the data in some way before passing it on to the next layer.
example: Consider a simple convolutional neural network (CNN) used for image recognition. If this CNN has three convolutional layers followed by one fully connected layer, we say it has a depth of three.

definition: A computing system inspired by biological neural networks, consisting of interconnected nodes (neurons) organized in layers. Each connection has a learnable weight, and each neuron applies an activation function to its weighted inputs. Neural networks can approximate any continuous function given sufficient width or depth, making them universal function approximators.
related_terms: Deep Learning (DL); Backpropagation (BP); Activation Function; Weight
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine a group of connected computers working together like neurons in your brain. These computers share information through wires, which we call 'weights.' They use special rules called 'activation functions' to decide what to do next based on the information they receive. This way, they can learn and improve their decisions over time.
example: Consider a simple neural network that learns to recognize handwritten digits. It starts with random guesses, then adjusts its guesses based on whether it got the digit right or wrong. With enough training, it can accurately identify digits from images.

definition: A point in a sparse region that density-based clustering assigns to no cluster.
related_terms: Density-Based Clustering; DBSCAN; Noise Contrastive Estimation; Clustering
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're looking at a map of a city where some areas are very crowded (dense) and others are empty (sparse). In a type of clustering called Density-Based Clustering, like DBSCAN, if you find an area that's too empty to be part of any dense area, we call it a noise point. It's like finding a lone tree in a forest where all the other trees are close together.
example: Consider a dataset representing the locations of people in a city. If you use DBSCAN to cluster these points, a noise point would be someone who is far away from any group of people, perhaps because they live in a completely different neighborhood.

definition: A game character controlled by software rather than a human player.
related_terms: Behaviour Tree in Games; Game AI; Game Balancing; Navigation Mesh
student_friendly_explanation: In video games, a Non-Player Character (NPC) is a virtual entity that interacts with players but is controlled by computer code instead of being controlled by another player. NPCs can perform actions like walking, talking, or attacking based on pre-programmed rules.
example: An NPC in a role-playing game might follow a path determined by a navigation mesh, interact with the player based on a behavior tree, and adjust its behavior according to game balancing rules.

definition: The bell-shaped distribution characterized by mean and variance, arising as the limit of many summed effects.
related_terms: Standard Normal Distribution; Multivariate Normal Distribution; Law of Total Variance; Cauchy Distribution
student_friendly_explanation: A normal distribution is a symmetrical graph that looks like a bell, centered around a mean value. It's formed when you add up many small, independent random effects, and it tends to form this shape as the number of added effects increases.
example: Imagine you're measuring the heights of people in a large city. If you take many samples and plot their average height, you might get a normal distribution curve. This curve shows that most people's heights are close to the average, but some are taller or shorter than usual.

definition: A canonical Unicode representation chosen so visually identical text compares equal.
related_terms: Unicode Normalization; Normalization of Text; Text Normalization for Speech; Normalization of Extracted Values
student_friendly_explanation: Normalization forms standardize character sequences.
example: NFC normalizes 'á' (precomposed) to the same form as 'á'.

definition: Converting extracted text into canonical typed values such as dates and amounts.
related_terms: Validation of Extraction; Unicode Normalization; Normalization Form; Text Normalization for Speech
student_friendly_explanation: Normalization of extracted values is the process of converting raw text data, like dates and numbers, into standardized forms that can be easily processed and compared. This helps ensure consistency and accuracy when dealing with different sources of information.
example: When extracting dates from various documents, normalization might convert '03/04/2023' to '2023-03-04', making it easier to store and compare across different formats.

definition: Standardizing text by lowercasing, stripping accents, or unifying Unicode forms before processing.
related_terms: Unicode Normalization; Normalization Form; Text Normalization for Speech; Normalization of Extracted Values
student_friendly_explanation: Normalization of text is the process of making text consistent and uniform before it's processed. This includes converting all letters to lowercase, removing any special characters or diacritical marks (like accents), and ensuring that all characters are in their standard form as defined by Unicode.
example: When we normalize text, we might convert 'Hello World!' to 'hello world!' and remove any emojis or other non-standard characters, preparing the text for further analysis.

definition: Performance rescaled against reference baselines so results across tasks can be averaged.
related_terms: Human-Normalized Score; Baseline Subtraction; Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG); Human Baseline
student_friendly_explanation: Normalized Score is a way to adjust scores from different tasks so that we can compare them fairly. Imagine you have several tests, and each test has its own score. By using Normalized Score, we make all scores comparable by adjusting them based on a common standard, like subtracting a baseline score or using a special formula.
example: Suppose you're evaluating search engine results for a project. Each result might have a score based on relevance, but the scores vary widely. To normalize these scores, you could subtract a human baseline score (like the average score given by humans) or use a Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) formula to account for the order of results. This way, you get a fair comparison of how good each result is, regardless of which task it came from.

definition: A computer vision task that identifies and localizes objects within images or video by predicting bounding boxes and class labels. Modern architectures include two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN), one-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD), and transformer-based detectors (DETR). Applications span autonomous driving, surveillance, medical imaging, and retail analytics.
related_terms: Computer Vision (CV); Image Recognition; YOLO (You Only Look Once); Transformer
student_friendly_explanation: Object detection is a computer vision task that helps computers recognize and locate objects in images or videos. It does this by using special algorithms to find and mark objects with boxes and labels.
example: In an image of a city street, object detection can identify cars, bikes, and pedestrians, and draw bounding boxes around them to show where each object is located.

definition: Following an object's position across successive video frames.
related_terms: Object Permanence in Tracking; Tracking by Detection; Multi-Object Tracking (MOT); Frame Differencing
student_friendly_explanation: Object tracking is the process of following the movement of objects from one frame to the next in a series of videos. It helps us understand where objects go and how they move over time.
example: Imagine you have a video camera filming a bird flying through a park. Object tracking would allow us to see the bird's path as it moves from one frame to the next, showing us its trajectory and speed.

definition: The surface an optimizer traverses, whose shape determines how hard a problem is.
related_terms: Clipped Surrogate Objective; Surrogate Objective; Lion Optimizer; Unbounded Problem
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're trying to find the lowest point in a hilly landscape. The objective landscape is like that whole area of hills and valleys where your search starts. It's shaped differently depending on the problem, making some problems harder to solve than others.
example: Consider a simple optimization problem where you want to minimize a function that looks like a bowl-shaped valley (convex). In this case, the objective landscape is easy to navigate because there's only one lowest point. However, if the function looks more like a mountain range with many peaks and valleys (non-convex), finding the absolute lowest point becomes much harder.

definition: Monitoring commitments a contract creates and when they come due.
related_terms: Regulatory Change Monitoring; Contract Analysis; Contract Lifecycle Management (CLM); Livestock Monitoring
student_friendly_explanation: Obligation Tracking is like keeping track of promises made in a contract. It involves watching over the commitments a contract makes and when those commitments need to be fulfilled.
example: A company might use Obligation Tracking software to monitor when employees need to meet their performance targets and deadlines, ensuring everyone stays on schedule and meets their obligations.

definition: The set of possible perceptions an agent can receive from its environment.
related_terms: Perception Module; Action Space for Agents; Environment Reset; Environment
student_friendly_explanation: The observation space is like a list of all the things an AI can see or sense in its environment. It's what the AI perceives as it interacts with the world.
example: Imagine you're building a robot that needs to navigate a maze. The observation space would include all the different shapes, colors, and textures the robot might encounter as it moves through the maze.

definition: Measuring how prediction changes as parts of an image are hidden.
related_terms: Occlusion Handling; Random Erasing; DeepSORT; Occlusion Culling
student_friendly_explanation: Occlusion sensitivity is a measure of how much the output of a computer vision model changes when certain parts of an image are obscured or hidden. It helps the model understand what it's seeing even when parts of the scene are not visible.
example: Imagine a computer vision system that detects pedestrians in a video. If part of a pedestrian's body is occluded (hidden), the system's ability to recognize them might change slightly. This sensitivity allows the system to still identify the pedestrian even if some of their body is out of view.

definition: Building applications that function without a reliable network connection.
related_terms: Generative Design; Bandwidth-Aware Design; Identity System Design; AI for Science
student_friendly_explanation: Offline-First Design is a strategy where applications are built to work even when there's no internet connection. This means the app can still perform tasks like data storage and basic operations without needing an active network.
example: A weather app using Offline-First Design will store current weather conditions locally on your device, allowing you to check the forecast even if you're offline.

definition: Comparing ranking changes against stored judgements before exposing them to users.
related_terms: Online Ranking Experiment; Feature Store for Ranking; Pairwise Ranking; Model Serving for Ranking
student_friendly_explanation: Offline ranking evaluation is a method where we compare how a model's rankings change when it's given new data, but we don't show these changes to anyone until after we've stored our judgments about the correct order of items. This allows us to see if the model's performance improves over time without bias.
example: Imagine you have a list of movies ranked by your movie recommendation system. In offline ranking evaluation, you would rank these movies based on your personal preferences and store those rankings. Later, you can compare this stored ranking with the system's new rankings to see if it has learned from additional data.

definition: An object detector predicting classes and boxes in a single pass, favouring speed.
related_terms: Object Detection; SSD Detector; FAST Detector; Two-Stage Detector
student_friendly_explanation: A one-stage detector is a type of object detection system that quickly predicts both the class (what the object is) and the bounding box (where the object is located) in an image all at once, without needing to refine its predictions multiple times.
example: Imagine you have a camera that can instantly recognize and outline objects in your photos. A one-stage detector would be like this camera, which can identify and draw a box around cars, trees, and people in a single step, rather than taking several steps to get more precise results.

definition: A quality measure computed from live traffic after deployment.
related_terms: Offline Metric; Metric Sensitivity; Model Deployment Pattern; Metrics Cardinality
student_friendly_explanation: An online metric is a way to check how well an AI system is working right away after it's put into use. It looks at real data coming through the internet to see if the system is doing what it should.
example: Imagine you have a chatbot that helps people find information. An online metric could tell you how often the chatbot correctly answers questions as soon as it starts working.

definition: Measuring a ranking change's effect using live user behaviour.
related_terms: Offline Ranking Evaluation; Feature Store for Ranking; Pairwise Ranking; Model Serving for Ranking
student_friendly_explanation: An online ranking experiment measures how changes in rankings affect real users' behavior in real time. It's like testing if a new sorting system makes people click on certain items more often than before.
example: Imagine you have a list of books sorted by popularity. An online ranking experiment might show you how quickly people scroll through different sections of the list after you shuffle the order of the books. This helps you understand which changes in the list make people interested.

definition: Conversational systems handling unrestricted topics without a fixed task.
related_terms: Dialogue Evaluation Metric; Dialogue State Tracking (DST); Conversational Memory; Task-Oriented Dialogue
student_friendly_explanation: Open-domain dialogue refers to conversations where the system can handle any topic without being limited to specific tasks. It's like having a chatbot that can talk about anything, from movies to news, without needing to know what you're going to say next.
example: A virtual assistant that can respond to questions about various subjects, such as 'What's the latest movie release?' or 'Tell me a joke.' It doesn't need to be told beforehand what kind of information it will provide.

definition: Erosion followed by dilation, removing small objects while preserving larger shapes.
related_terms: Closing; Erosion; Dilation; Morphological Operation
student_friendly_explanation: Opening is a process in image processing where we first remove small details (erosion) and then fill in large areas (dilation). It's like cleaning up a messy room by sweeping out the dust and then filling in the gaps.
example: Imagine you have a black-and-white image of a tree trunk surrounded by leaves. Opening would first remove all the tiny leaf details, leaving just the outline of the trunk. Then, it would fill in any small gaps or missing parts, making the trunk shape clearer.

definition: A public ranking of open models across a fixed benchmark suite with reproducible settings.
related_terms: Leaderboard Overfitting; Benchmark Suite Aggregation; Leaderboard Gaming; OGB
student_friendly_explanation: An OpenLLM Leaderboard is like a list where different computer programs (called models) compete against each other on a set of tasks (benchmark suite). Everyone can see how well they did, and it helps researchers understand which model is better at solving problems.
example: Imagine you have a bunch of different AI tools, and you want to know which one is best at recognizing images. An OpenLLM Leaderboard would be a place where all these tools show their scores on an image recognition test, so people can compare them easily.

definition: The specific threshold at which a model is deployed, chosen for the costs of each error type.
related_terms: Threshold Selection; Cost Matrix; Expected Cost; Confidence Threshold
student_friendly_explanation: An operating point is the particular setting where an AI model starts working, based on how much we're willing to pay for mistakes it makes. It's like picking a price for a service based on how costly it is to have errors.
example: Imagine you have a model that predicts if someone will buy a product. If the model predicts incorrectly, it might cost you money (like losing sales). An operating point would be the level of confidence you set for the prediction, deciding when you think the model has enough certainty to make a sale.

definition: A means by which creators can exclude their content from training datasets.
related_terms: Opt-Out Registry; Economic Harm to Creators; Opt-Out Design; Consent for Training
student_friendly_explanation: An opt-out mechanism allows creators to remove their work from training datasets used to develop artificial intelligence models. This ensures that creators have control over their content being used for training purposes.
example: For instance, a music composer can use an opt-out registry to notify developers of their music, thereby preventing it from being included in a dataset used to train a speech recognition system.

definition: The difference between the best known solution and a proven bound on the optimum.
related_terms: Relative Gap Tolerance; Second-Order Optimality Condition; First-Order Optimality Condition; Duality Gap
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're trying to find the absolute best way to solve a problem, like finding the shortest route to school. The optimality gap is the difference between the best solution you've found and the very best solution possible. It's like if you thought you had the fastest way to school, but then someone else found an even faster one.
example: Consider a scenario where you're optimizing a machine learning model to minimize errors. After running several iterations, you find a solution that minimizes errors to 5%. However, through further analysis, you discover that theoretically, you could reduce errors to 3%. The optimality gap here would be 2 percentage points, showing how much more you can improve your model.

definition: The auxiliary buffers an optimizer maintains, such as momentum and second-moment estimates, often dominating memory.
related_terms: 8-Bit Optimizer; Muon Optimizer; Quantized Optimizer; Lion Optimizer
student_friendly_explanation: An optimizer state is like a set of helper tools that an optimizer uses to improve itself during training. These tools, such as momentum and second-moment estimates, can take up a lot of memory, which is why they're important but also need careful management.
example: Imagine you're trying to find the lowest point in a hilly landscape. An optimizer state acts like a map that helps the optimizer (like a smart robot) move efficiently through this landscape, adjusting its path based on past steps to reach the bottom faster.

definition: Mapping categories to integers, appropriate only when the ordering is genuine.
related_terms: Ordinal Classification; Ordinal Feature; Target Encoding; Frequency Encoding
student_friendly_explanation: Ordinal encoding is a method used in machine learning where we assign unique integer values to different categories based on their order or rank. This technique is useful when the order of the categories matters and there's a genuine way to rank them.
example: Suppose you have a dataset of customer feedback ratings (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) for product quality. Ordinal encoding would convert these ratings into integers like {1: 0, 2: 1, 3: 2, 4: 3, 5: 4}, ensuring that higher numbers correspond to better quality.

definition: A rotatable rectangle fitting an object more tightly than an axis-aligned box.
related_terms: Bounding Box; Anchor Box; Face Detection; Visual Prompt
student_friendly_explanation: An Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) is like a flexible rectangle that can rotate to fit around an object more snugly than a fixed rectangle. It's used in computer vision to better understand shapes and objects.
example: Imagine you have a robot arm that needs to grasp an irregularly shaped object. An OBB can be adjusted to rotate and shrink around the object, ensuring it fits perfectly without gaps.

definition: Judging an agent solely by whether the end state satisfies the goal.
related_terms: Trajectory Evaluation; Capability Evaluation; Prompt Evaluation; Dangerous Capability Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: Outcome evaluation is when we judge if an AI system has reached its intended goal based on the final result it produces. It's like checking if you've completed your homework by looking at the grade you got, not by how much effort you put into it.
example: In a self-driving car system, outcome evaluation would involve checking if the car successfully reached its destination without accidents, rather than evaluating the car's performance during the journey.

definition: Identifying unusual points within a dataset that may itself contain contamination.
related_terms: Local Outlier Factor; Contamination Filtering; Novelty Detection; Near-Duplicate Detection
student_friendly_explanation: Outlier detection is like finding the odd one out in a group of data. It helps us spot values that don't fit with the rest of the information, which might be due to errors or unique events.
example: Imagine you have a list of test scores from your classmates. If one score is much lower than all the others, it could be an outlier. This score might indicate a student who didn't study well or had a special circumstance that day.

definition: The final stage of a network, producing predictions in the form the task requires.
related_terms: Layer; Input Layer; Hidden Layer; Compute Allocation Across Layers
student_friendly_explanation: The output layer is the last part of a neural network where it makes predictions based on the information it has processed. It takes data from all the hidden layers below it and uses this information to generate outputs that match what the task requires.
example: In a simple neural network designed to classify images into cats and dogs, the output layer would take the final processed data from the hidden layers and use a function (like a sigmoid or softmax) to decide whether the image is a cat or a dog.

definition: Discarding a generated result that a safety check flags before delivery.
related_terms: Prompt-Level Blocking; NSFW Filter; Classifier-Based Prevention; Blocking
student_friendly_explanation: Output-Level Blocking is when a system automatically discards an output it generates if a safety check flags something as unsafe or inappropriate before sending it out.
example: A chatbot might use Output-Level Blocking to discard explicit content from messages, ensuring users receive safe and appropriate responses.

definition: A formal specification the model's response must satisfy, often expressed as JSON Schema.
related_terms: Tool Schema; Schema Validation; Structured Tool Output; Model Specification
student_friendly_explanation: An output schema is like a set of rules that defines what kind of information an AI system should provide. It's a way to ensure that the model's response matches the expected format, usually described using JSON Schema, which is a language for describing data structures.
example: For instance, if you ask an AI tool to generate a list of steps for a machine learning project, the output schema might specify that the response should be a JSON object with keys like 'project_name', 'steps', and 'estimated_time'. This ensures that the tool always provides the same structure of information.

definition: An agent reporting success when the goal was not actually achieved.
related_terms: Verification Before Completion; Safe Completion; Success Rate; Streaming Response
student_friendly_explanation: Overconfident Completion happens when an AI system claims it has completed a task successfully even if it hasn't actually succeeded. This can lead to incorrect information being reported.
example: A self-driving car's AI system reports it has reached the destination, but it missed a stop sign. Despite reaching the destination, the system is overconfident because it didn't verify the stop sign.

definition: A modeling error that occurs when a machine learning model learns the training data too well, including its noise and random fluctuations, resulting in poor generalization to new data. The model performs excellently on training data but poorly on validation or test data. Techniques to combat overfitting include regularization, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, and cross-validation.
related_terms: Underfitting; Regularization; Cross-validation; Data Augmentation
student_friendly_explanation: Overfitting happens when a machine learning model learns the training data too well, even the noise and random fluctuations, instead of learning the underlying pattern. This makes the model perform very well on the training data but poorly on unseen data.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of images of cats and dogs. An overfit model might learn every tiny detail of the cat's whiskers and dog's fur, which is great for recognizing cats and dogs but won't generalize well to new, unseen images.

definition: Extra border values added before convolution so output size and edge treatment can be controlled.
related_terms: Same Padding; Valid Padding; Padding Token; Dilated Convolution
student_friendly_explanation: Padding is adding extra values around the edges of an input layer in a neural network. This helps control the size of the output and prevents the network from losing information at the borders.
example: Consider a 3x3 input image. Without padding, a 3x3 filter would leave a 1x1 output. With padding, say 2 pixels, the filter sees a 5x5 area, resulting in a 4x4 output, which keeps more information about the image's edges.

definition: A filler token added so sequences in a batch share a length, masked out of loss and attention.
related_terms: Same Padding; Valid Padding; Padding; Special Token
student_friendly_explanation: Padding tokens are extra placeholders added to make all sequences in a batch the same length. These tokens are not used in calculations but are included to ensure all data can be processed together. They are often used when preparing text data for models like neural networks.
example: Suppose we have three sentences: 'The cat', 'The dog', and 'The bird'. To feed them into a model, we might add padding tokens to make all sentences the same length, say five words. So, the padded sentences would look like this: '[PAD] The cat', '[PAD] The dog', '[PAD] The bird'. This ensures all sentences are treated equally during training.

definition: Assessing models by which of two outputs raters prefer rather than by absolute scores.
related_terms: Pairwise Preference Data; Rubric-Based Evaluation; Bradley-Terry Model; Annotator Agreement
student_friendly_explanation: Pairwise comparison evaluation is a method where we compare two outputs and decide which one we like better, instead of giving them numerical scores. It's used to assess models by asking raters to pick their preferred output.
example: Imagine you have two different image recognition models. Instead of giving each model a score based on some metric, you ask a group of people to look at the images produced by each model and tell you which one they think performs better. This way, you gather preferences without using absolute scores.

definition: Annotations recording which of two outputs a rater preferred, the raw material of alignment training.
related_terms: Pairwise Comparison Evaluation; Iterative Preference Optimization; Bradley-Terry Model; Preference Pair
student_friendly_explanation: Pairwise preference data involves collecting information from raters about their preferences between two options. For instance, if you're comparing two different machine learning algorithms, pairwise preference data would record which algorithm a rater prefers.
example: Imagine you have two machine learning models, Model A and Model B. If a rater prefers Model A over Model B, this is recorded as a preference. This type of data is used to train models that can make decisions based on preferences, like which model performs better.

definition: Learning to rank by predicting which of two documents is more relevant.
related_terms: Pointwise Ranking; Offline Ranking Evaluation; Feature Store for Ranking; Online Ranking Experiment
student_friendly_explanation: Pairwise Ranking is a method used in Information Retrieval where we predict which of two documents is more relevant to a query. It's like deciding which movie review is better based on a set of criteria, but instead, it deals with documents and their relevance scores.
example: Imagine you have a list of 10 articles about AI. A Pairwise Ranking system would compare each pair of articles (10 pairs) and decide which one is more relevant to a given topic, such as 'Artificial Intelligence Ethics', by analyzing factors like the number of times key terms appear and the overall quality of the article.

definition: Aligned text in two languages used to train translation systems.
related_terms: Corpus; Retrieval Corpus; Corpus Linguistics; Unsupervised Machine Translation
student_friendly_explanation: A parallel corpus is like a pair of books where one book is written in English and the other in another language, but they have the same content. This helps computers learn to translate from one language to another by comparing the words and their meanings in both versions.
example: Imagine you have a book about AI in English and another identical book in Spanish. A parallel corpus would include these two books, allowing a machine learning algorithm to understand how similar phrases and sentences are translated between English and Spanish.

definition: Invoking several independent tools simultaneously to reduce total latency.
related_terms: Sequential Tool Calls; Tool Result; Type Coercion in Tool Calls; Tool Call Retry
student_friendly_explanation: Parallel tool calls allow you to run multiple tools at the same time, which can make your work faster. Imagine if you had to type a document, proofread it, and then edit it one after another. With parallel tool calls, you could type, proofread, and edit all at once, saving time.
example: When using an AI writing assistant, parallel tool calls might involve running a text correction tool, a grammar checker, and a readability analyzer simultaneously. This way, the assistant can quickly provide feedback on different aspects of the text, making the overall process more efficient.

definition: The internal variables of a model that are learned from training data, such as weights and biases in neural networks. The number of parameters is often used as a rough measure of model capacity (e.g., GPT-4 is rumored to have over a trillion parameters). More parameters generally enable more capable models but require more compute, memory, and data.
related_terms: Hyperparameter; Weight; Neural Network (NN); Compute
student_friendly_explanation: Parameters are like the recipe ingredients for a machine learning model. They're the numbers that tell the model how to make decisions based on the data it sees. In a neural network, these numbers change during training to learn patterns in the data.
example: Imagine you're teaching a computer to recognize cats in pictures. Each parameter is like a tiny knob that adjusts how the computer looks at different parts of the picture to decide if it's a cat.

definition: The statistical family from which a network's starting weights are drawn.
related_terms: Weight Initialization Scheme; He Initialization; Bias Initialization; LeCun Initialization
student_friendly_explanation: Parameter initialization distribution refers to the statistical method used to set the starting values of a neural network's weights. It's like choosing a recipe (distribution) to bake your first batch of cookies (initialize weights), ensuring the network starts learning effectively.
example: In He Initialization, we use a normal distribution with a mean of zero and a variance of 2/n for each weight, where n is the number of input connections to the neuron. This helps ensure that the initial weights are not too large or too small, promoting better learning.

definition: Deciding whether two texts express the same meaning in different words.
related_terms: Paraphrase Generation; Paraphrase Attack on Watermarks; Data Augmentation for Text; Back-Translation Augmentation
student_friendly_explanation: Paraphrase detection is about figuring out if two pieces of text mean the same thing but use different words. It's like translating a sentence into another language, but instead of changing the meaning, it checks if the original and translated versions convey the same idea.
example: Imagine you have two sentences: 'The cat is sleeping' and 'The feline is at rest'. A paraphrase detector would recognize that these sentences have the same meaning even though they use different words.

definition: Producing alternative wordings that preserve a sentence's meaning.
related_terms: Paraphrase Detection; Paraphrase Attack on Watermarks; Data Augmentation for Text; Back-Translation Augmentation
student_friendly_explanation: Paraphrase generation is about creating different ways to say something while keeping the same meaning. It's like when you tell a story in multiple versions but still convey the same message.
example: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog can be paraphrased as 'A swift, colorful fox leaps over a dozy dog.' Both versions express the same idea but use different words.

definition: The set of solutions where no objective can improve without another worsening.
related_terms: Weighted Sum Method; Pareto Improvement in Modelling; Pareto Optimality; Pareto Distribution
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you have a set of options, and each option has different qualities like speed, cost, and efficiency. The Pareto Front is a list of the best options where you can't make one quality better without making another worse. It's like finding the sweet spot where you balance all your needs.
example: Consider designing an AI system for autonomous vehicles. You want it to be fast (low latency), cheap (low cost), and safe (low risk). The Pareto Front would show you the most efficient designs where you can't improve one aspect without worsening another. For instance, a design might be very fast but expensive, or very cheap but slow.

definition: Updating only selected layers while freezing the rest to save memory and reduce forgetting.
related_terms: Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning; Full Fine-Tuning; Layer Freezing; Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
student_friendly_explanation: Partial fine-tuning is when we tweak only some parts of a big learning model, leaving the rest untouched. This helps save space and prevents the model from forgetting what it learned before.
example: Imagine you have a super smart AI that can recognize cats and dogs. With partial fine-tuning, you could teach it to recognize birds without starting over from scratch, saving time and resources.

definition: The condition where an agent cannot see the full state of its environment.
related_terms: Agent Observability; Partial Tool Result; Data Observability; Sampling for Observability
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're playing a game where you can't see all the pieces on the board. In AI, partial observability means that an agent (like a character in the game) can't see the complete information about its environment (the board). This makes it harder for the agent to make decisions.
example: In a simple AI game, if you can't see which pieces your opponent has placed on the board, but you know they have some pieces hidden, this is an example of partial observability.

definition: An incomplete output an agent must decide whether to use or discard.
related_terms: Tool Result; Sequential Tool Calls; Partial Observability; Tool Use Accuracy
student_friendly_explanation: A partial tool result is when an AI system produces some but not all of the information it needs to complete a task. It's like if you asked your robot friend to find you a book, but instead of just showing you the book, it also showed you a map of the library where the book is located.
example: When using a search engine to find information about a topic, sometimes the search engine might return only part of the data needed to fully understand the topic. For instance, it might show you a few articles but not the full text of the most relevant article.

definition: The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts solves a task.
related_terms: Least Privilege for Agents; Pass at One; Forward Pass; Training Step
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you have a group of k friends trying to solve a puzzle. The pass at K is like checking if at least one of them can solve it. It's about the chance that at least one of your attempts will work.
example: Suppose you have 3 different algorithms (k=3) to classify images. If the pass at K is 0.95, it means there's a 95% chance that at least one of these algorithms will correctly classify an image.

definition: The probability a model solves a task on its first attempt, the honest deployment measure.
related_terms: Unbiased Pass at K Estimator; Score Variance Across Runs; Staleness of Model Knowledge; Pass at K
student_friendly_explanation: Pass at One is a measure used to evaluate how often an AI model gets a task right on its very first try. It's like checking if you can solve a puzzle correctly without any practice or learning.
example: Imagine you have a robot that needs to identify cats in pictures. If the robot can correctly identify a cat in its first picture it sees, then it has passed the task 'at one'. This helps us understand how well the robot can perform without needing to learn from previous examples.

definition: The linear projection converting an image patch into a token vector.
related_terms: Vision Transformer Patch; Embedding Model; BEiT; E5 Embedding Model
student_friendly_explanation: Patch Embedding is a process where small parts of an image (called patches) are transformed into numerical vectors. These vectors represent the information contained within each patch, which can then be used as input for machine learning models.
example: Imagine you have a small section of an image, like a part of a cat's face. This section is broken down into tiny pixels, and each pixel's color information is converted into a number. These numbers form a vector that represents this part of the image. This vector can then be fed into a model to help it learn patterns from the image.

definition: Tools helping learners give each other useful structured feedback.
related_terms: Structured Interview Support; Feedback Generation for Learners; Mental Health Support Tool; Technology-Assisted Review (TAR)
student_friendly_explanation: Peer Review Support is a tool designed to help students provide each other with useful and structured feedback. It guides them on how to give constructive criticism in a way that is clear and helpful.
example: A peer review support system might prompt students to evaluate each other's projects based on criteria like clarity of explanation, correctness of implementation, and effectiveness of results. This helps ensure that feedback is both specific and beneficial.

definition: A request for user authorization before an agent performs a restricted action.
related_terms: Standing Authorization; Permission Scope; Prompt Evaluation; Prompt Optimization
student_friendly_explanation: Permission Prompt is a process where a user asks for permission from an AI agent before it can perform actions that might be restricted or sensitive. It's like asking for a 'go-ahead' before the AI does something that could have consequences.
example: When using a chatbot for sensitive data, the system first checks if you have given permission to access your personal information. If you grant permission, the chatbot can then proceed to ask for more details or perform actions based on your consent.

definition: The breadth of what a single approval authorizes, which should be narrow and specific.
related_terms: Permission Prompt; Write Tool; Least Privilege for Agents; Scope Statement
student_friendly_explanation: Permission scope is about limiting what a single approval can cover. It's like setting boundaries for what an AI agent can do based on the permission it has. This ensures that actions are clear and controlled.
example: Imagine you have a permission scope that allows an AI agent to edit documents but not to access personal information. This way, the agent can perform its task without overstepping its authority.

definition: Adjusting medication amount to an individual's characteristics and response.
related_terms: Personalized Learning Content; Medication Reconciliation; Personalized Search; Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR)
student_friendly_explanation: Personalized dosing is about adjusting the amount of medication you take based on your unique body characteristics and how your body reacts to the drug.
example: A doctor uses a machine learning algorithm to analyze a patient's genetic information and past medical history to determine the most effective dosage of a new medication.

definition: Educational material adapted to an individual's current understanding.
related_terms: Personalized Dosing; AI in Education; Educational Technology; AI Companion
student_friendly_explanation: Personalized Learning Content refers to educational materials that are customized based on a student's current level of understanding. This means the content is tailored to fit the student's needs, making learning more effective and engaging.
example: An AI system analyzes a student's performance in a course, such as machine learning, and adjusts the difficulty and pace of the lessons to match the student's grasp of the subject matter.

definition: Whether a generated scene obeys a single coherent viewpoint geometry.
related_terms: Narrative Consistency; Multi-View Consistency; Character Consistency; Lighting Consistency
student_friendly_explanation: Perspective consistency ensures that all parts of a generated scene are viewed from the same angle, making the scene appear coherent and realistic.
example: When training a generative model to create images of a room, perspective consistency means that every part of the room (like walls, furniture, and windows) is captured from the same camera position, creating a seamless and believable environment.

definition: Monitoring medicines after approval to detect previously unknown safety issues.
related_terms: Signal Detection in Safety Data; Sentiment Monitoring; Shelf Monitoring; AI in Healthcare
student_friendly_explanation: Pharmacovigilance is like being a detective for medicines. After new drugs are approved, pharmacovigilance helps find out if there are any hidden dangers that weren't seen before.
example: Doctors and researchers use special software to track side effects of medications. When they notice unusual patterns, they alert the drug company and regulators to take action.

definition: Fitting preprocessing on the full dataset before splitting, letting test statistics influence training.
related_terms: Temporal Leakage; Duplicate Leakage; Target Leakage; Feature Scaling Pipeline
student_friendly_explanation: Pipeline leakage occurs when you preprocess all your data at once before splitting it into training and testing sets. This means that the test set can see some information from the future, which is not supposed to happen during training.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of weather measurements over time. If you preprocess (like normalizing values) the entire dataset before splitting it into training and testing sets, and then use this preprocessed data to train your model, the test set might inadvertently include some future weather data. This can lead to misleading results because the model learns patterns based on future information.

definition: The smallest addressable element of a digital image, holding one colour or intensity value.
related_terms: RGB; Histogram Equalization; Photometric Loss; Image Filter
student_friendly_explanation: A pixel is like a tiny dot in an image that can show different colors or shades of gray. It's the smallest part of the image that can be changed individually.
example: Imagine you have a picture of a red ball. Each small dot (pixel) in this picture can be made to look slightly darker or lighter than it was before, changing the overall appearance of the ball.

definition: Carrying out a planned action sequence while monitoring for deviations.
related_terms: Plan Cost Model; Execution Feedback; Replanning; Executor Agent
student_friendly_explanation: Plan execution is about carrying out a series of actions as planned, but it also involves checking if things go wrong along the way and making adjustments if necessary.
example: An AI agent plans to navigate through a maze. It follows a pre-defined path (the plan), but if it encounters an obstacle, it replans a new route based on the feedback it receives.

definition: Inferring a player's skill, style, and preferences to adapt the experience.
related_terms: Skill Rating System; Matchmaking; Health Economics Modelling; Catastrophe Modelling
student_friendly_explanation: Player modelling is like understanding what kind of player you are - whether you're good at certain tasks, prefer certain types of games, or have specific strategies. This helps the game adjust to make your experience more fun and challenging.
example: In a video game, the system learns from your actions and decides which level is best suited for you based on how well you've done in previous levels and what kinds of challenges you enjoy.

definition: Identifying illegal activity in protected areas from sensors and patrol data.
related_terms: Illegal Mining Detection; Defect Detection; Claim Detection; Signal Detection in Safety Data
student_friendly_explanation: Poaching detection is like using special tools and watching eyes to find out if someone is taking things from nature without permission. It helps protect animals and plants in their natural homes.
example: Scientists use cameras and microphones to watch over national parks. When they see unusual behavior, such as people moving around a lot or making loud noises, it might mean poachers are there. They then alert park rangers to come check.

definition: A set of 3D data points in space, typically representing the external surface of objects or environments. Point clouds are generated by LiDAR sensors, stereo cameras, or 3D scanners. Neural networks like PointNet and PointNet++ directly process point clouds for 3D classification, segmentation, and object detection.
related_terms: 3D Vision; LiDAR; Lidar Point Cloud; PointNet
student_friendly_explanation: A point cloud is a collection of dots in 3D space that represent the shape of an object or environment. These dots are collected by special sensors like LiDAR, which measure distances to various points in space. Point clouds are used in computer vision tasks to understand and analyze 3D scenes.
example: Imagine you have a 3D model of a building. A point cloud would be a bunch of tiny dots spread out in space, each dot showing where it was measured from the building's surface. This information can then be used by AI algorithms to recognize different parts of the building or even detect if someone is standing near it.

definition: Helping write internal rules that are consistent and complete.
related_terms: Contract Drafting Assistance; Clinical Documentation Assistance; Writing Assistance; Policy Question Answering
student_friendly_explanation: Policy Drafting Assistance helps create internal rules that are both well-thought-out and comprehensive.
example: A legal team uses Policy Drafting Assistance software to ensure all company policies are clear, enforceable, and cover all necessary aspects, such as employee conduct, safety protocols, and confidentiality guidelines.

definition: Computing the expected return of a fixed policy from each state.
related_terms: Policy Iteration; Behaviour Policy; Stochastic Policy; Target Policy
student_friendly_explanation: Policy evaluation is like calculating the average reward you can expect to get if you stick to a particular decision-making strategy (policy) in a game or situation (state). It's about figuring out what your long-term gains will be based on your chosen actions.
example: Imagine you're playing a video game where you have to make decisions to reach the end goal. Policy evaluation would help you estimate how many points you could score on average if you always made the same decision throughout the game.

definition: Alternating policy evaluation and improvement until the policy stops changing.
related_terms: Policy Evaluation; Policy Improvement; Behaviour Policy; Stochastic Policy
student_friendly_explanation: Policy iteration is like taking turns between evaluating a policy (guessing what action to take) and improving it (making better guesses). You keep doing this until your guesses don't change anymore, which means you've found the best policy.
example: Imagine you're playing a game where you have to guess the color of a ball in a box. At first, you might guess randomly. Then, you look at all the times you guessed wrong and try to guess more accurately next time. You keep doing this until you can't guess any better, and then you stick with that perfect guessing strategy.

definition: Answering questions about internal rules with citations to authoritative sources.
related_terms: Internal Helpdesk Automation; Policy Drafting Assistance; Knowledge Graph (KG); Citation Verification
student_friendly_explanation: Policy Question Answering is a system that helps answer questions about internal rules by using authoritative sources as references.
example: A university uses a Policy Question Answering system to quickly find answers to questions about student conduct policies, citing relevant university regulations.

definition: The structured categorization of content violations a moderation system enforces.
related_terms: Content Moderation at Scale; Appeals in Moderation; Policy Drafting Assistance; Taxonomy
student_friendly_explanation: A policy taxonomy is like organizing rules into different categories. Imagine you have a set of guidelines for what kind of content should be allowed on a platform. A policy taxonomy helps sort these guidelines into groups based on their type, such as whether they're about language use, inappropriate behavior, or other issues. This makes it easier to understand and enforce the rules.
example: In a social media platform, a policy taxonomy might classify content violations into categories like 'offensive language', 'spam', and 'harassment'. This allows the moderation team to quickly identify which category a post falls under and take appropriate action, such as removing the content or sending it to an appeals panel.

definition: A kernel corresponding to all feature products up to a chosen degree.
related_terms: Kernel Methods; String Kernel; Sigmoid Kernel; Kernel PCA
student_friendly_explanation: A polynomial kernel compares how similar two input vectors are based on their polynomial interactions, not by fully expanding those interactions into new features.
example: For a degree of 2, gamma of 1, and coef0 of 1, if two vectors have a dot product of 2, their kernel value is 9, calculated as (2 + 1)².

definition: A downsampling operation in CNNs that reduces the spatial dimensions of feature maps while retaining important information. Max pooling takes the maximum value in each pooling window; average pooling takes the mean. Pooling reduces computation, provides translation invariance, and helps prevent overfitting.
related_terms: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN); Feature Map; Downsampling; Average Pooling
student_friendly_explanation: Pooling is a process used in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to reduce the size of the feature maps. It involves dividing the image into smaller regions called pooling windows and then applying a function to find the most significant values within those windows. This process helps in making the network more efficient and less prone to overfitting.
example: Imagine you have an image of a cat, and you want to extract features from it using a CNN. After the convolution step, you get a large feature map. By applying max pooling, you divide this map into smaller sections and select the highest value in each section. This way, you reduce the number of parameters and make the model simpler without losing crucial information about the cat's features.

definition: Recommending the most popular items to everyone, a surprisingly strong reference point.
related_terms: Popularity Bias; Cold Start for Items; Collaborative Filtering (CF); Item Embedding
student_friendly_explanation: A popularity baseline is a method used in recommender systems where the system recommends the most popular items to all users. This approach can be effective because it leverages the fact that popular items are likely to be of interest to many people, but it can also lead to bias if less popular items are not considered.
example: Imagine a movie recommendation system using a popularity baseline. It would recommend the most watched movies to all users, assuming that these movies are popular and thus likely to be enjoyed by many people. However, this might overlook movies that are not as widely watched but could still be interesting to some users.

definition: Detecting position and orientation of body parts in images or video. Top-down methods detect person first; bottom-up detect all keypoints then group. Applications include sports analytics, animation, and fitness tracking.
related_terms: Computer Vision (CV); Action Recognition; Bottom-Up Pose Estimation; Top-Down Pose Estimation
student_friendly_explanation: Pose estimation is about figuring out where different parts of a person's body are located in an image or video. It can be done top-down, starting with the whole person and then identifying individual body parts, or bottom-up, where all body parts are identified first and then grouped together.
example: In a video of a basketball player, pose estimation could track the movement of their arms and legs as they shoot the ball, allowing us to analyze their technique and speed.

definition: The tendency of users to click higher-ranked results regardless of their actual relevance.
related_terms: Click Model; Click Position Debiasing; Presentation Bias; Title Relevance
student_friendly_explanation: Position Bias is when people tend to click on search results that appear at the top of a list, even if those results might not be the most relevant to what they're looking for. It's like preferring a book you see first in a bookstore over one you read about online.
example: Imagine searching for 'Artificial Intelligence' articles. If the top result is from a well-known AI expert but not necessarily the most recent or relevant, many users might click on it because it's at the top. This can lead to a situation where the most relevant article isn't as popular or clicked on.

definition: The stages after pretraining, including supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.
related_terms: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ); Mid-Training; Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT); Domain-Adaptive Pretraining
student_friendly_explanation: Post-training is what happens after the initial training phase of a model. It includes using labeled data to make the model learn more specific things and adjusting the model based on preferences given to it.
example: Imagine you have a model that can recognize cats and dogs in pictures. Post-training might involve showing it many more pictures of cats and asking it to focus more on recognizing cats, making it better at this task.

definition: Reducing a trained model's numeric precision without further training.
related_terms: Post-Training; Activation Quantization; GPTQ; Weight-Only Quantization
student_friendly_explanation: Post-Training Quantization is a technique used after a neural network has been trained. It involves changing the way numbers are stored in the model's weights and activations to make them simpler and faster to process, without needing additional training.
example: Imagine you have a complex model that can classify images very well. Post-Training Quantization would convert the floating-point numbers representing the model's parameters into smaller, integer values, making it more efficient to run on devices with limited processing power.

definition: The list of documents and positions where a particular term appears.
related_terms: Term Dictionary; Index Compression; Judgment List; Skip Pointer
student_friendly_explanation: A posting list is a list that shows which documents contain a specific word or term. It's like a directory that tells you where to find information about a word.
example: For instance, if we search for the term 'AI' in a document collection, the posting list would show us which documents contain this term and at what positions within those documents.

definition: The initial phase of training a foundation model on a large, diverse dataset to learn general-purpose representations before specialization. For language models, pre-training typically involves next-token prediction on trillions of tokens from the internet. The pre-training phase requires enormous compute resources (thousands of GPUs for weeks to months) and determines the model's base capabilities.
related_terms: Fine-tuning; Foundation Model; Transfer Learning (TL); Next-Token Prediction
student_friendly_explanation: Pre-training is the first step in training a big, smart model. It uses lots of information from the internet to teach the model how to understand words and their meanings. This helps the model learn general things it can use later, even if it's not trained specifically on AI stuff.
example: Imagine you have a magic book that learns from everything you read. Pre-training is like giving this book a huge amount of text to read, so it can understand new words and their meanings better when you ask it about them.

definition: The fraction of the top k results that are relevant.
related_terms: Mean Average Precision (MAP); Context Precision; Pseudo-Relevance Feedback (PRF); Recall at Depth
student_friendly_explanation: Precision at K is a measure used in information retrieval to assess how well a search engine retrieves relevant items from a list of top K results. It calculates the proportion of the first K items that are actually relevant.
example: Suppose you have a list of 10 search results for 'Artificial Intelligence'. If the top 3 results are all about AI research papers, then the precision at K would be 1 (or 100%) because all the top 3 are relevant. However, if the top 3 include some non-relevant results, say 2 out of 3 are relevant, then the precision at K would be 2/3 or approximately 67%.

definition: The inverse relationship between avoiding false positives and catching all positives.
related_terms: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC); False Positive (FP); True Positive (TP); Partial AUC
student_friendly_explanation: Precision-Recall Tradeoff is about balancing the need to avoid false positives (things incorrectly labeled as positive) with the goal of catching all true positives (correctly labeled things). It's like trying to catch all fish without getting any rocks.
example: Imagine you're using a spam filter on emails. If you set it too high for precision (fewer false positives), it might miss some actual spam emails (false negatives). But if you lower the precision, it catches more spam but also includes more non-spam emails (false positives). This tradeoff shows why it's hard to get both right.

definition: Anticipating equipment failures in energy infrastructure before outages occur.
related_terms: Predictive Maintenance; Energy Grid Optimization; Risk Register Maintenance; AI in Manufacturing
student_friendly_explanation: Predictive grid maintenance uses AI to foresee when equipment might break down in power systems, allowing engineers to fix issues before the system goes down, ensuring reliable electricity.
example: An AI system analyzes data from sensors on power lines, predicting when a transformer might fail based on patterns of wear and tear. This allows technicians to replace it before it stops working, preventing widespread blackouts.

definition: AI predicting equipment failures by analyzing sensor data, vibration, temperature, and maintenance records. Identifies degradation patterns and estimates remaining life. Reduces unplanned downtime and optimizes costs.
related_terms: Anomaly Detection; Time Series; Predictive Grid Maintenance; Risk Register Maintenance
student_friendly_explanation: Predictive maintenance uses artificial intelligence to forecast when machines might break down based on information from sensors, vibrations, temperatures, and past repair logs. It recognizes signs of wear and tear and predicts how long the machine can keep working before it needs fixing.
example: A factory uses predictive maintenance software to monitor the health of its machinery. When the system detects unusual patterns in the data from sensors, it alerts technicians to replace parts before a failure occurs, thus avoiding costly downtime.

definition: The total spread of a model's predictive distribution, combining epistemic and aleatoric sources.
related_terms: Epistemic Uncertainty; Aleatoric Uncertainty; Posterior Predictive Distribution; Prior Predictive Distribution
student_friendly_explanation: Predictive uncertainty is about how much we don't know about our predictions. It includes both what we don't understand (epistemic) and random factors (aleatoric). Imagine you're trying to predict the weather, and your model might be wrong because you don't have all the information (epistemic) or because there are unpredictable elements like sudden storms (aleatoric). Together, these uncertainties tell us how confident we should be in our predictions.
example: Suppose you're using a machine learning model to predict stock prices. If the model is uncertain about the exact price due to lack of data (epistemic) or because stock prices can suddenly change without clear patterns (aleatoric), then the predictive uncertainty gives you a range of possible outcomes, helping you make a more informed decision.

definition: An input measurement used by a model to explain or forecast the target.
related_terms: Target Variable; Latent Variable; Latent Variable Model; Factor Analysis
student_friendly_explanation: A predictor variable is like a tool a model uses to understand or predict something it's interested in, called the target variable. It helps the model learn patterns from data.
example: In a study predicting house prices based on various factors, the size of the house (predictor variable) might help the model estimate how much a house costs.

definition: Two candidate responses to the same prompt, one marked better, used to train reward models and policies.
related_terms: Reward Modelling; Length Bias in Reward Models; Pairwise Preference Data; Iterative Preference Optimization
student_friendly_explanation: Preference Pair is a pair of options given to a model to learn from. One option is considered 'better' than the other, and this helps the model understand which response is more appropriate.
example: Imagine you have two sentences: 'The cat sat on the mat' and 'The dog jumped over the fence'. A model trained on Preference Pairs might learn that describing actions (like 'sat' or 'jumped') is more informative than just stating locations ('on the mat' or 'over the fence').

definition: The initial forward pass over an entire prompt that populates the key-value cache before generation begins.
related_terms: Forward Pass; Training Step; Key-Value Memory; Stem
student_friendly_explanation: Prefill is like a first look at all the information in a puzzle before you start solving it. It's a quick scan of the whole problem to fill up some memory space that helps solve the puzzle more efficiently later.
example: Imagine you have a big jigsaw puzzle. Prewrite (prefill) is like looking at every piece of the puzzle at once before you start putting them together. This way, when you start assembling the pieces, you can quickly find where they fit without having to look at every single one again.

definition: An agent stopping before the task is genuinely complete.
related_terms: Termination Condition; Episode; Failure Taxonomy for Agents; Premature Optimization
student_friendly_explanation: Premature termination occurs when an AI system stops executing its task before it has fully completed what it was supposed to do. This can happen if the system detects an error early on or decides to stop based on some predefined conditions.
example: Consider a machine learning model training on a dataset. If the model's performance starts to degrade significantly after a certain number of epochs (episode), the training might be prematurely terminated to save time and resources.

definition: How much demand changes in response to a price change.
related_terms: Demand Response; Slippage; Reserve Price; Dynamic Pricing
student_friendly_explanation: Price elasticity measures how much the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its price. It's calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded relative to the percentage change in price.
example: If you raise the price of a product by 10%, and the quantity demanded decreases by 20%, then the price elasticity of demand is -2 (a negative value indicates an inverse relationship between price and quantity).

definition: Processing insurance approval requests for medical treatment.
related_terms: Procurement Automation; Border Processing Automation; Underwriting Automation; Customer Support Automation
student_friendly_explanation: Prior authorization automation is a system that helps doctors and hospitals quickly get permission from insurance companies before providing certain treatments. This process ensures that patients receive necessary care while also managing insurance costs effectively.
example: A hospital uses an automated system to request prior authorizations for expensive procedures. When a patient needs a costly surgery, the hospital's system automatically sends the required information to the insurance company, streamlining the approval process and ensuring timely access to care.

definition: A benchmark whose questions are never published, preventing contamination and targeted tuning.
related_terms: Held-Out Test Set; Evaluation Cost; LM Evaluation Harness; Natural Questions
student_friendly_explanation: The Private Evaluation Set is a special part of your dataset that you don't share with others. This way, it stays pure and doesn't get influenced by outside knowledge, which helps make sure your AI system really works well on unseen data.
example: Imagine you have a magic box (your model) that can answer questions. A Private Evaluation Set is like a secret test where you ask the box questions without showing them to anyone else. This way, you can be sure the box really knows what it's doing, not just memorizing the questions.

definition: A function giving the probability of each value of a discrete random variable.
related_terms: Law of Total Probability; Marginal Probability; Probability Density Function (PDF); Joint Probability
student_friendly_explanation: The Probability Mass Function (PMF) is like a map that tells you how likely it is to find a specific outcome in a set of possible outcomes. It's used for discrete random variables, which means the outcomes can be counted, like rolling a die or flipping a coin.
example: Imagine you have a bag with 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. If you draw one ball at random, the PMF would tell you the probability of drawing each color. For instance, the PMF might show that there's a 0.6 chance of drawing a red ball and a 0.4 chance of drawing a blue ball.

definition: A function assigning each event a number between zero and one, additive over disjoint events and summing to one overall.
related_terms: Event; Conditional Probability; Mutually Exclusive Events; Marginal Probability
student_friendly_explanation: A probability measure is like a rule that tells you how likely something is to happen. It takes an event (something that can happen) and gives it a number between 0 and 1. This number shows how probable the event is. The rule has some special rules: it always gives a number between 0 and 1, and if two things can't both happen at the same time (mutually exclusive), the rule adds their numbers together. Also, if you add up all the numbers for every possible outcome, it will be 1.
example: Imagine flipping a coin. A probability measure would assign a 0.5 to the event 'heads' and another 0.5 to the event 'tails'. If you flip the coin twice, the probability measure would add the probabilities of getting heads both times (0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25) and the probability of getting tails both times (0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25). Adding these up gives 0.5 + 0.5 = 1, which means the total probability is 1.

definition: Creating content algorithmically from rules and seeds rather than by hand or by learned models.
related_terms: Seed; Seed Variation; Hand Rendering Problem; Asset Variation
student_friendly_explanation: Procedural Content Generation (PCG) is a method where we create content using algorithms based on rules and starting points called seeds, instead of making it manually or by learning from existing data. It's like generating a story or a level in a video game where the rules dictate how things change but not what happens.
example: Imagine you're creating a video game. Instead of drawing every single tree, house, or character by hand, you use a PCG system. This system has rules about how trees grow, houses are built, and characters move. Then, it uses random seeds to generate unique versions of these elements each time the game is played, making the experience different every time.

definition: Streamlining purchasing workflows from request through approval and ordering.
related_terms: Prior Authorization Automation; Customer Support Automation; Compliance Automation; Robotic Process Automation (RPA)
student_friendly_explanation: Procurement automation is about making the process of buying things more efficient. It includes getting requests for purchases, checking if you need permission to buy them (prior authorization), and then placing orders automatically.
example: A university uses procurement automation to streamline the process of ordering textbooks. When a student submits a request for books, the system checks if prior authorization is needed and then automatically places the order without human intervention.

definition: Sequencing manufacturing operations to meet demand within capacity constraints.
related_terms: Scheduling Optimization; Production system (computer science); Job Shop Scheduling (JSSP); Constraint-Based Scheduling
student_friendly_explanation: Production scheduling is about figuring out the best order to make things in a factory to meet the number of items customers want to buy without running out of space or workers.
example: Imagine you have a small toy factory making cars and planes. You need to decide which car parts to make first, then which plane parts, all while keeping track of how many workers you have and how much space you have in your workshop.

definition: A production system (or production rule system) is a computer program typically used to provide some form of artificial intelligence, which consists primarily of a set of rules about behavior, but also includes the mechanism necessary to follow those rules as the system responds to states of the world. Those rules, termed productions, are a basic knowledge representation found useful in automated planning and scheduling, expert systems, and action selection.
related_terms: Production Scheduling; Root Cause Analysis in Production; Business rules engine; Cleverpath AION Business Rules Expert
student_friendly_explanation: A production system is like a set of instructions that a computer uses to make decisions based on what it sees happening around it. These instructions are called productions, and they tell the system how to act in different situations. It's like having a rule book for a game, but instead of playing against other people, the system plays against itself to figure out the best way to solve problems.
example: Imagine you have a robot that needs to clean a room. The production system would be the set of rules that tells the robot how to move around the room, pick up toys, and put them away. Each rule is a production, and together they help the robot learn and improve over time.

definition: A measure indicating whether an agent is converging on its objective.
related_terms: Incremental Progress Check; Subgoal; Checkpointing Agent State; Differential Progress
student_friendly_explanation: A progress metric for agents is a way to see if the AI system is getting closer to what it aims to achieve. It's like checking if you're moving towards your goal in a race.
example: Imagine an AI learning to recognize images. A progress metric could be the accuracy of its guesses over time. If the AI starts guessing correctly more often, it means it's making progress.

definition: How faithfully generated output matches the details requested in its prompt.
related_terms: Prompt Length Effect; Prompt Weighting; Prompt Sharing; Caption Quality
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt Adherence refers to how closely the output generated by a generative AI system matches the specific details provided in its prompt. It's about ensuring that the AI generates information that aligns perfectly with what was asked for, without adding irrelevant details or missing important points.
example: When using a language model to generate text based on a given prompt, if the prompt asks for a detailed analysis of a specific machine learning algorithm, the model should adhere to this request and provide a thorough analysis rather than generating unrelated content.

definition: The practice of crafting and optimizing input text (prompts) to elicit desired outputs from language models. Techniques include few-shot examples, chain-of-thought reasoning, system prompts, role-playing, and structured output formatting. As models become more capable and agentic systems proliferate, prompt engineering is evolving into the broader discipline of 'context engineering.'
related_terms: Large Language Model (LLM); Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting; Context Window; Structured Output
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt engineering is the art of creating and refining text inputs to get the desired output from artificial intelligence models. It involves techniques like using examples, logical reasoning, and specific model configurations to guide the AI in generating the right response.
example: A researcher uses prompt engineering to fine-tune a large language model (LLM) to generate detailed explanations for complex scientific concepts. By providing clear, structured prompts, the model can produce coherent and informative responses.

definition: Automatically rewriting a short user prompt into a richer one before generation.
related_terms: Prompt Weighting; Face Enhancement; Detail Enhancement Pass; Prompt Length Effect
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt Enhancement is a process where a computer system automatically modifies a short initial message from a user (the prompt) into a more detailed and informative one before it generates an answer or response. This enhancement can include adding relevant details, clarifying ambiguous information, or incorporating additional context that wasn't explicitly stated in the original prompt.
example: For instance, if a user asks 'What is AI?', the system might enhance the prompt to 'Could you please provide more information about the different types of artificial intelligence and their applications?' This way, the system provides a richer and more comprehensive response.
