definition: Systematically measuring how prompt variants affect output quality.
related_terms: Prompt Optimization; Prompt Versioning; Automatic Prompt Engineering; Prompt Registry
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt evaluation is the systematic process of assessing how different versions of initial input (prompts) influence the quality of the final output generated by an AI system. It helps researchers and developers understand which variations of prompts lead to better results.
example: In a language model, prompt evaluation might involve testing various ways to introduce a question or instruction at the start, such as 'What is the capital of France?' versus 'The country of France, what is its capital?' to see which leads to more accurate and concise answers.

definition: How the amount of detail in a prompt changes generation fidelity and variability.
related_terms: Prompt Ordering Effect; Prompt Weighting; Prompt Adherence; Prompt Sharing
student_friendly_explanation: The prompt length effect refers to how increasing the number of words or details in a prompt can affect the quality and diversity of the generated response. Longer prompts can lead to more detailed and specific responses, but they might also make the system less flexible in generating varied outputs.
example: When training a language model to generate code snippets, a shorter prompt like 'Write a function' might result in a variety of different but correct code snippets, while a longer prompt such as 'Write a function that takes an array of integers and returns their sum' will likely produce fewer but more specific examples.

definition: Refusing a generation request based on its input before any output is produced.
related_terms: Output-Level Blocking; Classifier-Based Prevention; NSFW Filter; Blocking
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt-Level Blocking is when a system decides not to generate an answer based on the prompt given before it has even started producing an output. It's like if you ask a question, but the system doesn't respond because it thinks your question might be inappropriate or too broad.
example: Imagine you're using a language model to generate code snippets. If the model detects that your prompt contains sensitive information or is too vague, it might block generating the code snippet until you provide more specific details.

definition: A managed store of production prompts with metadata and version history.
related_terms: Prompt Evaluation; Tool Registry; Prompt Optimization; Prompt Versioning
student_friendly_explanation: A prompt registry is like a digital catalog where AI systems can store and manage their input data (prompts) along with information about them and their versions. This helps in organizing and tracking different versions of prompts used in various AI applications.
example: Imagine you're developing an AI chatbot. A prompt registry would allow you to keep track of all the questions and responses your chatbot uses, including which version was last updated and any changes made. This way, you can easily manage and update the chatbot's knowledge base.

definition: The practice of publishing effective prompts so others can reproduce results.
related_terms: Prompt Weighting; Prompt Length Effect; Prompt Adherence; Prompt Enhancement
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt sharing is the act of publicly posting examples of effective input (prompts) used to generate desired outputs, allowing others to use similar inputs to achieve similar results.
example: A researcher publishes a list of successful prompts used to fine-tune a language model for natural language understanding tasks, enabling other researchers to improve their own models by using similar prompts.

definition: Tracking changes to prompts over time so behaviour regressions can be traced.
related_terms: Prompt Evaluation; Prompt Optimization; Automatic Prompt Engineering; Prompt Registry
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt versioning is a method of tracking changes to prompts as they evolve over time, allowing researchers to identify when behavior changes occur and understand their causes.
example: A prompt registry system logs every version of a prompt used in an AI project. When a new version introduces unexpected behavior, the system can trace back to the last stable version, helping to pinpoint the change that caused the issue.

definition: Adjusting the influence of individual words or phrases within a generation prompt.
related_terms: Token Weighting Syntax; Prompt Syntax; Iterative Prompt Refinement; Prompt Ordering Effect
student_friendly_explanation: Prompt weighting is like giving some words more importance than others when you're starting to generate text. It's about adjusting how much each word or phrase counts in your input, which can help the system understand what you want better.
example: For example, if you're writing a paper on natural language processing (NLP), you might use prompt weighting to make sure the words 'NLP', 'algorithm', and 'machine learning' appear more frequently in your generated text compared to other unrelated terms.

definition: The difficulty of choosing pronouns when the source language does not mark them.
related_terms: Pronoun Resolution; Lexical Ambiguity; Syntactic Ambiguity; Cohesion
student_friendly_explanation: When translating from one language to another, pronouns can be tricky because the source language doesn't always mark them. This means that the translator needs to guess which pronoun to use based on context clues.
example: In English, 'he' and 'she' might refer to the same person in a sentence like 'He/She likes apples,' but without additional context, it's hard to know if 'he' or 'she' is being used.

definition: Determining which entity a pronoun refers to.
related_terms: Pronoun Ambiguity in Translation; Winograd Schema; Cohesion; Anaphora
student_friendly_explanation: Pronoun resolution is the process of figuring out which person, number, and referent a pronoun is talking about in a sentence. It's like solving a puzzle where you need to match the pronoun with the noun it's referring to.
example: In the sentence 'He went to the store, and she bought some groceries,' pronoun resolution helps us understand that 'he' refers to the same person as 'He' and 'she' refers to the same person as 'her.'

definition: The public archive of experimentally determined biological macromolecule structures.
related_terms: CASP; UniProt; Bank Conflict; Protein Design
student_friendly_explanation: The Protein Data Bank (PDB) is an online repository where scientists store detailed images of protein molecules. These images are created using advanced technology that captures the shape and structure of proteins, which helps researchers understand how these molecules work in living organisms.
example: Scientists can use PDB to visualize the three-dimensional structure of a protein, such as hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in our blood. This visualization helps them study how the protein functions and interacts with other molecules.

definition: The shared systems needed for content origin claims to be widely verifiable.
related_terms: Content Provenance; Data Provenance Tracking; Data Provenance Standard; Provenance Metadata
student_friendly_explanation: Provenance infrastructure refers to the shared systems that help verify where data comes from. It ensures that information can be traced back to its original source, making it easier to trust the authenticity of the data.
example: A digital library uses provenance infrastructure to track the origins of all documents. This allows users to verify if a document is authentic and has not been tampered with, ensuring the integrity of the information.

definition: Embedded information recording how a piece of content was created and edited.
related_terms: Content Provenance; Data Provenance Tracking; Data Provenance Standard; Provenance Infrastructure
student_friendly_explanation: Provenance metadata is like a storybook that tells you how a document, image, or video was made and changed over time. It includes details about who created it, when they did it, and any changes they made.
example: A digital photo has provenance metadata that shows who took the picture, when it was taken, and any adjustments made to the image later on.

definition: Using data and automation to improve how government services reach people.
related_terms: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI); Customer Support Automation; Last Mile Delivery; Refugee Services Planning
student_friendly_explanation: Public Service Delivery uses technology like data and automation to make it easier for the government to provide services to people. This means using digital tools to help deliver services more efficiently and effectively.
example: A city government uses AI to streamline its service delivery process. By analyzing data on public needs, the city can predict where services are most needed and allocate resources accordingly, ensuring that essential services reach everyone.

definition: Planning routes and schedules to match demand within resource limits.
related_terms: Route Optimization; Demand Planning; Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI); Scheduling Optimization
student_friendly_explanation: Public transit optimization is about figuring out the best way to plan bus, train, or subway routes and schedules to meet the needs of people who want to use them, while also using the resources available like buses, trains, and tracks efficiently.
example: A city uses an algorithm to analyze past data on when and where people take public transportation. It then creates schedules and routes that minimize wait times and ensure all passengers can get where they need to go without overcrowding.

definition: A citation network of biomedical publications used in graph neural network evaluation.
related_terms: Reddit Graph Dataset; Cora Dataset; Citeseer Dataset; OGB
student_friendly_explanation: The PubMed Graph Dataset is a collection of biomedical papers connected through citations. It's used to test machine learning models that understand relationships between scientific articles.
example: Imagine you have a list of medical research papers. Each paper cites other papers. The PubMed Graph Dataset shows these citations as connections between nodes (papers). Researchers use this dataset to train their algorithms on how to recognize important papers and their relationships.

definition: A model-free RL algorithm learning the value of each action in each state, stored in a Q-table. Updates via Bellman equation. Deep Q-Learning (DQN) extends to continuous states using neural networks.
related_terms: Q-Function; Deep Q-Network (DQN); Bellman Equation; Q-Learning Update
student_friendly_explanation: Q-learning is a method used in artificial intelligence to learn the best actions to take in different situations. It does this by creating a table called a Q-table, which stores the value of each possible action in every state. This table is updated based on the results of actions taken, following a rule called the Bellman equation. Over time, it learns which actions lead to the best outcomes.
example: Imagine you're playing a game where you have to choose between two actions: move left or right. Q-learning would help you figure out which action leads to the most points by keeping track of the rewards you get from each choice and adjusting its estimate accordingly.

definition: An off-policy update moving a value estimate toward the reward plus the best next-state value.
related_terms: Q-Learning; Double Q-Learning; Conservative Q-Learning (CQL); Implicit Q-Learning (IQL)
student_friendly_explanation: Q-Learning Update is a method used in reinforcement learning where we adjust our estimate of the value of a state based on the immediate reward we receive and the best possible future reward we could get from the next state, without actually knowing the exact future rewards.
example: Imagine you're playing a game where you want to maximize your score. After each move, you get a reward. Q-Learning Update helps you decide how much to improve your current strategy based on the immediate reward and the best possible score you could achieve if you chose the best action at the next step.

definition: Removing low-quality documents from a corpus using heuristics or learned classifiers.
related_terms: Heuristic Filtering; Toxicity Filtering; Deduplication of Training Data; Perplexity Filtering
student_friendly_explanation: Quality filtering is a process where we remove documents that don't meet certain standards from a collection of texts. This is done using rules (heuristics) or machine learning models (learned classifiers) to decide which documents should be kept.
example: Imagine you have a large library of text data about AI research papers. Quality filtering could help you remove papers that are poorly written, contain errors, or are irrelevant to your study. This way, you can focus on high-quality resources that will improve your understanding.

definition: A threshold a candidate must clear to progress through a release process.
related_terms: Threshold Selection; Confidence Threshold; Release Readiness Review; Acceptance Criteria
student_friendly_explanation: A quality gate is like a checkpoint where a project or software release needs to meet certain standards before moving on to the next phase. It's a way to ensure that all necessary checks are done before something can be released.
example: Imagine you're working on a big software project. Before you can move on to testing, there might be a quality gate that requires your code to pass a series of tests. If it passes, you can proceed to the next stage, but if it fails, you need to fix issues before moving forward.

definition: Predicting the remainder of a search query as a user types.
related_terms: Query Rewriting; Query Expansion; Query Understanding; Query Focus
student_friendly_explanation: Query Autocomplete is a technique used in Natural Language Processing where a system predicts the remaining part of a search query based on the text you've already typed. It helps anticipate what you might type next, making the search process faster and more efficient.
example: As you start typing 'How can I improve my', the autocomplete feature suggests 'algorithm performance' or 'code optimization', suggesting relevant words to complete your query.

definition: Adding related terms to a query to retrieve documents that use different wording.
related_terms: Query Rewriting; Vocabulary Expansion; Query Autocomplete; Query Understanding
student_friendly_explanation: Query expansion is a technique used in natural language processing where we add related terms to a search query to help find documents that might use different words but convey the same meaning as the original query. This helps in retrieving more relevant information than using just the exact wording of the query.
example: For example, if you search for 'machine learning', query expansion can add synonyms like 'artificial intelligence' or 'deep learning' to your search, ensuring that documents discussing these topics are also included in the results.

definition: The classification of searches as navigational, informational, or transactional.
related_terms: Navigational Query; Informational Query; Transactional Query; Query Log Analysis
student_friendly_explanation: Query intent taxonomy is a way to categorize search requests into three main types: navigational, informational, and transactional. Navigational queries aim to find specific websites or pages, informational queries seek detailed information about topics, and transactional queries involve making purchases or completing actions online.
example: A user searching for 'best AI courses' on an e-learning platform would be classified as an informational query, while a user looking to buy a specific AI course from the same platform would be considered a transactional query.

definition: A store of complete result pages for frequently repeated searches.
related_terms: Blended Results; Zero Result Rate; Result Deduplication; Result Diversification
student_friendly_explanation: Query Result Cache is like a digital storage system that saves the complete results of common searches. Imagine it as a library where you can quickly find books you've borrowed before, without having to go through the whole process again.
example: When searching for information on machine learning algorithms, if the cache has already stored the results of previous queries, it can retrieve them instantly, saving time and effort.

definition: Reformulating a user query into a form that retrieves better results.
related_terms: Query Expansion; Query Autocomplete; Query Understanding; Query Focus
student_friendly_explanation: Query rewriting is the process of changing a user's original question into a more precise or broader version that helps search engines find relevant information more effectively.
example: A user might type 'what is deep learning' but the system could rewrite it as 'definition of deep learning' or 'explain deep learning', which would lead to better search results.

definition: Directing a query to the shards or replicas most likely to serve it well.
related_terms: Query Performance Prediction (QPP); Structured Query Generation; Query Likelihood; Query Suggestion
student_friendly_explanation: Query routing is like sending your homework to the printer closest to you instead of the farthest one. It helps computers send search requests to the parts of their system that can answer them best, making searches faster and more efficient.
example: Imagine a big library with many computers. When someone searches for information, query routing decides which computer has the most relevant books or files to show, similar to finding the nearest bookshelf.

definition: Proposing related searches that may better serve a user's underlying need.
related_terms: Trie-Based Suggestion; Information Need; Query Routing; Query Performance Prediction (QPP)
student_friendly_explanation: Query suggestion is about suggesting other search terms that might better match what you're looking for, based on the information you've already searched for or the context of your query.
example: When you search for 'Artificial Intelligence', the system might suggest 'AI applications' or 'machine learning' if it detects that you're interested in those topics.

definition: Interpreting a search query's intent, entities, and constraints before retrieval.
related_terms: Multi-Page Document Understanding; Query Expansion; Query Rewriting; Query Autocomplete
student_friendly_explanation: Query understanding is about figuring out what you really mean when you type something into a search engine or a system. It involves looking at the words you use, any numbers or special parts (like dates), and making sure the system knows exactly what information you want to find.
example: For instance, if you type 'AI research papers' into a search engine, query understanding helps it understand that you're looking for documents about AI research. It might also recognize that you want recent papers, even if you didn't explicitly add a date range.

definition: Predicting search demand to prepare content and capacity.
related_terms: Tail Query; Query Performance Prediction (QPP); Trending Query Detection; Structured Query Generation
student_friendly_explanation: Query Volume Forecasting is about predicting how many searches for certain topics will happen in the future. This helps universities and tech companies prepare their systems to handle more requests without slowing down.
example: A university uses historical data to forecast the number of times students will search for information on specific AI topics like neural networks or machine learning algorithms. Based on this prediction, they can adjust their online resources and training materials to meet the expected demand.

definition: An NLP task where systems automatically answer natural language questions. Types include extractive (selecting spans), abstractive (generating new text), open-domain, and closed-book QA. RAG systems enhance QA with retrieved context.
related_terms: Information Retrieval (IR); Reading Comprehension; Extractive Question Answering; Abstractive Question Answering
student_friendly_explanation: Question Answering (QA) is an NLP task where systems process natural language questions and generate answers. It can be categorized into different types like extractive and abstractive, which involve selecting or generating text to answer questions. QA systems also work with open-domain and closed-book scenarios, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve QA by using additional context from documents.
example: A QA system might answer a question like 'What is the capital of France?' by extracting information directly from a document or database, or it could generate an answer based on general knowledge, possibly supplemented with external data.

definition: Organizing waiting work or customers to balance throughput and fairness.
related_terms: Knowledge Management; Case Management; Algorithmic Management Transparency; Building Energy Management
student_friendly_explanation: Queue management is about organizing people or tasks in line to make sure everyone gets served fairly and quickly. It helps manage wait times and ensures that resources are used efficiently.
example: A bank uses queue management software to process customer requests. This system assigns tasks to tellers based on their availability and prioritizes urgent requests, ensuring all customers are attended to in an orderly manner.

definition: An open-weight multilingual model family with strong performance on Chinese and English tasks.
related_terms: Baichuan; DeepSeek; Falcon; Gemma
student_friendly_explanation: Qwen is an open-source multilingual model that performs well on Chinese and English language tasks. It's part of a family of models called Baichuan, DeepSeek, Falcon, and Gemma.
example: Qwen can be used to translate text between Chinese and English, understand natural language queries, and generate responses in both languages.

definition: Extracting a randomly positioned sub-region during training to encourage translation robustness.
related_terms: Center Crop; Image Augmentation; Random Erasing; Multi-Crop Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: Random Crop is a technique used in computer vision during training. It involves selecting a random part of an image to use as input, which helps the model learn from various parts of the image rather than just one fixed area.
example: Imagine you have a photo of a cat. Instead of always using the same part of the photo (like the head or the tail), Random Crop picks a random section of the photo, like cropping a book page, to train the model. This way, the model learns to recognize the cat no matter where it appears in the photo.

definition: Blanking a random rectangle during training to improve robustness to occlusion.
related_terms: Random Crop; Continual Learning for Vision; Occlusion Sensitivity; Occlusion Handling
student_friendly_explanation: Random Erasing is a technique used in training computer vision models. During training, a random rectangular region of the image is blanked out (or 'erased') to make the model more robust against situations where parts of the image might be hidden or obscured (occluded). This helps the model learn to recognize objects even when they are partially covered.
example: Imagine you have a photo of a bird flying over a tree. If part of the bird's wing is hidden by the tree, Random Erasing would randomly erase a small area of the image, forcing the model to focus on other parts of the bird to still recognize it.

definition: An ensemble learning method that constructs multiple decision trees during training, each on a random subset of features and data, then aggregates their predictions through majority voting (classification) or averaging (regression). Random forests are robust, require minimal tuning, handle missing values well, and remain among the strongest methods for tabular data despite the deep learning revolution.
related_terms: Decision Tree; Gradient Boosting; Classification; Deep Learning (DL)
student_friendly_explanation: Random Forest is like creating many decision trees at once, where each tree makes decisions based on different sets of features and some randomly selected data points. These trees work together to make predictions, and their collective wisdom helps improve accuracy compared to a single decision tree.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of emails, and you want to classify them as spam or not spam. A Random Forest would create several decision trees, each trained on a different subset of email features and a different set of emails. Each tree might predict an email as spam or not spam differently, but when combined, they can make more accurate predictions about whether an email should be flagged as spam.

definition: Sampling hyperparameter configurations at random, usually more efficient than grid search in high dimensions.
related_terms: Grid Search; Random Search Baseline; Hyperparameter Search Space; Random Field
student_friendly_explanation: Random Search is like flipping a coin to pick different settings for something called hyperparameters. It's quicker than trying every single possible setting, which can be very time-consuming when there are many options.
example: Imagine you're trying to find the best recipe for making cookies. Instead of testing every single ingredient combination (which would take forever), you could randomly pick some ingredients to see what works best. This way, you might find a good recipe faster than if you tested all possibilities.

definition: Deriving the distribution of a function of a random variable, requiring a Jacobian correction in the continuous case.
related_terms: Random Field; Random Walk; Variable Elimination; Moment
student_friendly_explanation: A random variable transformation is when we take a random variable (a variable whose values are determined by chance) and create a new random variable by applying a mathematical function to it. This process can change the distribution of the original random variable, and we need to adjust for this change using something called the Jacobian in continuous cases.
example: Suppose you have a random variable X representing the number of heads in two coin flips. Its possible outcomes are 0, 1, or 2. If we transform this into a new random variable Y = X^2, which represents the square of the number of heads, then Y could be 0, 1, or 4. The distribution of Y will be different from X, and we would need to calculate the new probabilities using the Jacobian if we were dealing with continuous variables.

definition: A process whose position changes by independent random increments, the simplest diffusion model.
related_terms: Brownian Motion; Random Field; Random Variable Transformation; Diffusion Process
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're walking randomly in a park without following any path. Each step you take is independent of the last, and the direction and distance of each step are chosen randomly. This kind of movement can be described as a random walk.
example: Consider a robot moving on a grid. At each time step, the robot moves one step in a random direction (up, down, left, right) from its current position. This simple action demonstrates a random walk.

definition: A cap on how many requests a client may make in a period.
related_terms: Step Limit; Success Rate; Throttling; Context Isolation
student_friendly_explanation: A rate limit is like a speed limit for your internet connection. It's a rule that tells you how many times you can ask for information from a server within a certain time frame. For example, if a website has a rate limit of 50 requests per minute, it means you can't send more than 50 requests to their server in one minute.
example: Imagine you're building an AI chatbot that sends requests to a language model API every second. If the API has a rate limit of 100 requests per minute, after 60 seconds, you would have sent 100 requests, which is the maximum allowed. Any additional requests would be ignored or might even trigger a 'throttle' event.

definition: Preparing evaluators so their judgements are consistent and aligned with the rubric.
related_terms: Rater Pool Diversity; Rubric Scoring; Attention Check; Blind Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: Rater training is a process where assessors are prepared to make consistent judgments according to a set of guidelines called a rubric. This ensures that everyone evaluates the same criteria in the same way.
example: In a peer review session for a research paper, rater training helps ensure that all reviewers use the same set of questions (rubric) to evaluate the paper's structure, clarity, and evidence, leading to more reliable and comparable feedback.

definition: Adjusting text complexity to match an intended audience's reading level.
related_terms: Readability Score; Domain Adaptation for Translation; Dialect Adaptation; Reading Order Detection
student_friendly_explanation: Readability Adaptation is about changing the way text is written to make it easier to understand for people who don't have much experience with the topic. It's like when you write instructions for someone who isn't as familiar with computers as you are.
example: A readability adaptation tool might change complex sentences into simpler ones, use more common words, and add examples to help readers grasp the concepts better.

definition: Answering questions about a provided passage, a core benchmark of language understanding.
related_terms: Extractive Question Answering; Reading Order Detection; Multi-Hop Question Answering; Abstractive Question Answering
student_friendly_explanation: Reading comprehension is the ability to understand and derive meaning from written text. It involves answering questions about a given passage, which tests your understanding of the information presented.
example: Given a passage about machine learning algorithms, you can answer questions like 'What is the main difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?' This requires you to comprehend the text and extract relevant information to form a correct answer.

definition: The fraction of true nearest neighbours appearing in an approximate method's top k results.
related_terms: Edited Nearest Neighbours (ENN); Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN); HNSW; Large Margin Nearest Neighbor
student_friendly_explanation: Recall at K is a measure used in machine learning to evaluate how well an algorithm can find the correct nearest neighbors among the top K results it returns. It calculates the proportion of correct nearest neighbors in the top K results.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of images of cats and dogs. An ANN algorithm might return the top 5 images that are closest to a new image you're trying to classify. If 3 out of those 5 images are actually cats, then the Recall at K would be 60% (3/5). This tells us how often the algorithm correctly identifies the nearest neighbors.

definition: AI predicting user preferences and suggesting relevant items. Approaches: collaborative filtering (user-item interactions), content-based (item features), and hybrid methods. Deep learning powers Netflix, Amazon, Spotify, YouTube.
related_terms: Collaborative Filtering (CF); Content-Based Filtering; Size Recommendation; Content Recommendation in Education
student_friendly_explanation: A recommendation system is an AI tool that predicts what users might like based on their past behavior or characteristics of the items. It suggests relevant things to them.
example: Imagine you often watch movies about space exploration. A recommendation system might notice this pattern and suggest other space-related movies to you.

definition: Flagging inputs an autoencoder fails to reconstruct well as likely anomalies.
related_terms: Autoencoder Anomaly Detection; Anomaly Detection; Anomaly Score; Denoising Autoencoder (DAE)
student_friendly_explanation: Reconstruction error anomaly detection is a method used in machine learning where an autoencoder, which is a type of neural network, tries to recreate input data. If the autoencoder struggles to create a perfect copy of the input, it flags this as an anomaly, indicating something might be wrong with the data.
example: Imagine you have a set of images, and you train an autoencoder on them. When the autoencoder can't perfectly recreate some images, it signals that there's an anomaly in those images, possibly due to noise or corruption.

definition: A neural network architecture designed for sequential data that maintains a hidden state updated at each time step. RNNs can theoretically capture long-range dependencies but suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients in practice. LSTM and GRU variants address gradient issues with gating mechanisms. RNNs have been largely superseded by transformers for most sequence tasks.
related_terms: Transformer; Neural Network (NN); Gradient; Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
student_friendly_explanation: A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is a type of neural network that processes sequential data by maintaining a hidden state that updates at each time step. This allows it to capture patterns over time, like predicting the next word in a sentence. However, RNNs can struggle with long-term dependencies because the hidden state can lose information over many steps. To overcome this, variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) use special mechanisms to control the flow of information better.
example: Consider a simple RNN model trained on a sequence of text. As it processes each word, the RNN updates its internal state based on the current input and the previous state. This helps the model learn to predict the next word in the sequence, such as predicting 'the' after seeing 'a' and 'cat'. The model uses this updated state to make more informed decisions about future predictions.

definition: An adversarial input designed to elicit unsafe or incorrect behaviour during testing.
related_terms: Automated Red Teaming; Prompt Versioning; Prompt Evaluation; Prompt Optimization
student_friendly_explanation: The red team prompt is an adversarial input crafted to provoke undesirable or incorrect behavior during tests. It's used to simulate real-world threats and improve AI systems' robustness.
example: A red team prompt might be a slightly altered version of a normal input that causes an AI system to make a mistake, such as misinterpreting a command or making a logical error.

definition: How strongly a supplied example constrains generated output.
related_terms: Style Strength; Style Reference; Denoising Strength; Reference-Guided Generation
student_friendly_explanation: The reference image strength is a measure of how much a given example image influences the generated output image. It's like how much you want your painting to look similar to a reference photo.
example: Suppose you have a reference image of a cat and you want to generate an image of a cat using a generative AI model. If the reference image strength is high, the generated cat will closely resemble the reference image. Conversely, if it's low, the generated cat might look more abstract or creative.

definition: A second generation stage that improves detail in an initial output.
related_terms: Detail Enhancement Pass; Iterative Prompt Refinement; Iterative Refinement Workflow; Batch Generation
student_friendly_explanation: The refinement pass is like making a first draft better. It's a step where you take the initial output and make it more detailed and accurate. Imagine you're writing a paper, and after your first draft, you go back and add more information, correct errors, and explain things more clearly.
example: In a machine learning project, after the first iteration of training a model, the refinement pass involves analyzing the model's performance and adjusting parameters to improve accuracy and reduce errors.

definition: Forecasting and allocating support for displaced populations.
related_terms: Public Service Delivery; Demand Planning; Workforce Planning; Customer Support Automation
student_friendly_explanation: Refugee Services Planning is about predicting and distributing resources to help people who have been forced to leave their homes. It involves estimating the needs of displaced individuals and then organizing services like food, shelter, and healthcare to meet those needs effectively.
example: A city uses data analytics to forecast the number of refugees it will receive based on past migration patterns. Then, they plan to allocate resources such as housing units, medical centers, and food banks to ensure all refugees have access to essential services.

definition: A model declining to fulfil a request it judges harmful or outside its policy.
related_terms: Refusal Calibration; Guardrail Policy; Over-Refusal; Model Selection Policy
student_friendly_explanation: When an AI agent, like a chatbot, decides not to respond to a request it deems too risky or off-topic based on its programmed rules, it's refusing the request. This decision is part of its 'Guardrail Policy' and helps ensure it stays within safe boundaries.
example: A language model might refuse to generate explicit content if it detects it could be harmful, even if the user requests it.

definition: A supervised learning task where the model predicts a continuous numerical value rather than a discrete class label. Types include linear regression, polynomial regression, and ridge/lasso regression. Evaluation metrics include mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and R-squared. Deep learning extends regression to high-dimensional outputs like image generation.
related_terms: Classification; Supervised Learning; Linear Regression; Mean Squared Error (MSE)
student_friendly_explanation: Regression is a type of machine learning where we try to predict a number that changes smoothly, like how tall you might be when you grow up. It's different from classification, which tells us if something belongs to one group or another.
example: Imagine you have a garden and you want to predict how many tomatoes will grow based on the amount of water and sunlight it gets. You could use a simple linear regression model to make this prediction.

definition: A final layer producing continuous values rather than class probabilities.
related_terms: Classifier Head; Reward Model Architecture; Class Token in ViT; Vision Backbone
student_friendly_explanation: The regression head is like a special part at the end of a model that predicts numbers instead of just saying yes or no. It's used when we want to know a specific value, like how many times something happens, rather than just categorizing it into different groups.
example: Imagine you have a model that predicts the temperature outside based on weather data. The regression head would output a single number representing the predicted temperature, which could be 22 degrees Celsius, 23 degrees Celsius, etc., rather than just telling you if it will be hot or cold.

definition: Techniques used to prevent overfitting by adding constraints or penalties to the learning process. Common approaches include L1 regularization (lasso, promotes sparsity), L2 regularization (ridge, penalizes large weights), dropout (randomly deactivating neurons during training), weight decay, and early stopping. The right regularization strategy depends on the model architecture and data characteristics.
related_terms: Overfitting; Dropout; Weight Decay; Early Stopping
student_friendly_explanation: Regularization is like adding a rule to your learning process to make sure you don't get too good at memorizing the training data instead of understanding the real pattern. It helps prevent your model from becoming too complex and overfitting, which means it performs well on practice but poorly on new unseen data.
example: Imagine you're trying to predict house prices based on their size. Without regularization, your model might learn every tiny detail about the houses, including the color of the paint, which doesn't help much in making accurate predictions. Regularization adds a penalty for these small details, making your model simpler and more reliable.

definition: Tracking rule updates and mapping them to affected internal obligations.
related_terms: Obligation Tracking; Regulatory Reporting; Livestock Monitoring; Sentiment Monitoring
student_friendly_explanation: Regulatory Change Monitoring is like keeping track of changes in rules made by authorities, and making sure your own actions follow those new rules. It's like when the school changes its rules, and you make sure you're still following all the guidelines.
example: Imagine a company that makes toys. When the government changes its safety regulations, the company needs to monitor these changes. They then adjust their internal processes to ensure they comply with the new rules, such as testing their products more rigorously.

definition: Producing the periodic submissions a supervisory authority requires.
related_terms: Regulatory Change Monitoring; Regulatory Capital Model; Compliance Automation; Model Explainability Requirement
student_friendly_explanation: Regulatory Reporting is the process of submitting regular reports to a supervisory authority as required by law. These reports provide information about a company's financial health, risk management, and other key aspects.
example: A bank submits monthly regulatory reports to the central bank detailing its loan portfolio, interest rates, and credit risk exposure, which helps the central bank monitor the stability of the banking system.

definition: A machine learning paradigm where an agent learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment. The agent receives rewards or penalties for its actions and learns a policy that maximizes cumulative reward over time. RL has achieved superhuman performance in games like Go and has applications in robotics, autonomous driving, and resource optimization.
related_terms: Q-Learning; Policy Gradient; Markov Decision Process (MDP); Policy
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're playing a game where you get points for doing well and lose points for doing poorly. Reinforcement Learning is like learning how to play this game by getting better at it over time. You learn from your mistakes and successes, and you try to always score the most points possible.
example: In a simple game, imagine you have a robot that can move left or right. The robot gets a point every time it moves towards a target and loses a point if it moves away. Over time, the robot learns which direction to move to get more points, just like a human player would.

definition: Alternative queries shown to help users explore a topic further.
related_terms: Query Suggestion; Session Success; Query Performance Prediction (QPP); Head Query
student_friendly_explanation: The Related Search feature shows alternative queries to help you find more information on a topic. It's like when you search for 'Artificial Intelligence' and it suggests other related terms like 'Machine Learning', 'Deep Learning', and 'Neural Networks'. This helps you explore the topic further and get a broader understanding.
example: When searching for 'Artificial Intelligence', the system might show suggestions such as 'Machine Learning', 'Deep Learning', and 'Neural Networks'. These suggestions are based on the query performance prediction (QPP) algorithm, which analyzes your search history and context to provide relevant alternatives.

definition: Identifying structured relationships between entities stated in text.
related_terms: Open Information Extraction (OpenIE); Information Extraction (IE); Zero-Shot Extraction; Event Extraction
student_friendly_explanation: Relation extraction is a process in natural language processing where we identify and understand the connections or relationships between different pieces of information mentioned in text. It's like finding out how different parts of a story are connected.
example: In a sentence like 'John gave a book to Mary', relation extraction would identify the relationship between John and Mary as the giver and receiver, and the relationship between the book and the action of giving.

definition: Error expressed as a fraction of the true value, comparable across scales.
related_terms: Error Distribution; Mean Absolute Error (MAE); Median Absolute Error (MedAE); Scale-Dependent Metric
student_friendly_explanation: Relative error is a way to measure how far off an estimated value is from the actual value, but it's adjusted so that it can be compared across different scales. It's calculated by dividing the absolute difference between the estimated value and the actual value by the actual value itself.
example: Suppose you estimate the weight of a bag of apples to be 5 kg, but the actual weight is 4.8 kg. The absolute error is 0.2 kg. To find the relative error, you divide this by the actual weight: 0.2 / 4.8 = 0.0417. This tells you that your estimate was about 4.17% off from the real weight.

definition: A structured assessment confirming a system meets all criteria before deployment.
related_terms: Acceptance Criteria; Quality Gate; Readiness Assessment; Security Review
student_friendly_explanation: A Release Readiness Review is like a final check-up for your project before it goes live. It's a structured way to make sure everything is working as it should and meets all the rules and requirements you need to have before you can use it.
example: Imagine you're building a new app. A Release Readiness Review would be like having a meeting with your team to go over all the features, fix any bugs, and make sure everything follows the company's guidelines before you let everyone download it.

definition: Improving results by incorporating a user's judgements about initial results.
related_terms: Graded Relevance; Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR); Relevance Engineer; Title Relevance
student_friendly_explanation: Relevance feedback is a method used in information retrieval to refine search results based on users' judgments of those results. It helps improve the quality of search outcomes by allowing users to indicate which parts of the retrieved documents are most relevant to their query.
example: Imagine you're searching for papers on deep learning. After seeing some initial results, you mark certain papers as 'relevant.' The system then uses this feedback to adjust future searches, showing you more papers that align better with your interests and understanding.

definition: A human assessment of how well a document satisfies a query.
related_terms: Judgment List; Graded Relevance; Query Performance Prediction (QPP); Title Relevance
student_friendly_explanation: Relevance judgment is when a person decides if a document is good enough to answer a question you ask about it. It's like checking if a book has information that matches what you're looking for.
example: Imagine you're searching for information on machine learning. A relevance judgment would be when someone looks at a document and decides if it contains useful details about machine learning concepts.

definition: Tracking health indicators from a patient's home between visits.
related_terms: Livestock Monitoring; Regulatory Change Monitoring; Sentiment Monitoring; Fisheries Monitoring
student_friendly_explanation: Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) is a technology that allows healthcare providers to track patients' health information, such as blood pressure or heart rate, using devices at home. This helps doctors stay informed about their patients' health without requiring frequent in-person visits.
example: A doctor uses an RPM system to monitor a patient's blood pressure readings taken at home. These readings are sent to the doctor's office, allowing the doctor to adjust medication or treatment plans based on the patient's health status.

definition: A decoding adjustment reducing the probability of tokens already generated.
related_terms: Presence Penalty; Frequency Penalty; KL Penalty in RLHF; Heuristic Filtering
student_friendly_explanation: Repetition Penalty is a technique used during the training of language models. It adjusts the model's output by making it less likely to repeat previously generated words, which helps in generating more varied and diverse text.
example: Imagine you're training a language model to generate text about AI. With Repetition Penalty, if the model generates 'AI' again, it becomes slightly less probable than other words, encouraging it to explore different aspects of AI rather than just repeating itself.

definition: A data structure in reinforcement learning that stores past experiences (transitions) and provides random samples for training. By breaking temporal correlations and enabling data reuse, replay buffers improve sample efficiency and training stability. Prioritized replay buffers weight important transitions more heavily for faster learning.
related_terms: Experience Replay; Deep Q-Network (DQN); Sample Efficiency; Prioritized Experience Replay
student_friendly_explanation: A replay buffer is like a digital memory bank for artificial intelligence systems. It saves all the information about what happened in previous situations, which helps the system learn better and faster. This way, it can practice making decisions without starting from scratch every time.
example: Imagine you're playing a video game where your character learns to navigate through levels. A replay buffer would be like saving all the paths you took in previous levels. When the AI system needs to make a decision, it can look at these saved paths to get a good idea of what might work, making the learning process quicker and more effective.

definition: Automatically producing written analysis from data and context.
related_terms: Motion Generation; Variation Generation; Conditional Generation; Hierarchical Generation
student_friendly_explanation: Report generation is the process of automatically creating written analyses based on given data and context. It involves using algorithms to analyze information and produce detailed reports without human intervention.
example: A natural language processing (NLP) system can generate a report analyzing customer feedback data, summarizing trends and issues, which can then be used by marketing teams to improve products.

definition: A unit whose output adds its input to a learned transformation, easing optimization of deep stacks.
related_terms: Bottleneck Block; Transformer Block; Residual Stream; Residual Post-Init Scaling
student_friendly_explanation: A residual block is a type of neural network layer that takes an input, applies a learned transformation (like a series of operations), and then adds this transformed input back to the original input. This process helps the network learn more complex patterns without getting stuck in local minima during training.
example: Imagine you have a function that maps inputs to outputs. A residual block might add a small tweak to the output before adding it back to the original input. This way, the network can learn subtle changes in the data without losing track of the overall structure.

definition: Fitting images to a fixed input size while preserving aspect ratio with padding.
related_terms: Resize Interpolation; Aspect Ratio Distortion; Aspect Ratio; Ratio Test
student_friendly_explanation: Resize and pad is a technique used in computer vision to make images fit into a standard size without distorting their proportions. This process involves scaling the image to a fixed width or height while maintaining the original aspect ratio by adding extra pixels (padding) around the edges.
example: Consider an image of a cat that is 400x300 pixels. To resize and pad it to 256x256 pixels, we first scale the image to 256x256 while keeping the original aspect ratio. Then, we add padding to ensure all sides are equal, resulting in a final image that looks similar to the original but fits within the new dimensions.

definition: The method used to compute pixel values when changing image dimensions.
related_terms: Resize and Pad; Bilinear Interpolation; Bicubic Interpolation; Nearest Neighbor Interpolation
student_friendly_explanation: Resize interpolation is a technique used to adjust the size of an image while maintaining its quality. It involves computing new pixel values based on the positions of existing pixels in the original image.
example: Consider an image resized from 640x480 pixels to 320x240 pixels. Resize interpolation calculates the new pixel values by averaging the colors of nearby pixels in the original image, ensuring the resized image looks smooth and consistent.

definition: Residual Network, a deep CNN introducing skip connections to enable training of very deep networks. By learning residual mappings, ResNets avoid degradation. Variants (ResNet-50, ResNet-101) remain standard computer vision baselines.
related_terms: Skip Connection; Residual Connection; Skip Connection Types; Residual Block
student_friendly_explanation: Residual Networks, or ResNets, are a type of deep neural network that helps train very deep models by adding shortcut connections. These shortcuts allow the network to learn residual mappings, which prevent the degradation of performance as the network becomes deeper.
example: Imagine you have a simple neural network that can recognize images. As you add more layers to make it deeper, it might start to forget earlier features. Residual Networks solve this by adding a shortcut connection that allows the network to pass through unchanged data from previous layers. This way, the deeper layers can learn new features without losing the information from the shallower layers.

definition: How generating above or below a model's training resolution affects coherence.
related_terms: Resolution Conditioning; Prompt Ordering Effect; Latent Upscaling; High-Resolution Fix
student_friendly_explanation: The resolution of a model's training refers to the level of detail it can capture during learning. Generating a model with too high or too low a resolution can affect how well the model understands and produces coherent outputs.
example: Training an image generation model at a high resolution allows it to produce images with finer details, which can lead to more coherent and realistic outputs. However, if the resolution is too low, the model might struggle to capture all the nuances present in the training data, resulting in less coherent images.

definition: Read-only data an agent can load through a protocol, distinct from an action it can invoke.
related_terms: Read-Only Tool; Action Space for Agents; Model Context Protocol Server; Agent Communication Protocol
student_friendly_explanation: A resource is like a tool you can use without changing anything. It's data that an AI agent can access using a special way of talking (protocol), but it doesn't change the agent's state or actions.
example: Imagine you have a robot that needs to find information about traffic conditions to navigate. The robot has a 'resource' that contains real-time traffic maps. This resource allows the robot to see the current traffic situation without altering its own decision-making process.

definition: The principles governing how limited care capacity is distributed.
related_terms: Resource Allocation; Equity in Resource Allocation; Care Gap Identification; Standard of Care
student_friendly_explanation: Resource allocation ethics are the rules that help decide how to share limited resources, like medical care, fairly among people who need them.
example: A hospital uses resource allocation ethics to decide which patients get life-saving treatments first, based on their health needs and other factors.

definition: The practice of designing, developing, and deploying AI systems in ways that are ethical, transparent, fair, accountable, and beneficial to society. Responsible AI frameworks encompass bias mitigation, explainability, privacy protection, security, environmental impact, and regulatory compliance. Major organizations including Google, Microsoft, and the EU have published responsible AI principles and guidelines.
related_terms: AI Ethics; AI Governance; Explainability; Bias
student_friendly_explanation: Responsible AI is about creating, improving, and using artificial intelligence in a way that respects people's rights, makes decisions clear, protects personal information, keeps everyone safe, and helps the environment. It includes making sure AI doesn't treat some groups unfairly, following rules, and being open about how it works.
example: A company uses a chatbot to help customers. They make sure the chatbot understands different languages and can answer questions clearly, which shows responsible AI in action.

definition: The practice of reporting security vulnerabilities, jailbreaks, or safety issues in AI systems to the developer before publicly sharing them, allowing time for fixes. Responsible disclosure helps improve AI safety while preventing malicious exploitation. Many AI companies have bug bounty programs and vulnerability reporting channels.
related_terms: AI Safety; Red Teaming; Jailbreaking; Responsible AI
student_friendly_explanation: Responsible Disclosure is like telling your friend about a small hole in their house before anyone else finds it. Instead of just saying 'Look at this hole!' you tell them first so they can fix it. This way, everyone stays safe and no one gets hurt.
example: A researcher discovers a flaw in an AI system that could be used to cause harm if exploited. They report this flaw to the developers, who then fix it before anyone else can use it. This way, the AI remains safe and secure.

definition: Removing near-identical entries so a result list is not dominated by one source.
related_terms: Blended Results; Query Result Cache; Zero Result Rate; Relevance Feedback
student_friendly_explanation: Result Deduplication is a process where similar search results are removed from a list of search outcomes. This helps ensure that the final list isn't heavily influenced by a single source, making it more balanced and diverse.
example: Imagine you're searching for information on machine learning algorithms. If you search three times, sometimes you might get the same set of papers about gradient descent algorithms. Result Deduplication would remove those duplicates, giving you a cleaner list of unique resources.

definition: Filtering job applications automatically, a use with significant fairness obligations.
related_terms: Sanctions Screening; Anti-Money Laundering Screening (AML); Obligation Tracking; Job Shop Scheduling (JSSP)
student_friendly_explanation: Resume screening is like a magic filter that looks at job applications automatically. It helps companies quickly find the best candidates by checking if their information matches what they need. This process has some rules about being fair to everyone involved.
example: Imagine a big company using resume screening software. When a new job opening comes up, the software goes through all the resumes it receives. It checks things like education, work experience, and skills. The goal is to find the most qualified people for the job without any bias.

definition: The document collection a retrieval-augmented system searches.
related_terms: Corpus; Corpus Linguistics; Parallel Corpus; Document
student_friendly_explanation: A retrieval corpus is a group of documents that a system can search through. It's like having a big library where a computer can look up information.
example: For a machine learning model to understand different languages, it needs to be trained on a retrieval corpus. This corpus could include books, articles, and web pages in various languages, which helps the model learn patterns and similarities across texts.

definition: Measuring whether retrieval supplies the evidence a generator actually needs.
related_terms: Boolean Retrieval; Learned Sparse Retrieval; Language Model for Retrieval; Probabilistic Retrieval Model
student_friendly_explanation: Retrieval Evaluation for RAG is about checking if the search results (retrieval) provide the information needed by the model (RAG) to generate the correct output.
example: Imagine you have a language model that generates text based on previous examples. If you ask it to generate a sentence about 'Artificial Intelligence', the evaluation checks if the search results about AI help the model understand the topic well enough to produce relevant text.

definition: Reattempting a failed operation after progressively longer waits to avoid overwhelming a service.
related_terms: Tool Call Retry; Idempotent Action; Jittered Backoff; Job Retry Policy
student_friendly_explanation: When an AI system fails to complete a task, it tries again later, but with increasing delays between attempts. This helps prevent the system from making too many requests at once, which could overwhelm the service.
example: A search engine might retry a query after a few seconds, then wait longer (e.g., 10 seconds, 30 seconds) before trying again if the first attempt doesn't find the information requested.

definition: The total accumulated reward from a point in time onward, usually discounted by how far in the future it arrives.
related_terms: Monte Carlo Return; N-Step Return; Reward Function; Distributional RL
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're playing a game where you get points for completing tasks. The return is like adding up all those points you've earned so far, but you might not get them right away. It's like having a piggy bank where you keep adding coins, but you can't take them out until later. This total amount of points is what we call the return, and it helps us understand how well you're doing in the game over time.
example: In a reinforcement learning task, if you earn 5 points for every correct answer and you get 3 more points for every additional correct answer, the return would be the sum of all these points, discounted based on how long ago you got them. If you get 10 points now, 15 points after 1 day, and 20 points after 2 days, the return would be the total points you've earned, adjusted for when you got them.

definition: Estimating which purchases are likely to be sent back.
related_terms: Treatment Response Prediction; Adherence Prediction; No-Show Prediction; Size Recommendation
student_friendly_explanation: Return Prediction is a type of machine learning model that predicts which items customers might return after purchasing them. It helps retailers understand customer behavior and make better inventory decisions.
example: A clothing retailer uses Return Prediction to analyze past purchase data. If the model predicts that a high percentage of customers return certain types of shirts, the retailer can adjust future stock levels accordingly.

definition: An agent checking another's work before it is accepted.
related_terms: Work Item; Reviewer Agreement with Model; Critic Model; Context Isolation
student_friendly_explanation: A reviewer agent is like a helper who checks someone else's work, making sure it meets the required standards before it can be accepted as correct. It acts as an AI that reviews documents, papers, or projects to ensure they follow the rules and guidelines.
example: Imagine you have written a research paper on artificial intelligence. A reviewer agent would check your paper to make sure it has all the necessary sections (introduction, methods, results, discussion), uses proper citations, and adheres to the formatting style guide. If everything is in order, the agent will approve your paper.

definition: The scalar feedback signal telling an agent how good its most recent transition was.
related_terms: Reward Function; Reward Tampering; Reward Hacking; Sparse Reward Problem
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're playing a game where you get points based on your actions. The reward is like getting a sticker or a gold star after you complete a level. It tells you how well you did in the last move, helping you learn and improve.
example: In a video game, if you collect coins, the number of coins you collect can be seen as a reward. If you reach a certain level, you might get a special bonus, which is another form of reward.

definition: In reinforcement learning, a function that provides numerical feedback (reward or penalty) to the agent based on its actions and the resulting state. The reward function encodes the desired behavior—the agent learns a policy that maximizes cumulative reward. Designing good reward functions is challenging and critical to RL success.
related_terms: Reinforcement Learning (RL); Reward Model (RM); Policy; Reward
student_friendly_explanation: A reward function in reinforcement learning assigns points to an agent based on its actions and the outcomes. It helps the agent learn what actions lead to better results, guiding it towards the best possible solution.
example: Imagine you're playing a game where you collect coins. Each time you collect a coin, you get a point. The more coins you collect, the higher your score. This score acts as a reward function, encouraging you to collect as many coins as possible.

definition: Writing a reward that does not capture the intended goal, leading to unintended optimized behaviour.
related_terms: Reward Function; Dense Reward; Reward Tampering; Reward
student_friendly_explanation: Imagine you're trying to teach a robot to navigate a maze. If your reward function (the rule that tells the robot how well it's doing) is misspecified, it might think that moving quickly is good, but you want it to find the safest path. This can lead the robot to take shortcuts that aren't always the best choice.
example: In a robotics competition, a team uses a reward function that rewards high speed over accuracy. As a result, their robot moves too fast and gets stuck in corners, failing to complete the course as intended.

definition: A colour model representing pixels by red, green, and blue intensities.
related_terms: Color Space; Pixel; Green Screen Keying; Histogram Equalization
student_friendly_explanation: RGB stands for Red, Green, and Blue. It's a way to describe colors using three primary colors. Each color is represented by a number between 0 and 255, which tells us how much of that color to use. These numbers together make up a pixel in an image.
example: Imagine you have a small square on a screen. To paint this square, you can set the red, green, and blue values independently. If you set all three to 255 (the maximum), it will be bright white. If you set them all to 0, it will be black. By changing the values, you can create any color you want.

definition: Linear regression with an L2 penalty that shrinks coefficients smoothly without zeroing them.
related_terms: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR); Regression; Softmax Regression; Lasso
student_friendly_explanation: Ridge Regression is a type of linear regression where we add a penalty to the sum of squared coefficients. This helps in making the model more stable and less prone to overfitting by shrinking the coefficients towards zero but not setting them to zero.
example: Imagine you have a dataset with many features, and you want to predict a continuous outcome. Instead of just adding up all the features' values to make your prediction, Ridge Regression adds a bit of extra cost based on the size of the numbers. This makes the model think twice before giving too much weight to any single feature, thus smoothing out the predictions.

definition: The legal interest a person holds in the commercial use of their likeness and voice.
related_terms: Commercial Use Rights; Consent for Likeness; Rights Clearance; Model Output Ownership
student_friendly_explanation: The right of publicity is like having control over how your image or voice can be used for money-making purposes. It's a type of legal permission that allows you to decide if and how people can use your likeness or voice for business.
example: A famous actor might have the right of publicity, which means they can decide if and how their image and voice are used in movies, commercials, or even on social media platforms.

definition: Confirming that necessary permissions exist before content is used commercially.
related_terms: Commercial Use Rights; Right of Publicity; Model Output Ownership; FDA Clearance
student_friendly_explanation: Rights clearance is a process where you make sure you have permission to use someone else's work for profit. It involves checking if there are legal agreements in place that allow your commercial use.
example: A movie studio needs to use a song in their film. They need to get rights clearance from the songwriter to ensure they can legally use the song without infringing on any copyrights.

definition: Keeping an updated record of identified risks, owners, and mitigations.
related_terms: Predictive Maintenance; Predictive Grid Maintenance; Risk Parity; Customs Risk Assessment
student_friendly_explanation: A risk register is like a list where you keep track of all the potential problems you might face in your project. It includes what those problems are, who's responsible for fixing them, and how you plan to fix them. This helps everyone stay on the same page and make sure nothing unexpected stops your project from succeeding.
example: Imagine you're building a smart home system. Your risk register might include a risk for software bugs that could cause the system to malfunction. You'd write down that it's a risk, who's in charge of fixing it (like a team of programmers), and how you'll test the system to catch any issues early.

definition: Requiring confirmation only for actions above a defined risk level.
related_terms: Human Approval Gate; Confirmation Prompt; Approval Fatigue; Destructive Tool
student_friendly_explanation: Risk-Tiered Approval is a system where actions are approved based on their risk level. Only actions that exceed a certain risk threshold need human approval. This ensures that high-risk activities are carefully reviewed while less risky ones can proceed without delay.
example: In an AI-driven project management system, tasks are automatically classified into different risk tiers. If a task's risk score exceeds a predefined threshold, it requires human intervention for final approval before proceeding.

definition: An optimized BERT variant trained longer on more data without the next sentence prediction objective.
related_terms: ALBERT; mBERT; FLAN-T5; DistilBERT
student_friendly_explanation: RoBERTa is an improved version of BERT that trains for a longer time on more data, focusing on improving its performance rather than adding a task like predicting the next sentence.
example: For instance, RoBERTa might be used to better understand the context between words in a sentence, which can help in tasks like text classification or question answering.

definition: Software automating repetitive rule-based tasks across existing application interfaces.
related_terms: Compliance Automation; Underwriting Automation; Customer Support Automation; Fact Checking Automation
student_friendly_explanation: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is like having a smart robot that can do the same things over and over again, just like you might do your homework. This robot uses special software to follow rules and work with different computer programs, making it easier to handle routine tasks.
example: Imagine a bank using RPA to process loan applications. The system can automatically fill out forms, check documents, and even verify signatures, all without human intervention. This saves time and reduces errors compared to manual processing.

definition: Instructions establishing an agent's responsibilities within a larger system.
related_terms: Prompt Evaluation; Prompt Optimization; Prompt Versioning; Automatic Prompt Engineering
student_friendly_explanation: A role prompt for agents is a set of instructions that defines what an AI system or agent should do within a larger context. It specifies the responsibilities and tasks of the agent, ensuring it operates effectively within the system.
example: In a chatbot designed to assist with university course inquiries, a role prompt might instruct the bot to answer questions about course requirements, upcoming deadlines, and available resources, thereby guiding its behavior and interactions.

definition: The square root of average squared error, penalizing large mistakes disproportionately.
related_terms: Mean Absolute Error (MAE); Error Distribution; Relative Error; Median Absolute Error (MedAE)
student_friendly_explanation: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) is a measure of how well a model's predictions match actual values. It calculates the square root of the average of the squared differences between the predicted and actual values. This means it penalizes larger errors more than smaller ones, making it useful when you want to see how far off your model's predictions are from the real data.
example: Suppose you have a model predicting house prices based on their size. If the model predicts a house price of $500,000 but the actual price is $450,000, the absolute error is $50,000. However, if the model predicts $1,000,000 and the actual price is $950,000, the absolute error is $50,000. In RMSE, both errors contribute equally, but since the first prediction was further off ($50,000), it gets a higher weight in the final calculation.

definition: Computing efficient delivery paths subject to time, capacity, and cost constraints.
related_terms: Public Transit Optimization; Order Fulfilment Optimization; Scheduling Optimization; Inventory Optimization
student_friendly_explanation: Route Optimization is about finding the best way to deliver something while considering when it needs to be done, how much space it takes up, and how much it costs.
example: A delivery company uses Route Optimization to find the fastest and most cost-effective route to deliver packages to multiple locations, taking into account traffic, distance, and the number of packages.

definition: Routing users showing acute risk to human professional support.
related_terms: Escalation Rate; Moderator Wellbeing; Signal Detection in Safety Data; APPS
student_friendly_explanation: Safety Escalation in Wellbeing Apps is a system that automatically alerts users when their mental health might be at a critical level, indicating they need immediate help from professionals.
example: If a user's wellbeing app detects unusual patterns in their mood tracking data (like a sudden drop in happiness scores), it will trigger an escalation alert, notifying the user to seek help from a mental health professional.

definition: Systematic testing of what prohibited content a generative model can be induced to produce.
related_terms: Safety Fine-Tuning for Generators; Generator; Masked Generative Model; Class-Conditional Model
student_friendly_explanation: Safety evaluation for generators is like checking if a machine that creates text (like writing stories) can make things it shouldn't say, such as inappropriate words or ideas.
example: Imagine you have a toy that writes stories. Safety evaluation would be like watching it write stories and making sure it doesn't write scary or offensive things.

definition: Extra inventory held to absorb demand and supply variability.
related_terms: Inventory Optimization; Assortment Planning; Signal Detection in Safety Data; Demand Planning
student_friendly_explanation: Safety stock is like having extra cookies in the cookie jar. It's extra inventory you keep on hand to help when regular orders don't come in as expected or when there's a sudden rush of customers.
example: A bakery might have a safety stock of flour to ensure they can quickly make cakes if a popular flavor suddenly becomes very popular among customers.

definition: Padding chosen so the output spatial size matches the input.
related_terms: Valid Padding; Padding; Padding Token; Special Token
student_friendly_explanation: Same padding is a technique used in deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where padding is added to the input so that the output has the same spatial size as the input. This ensures that the feature maps generated from the convolutional layers have the same dimensions, which can be crucial for maintaining the spatial resolution of the data.
example: Consider a 3x3 input image. Without padding, a 5x5 filter would result in an output of 4x4 pixels. With same padding, the filter will slide over the entire 3x3 input, producing an output of 3x3 pixels, matching the input's size.

definition: How much a model improves per training example consumed.
related_terms: Parameter Efficiency of Architectures; Batch Inference Efficiency; Sample Weighting; Chunked Recurrence
student_friendly_explanation: Sample efficiency is about how much a model learns from each new piece of data it gets. It's like how quickly you can solve a puzzle with each new piece you add.
example: Imagine you're trying to teach a machine learning model to recognize cats in pictures. If the model learns very fast from each new picture (sample), it has high sample efficiency. This means it can improve quickly as it sees more examples.

definition: The number of items needed to distinguish models reliably at a given effect size.
related_terms: Evaluation Cost; LM Evaluation Harness; Private Evaluation Set; Statistical Significance in Evaluation
student_friendly_explanation: The sample size is the number of data points you need to tell different AI models apart with a certain level of confidence. It's like having enough pieces of evidence to decide which model performs better.
example: Imagine you have two AI models predicting house prices. To decide which one is better, you might use a sample size to ensure your test results are reliable. If you have too few houses (small sample size), you might not see a clear difference between the models' predictions. But if you have many houses (large sample size), you're more likely to spot any real differences in their performance.

definition: Assigning different importance to training examples according to quality or source.
related_terms: Sample Efficiency; GELU; Head Importance Score; Grad-CAM
student_friendly_explanation: Sample weighting is like giving some training examples more attention than others based on their quality or where they come from. It's a way to make sure the model learns better from the most useful data.
example: Imagine you have a dataset of images of cats and dogs. Some images might be taken under good lighting while others are blurry. By using sample weighting, you could assign higher weights to the clearer images to help the AI learn more effectively from them.

definition: The number of denoising iterations used to generate one output, trading quality against speed.
related_terms: Step Count Tuning; Denoising Step; Inference Steps Tradeoff; Steps per Second
student_friendly_explanation: Sampling steps refer to the number of times we use a process called denoising to improve the quality of our generated output. This process helps reduce errors or noise in the data, but it also takes more time and computational power.
